If the contest pushes policy expectations toward higher welfare commitments, looser fiscal discipline or weaker control of public spending, sterling swap rates could remain higher for longer. That matters directly for listed real estate: higher swaps increase refinancing costs, reduce the relative attraction of the sector's dividend/EPS yields versus bonds and other asset classes, and potentially put pressure on property valuation yields. The sector has already spent several years repricing to a higher-rate world; any renewed increase in UK-specific risk premia would likely delay the recovery in investor appetite for REITs and property equities. Lower growth confidence means weaker occupier confidence The second channel is growth expectations. Real estate demand is ultimately a function of economic activity, corporate confidence and investment intentions. A political backdrop associated with higher welfare spending, more regulation and weaker fiscal credibility is unlikely to improve external investors' view of UK growth. If corporates see the UK as a less attractive place to invest, expand or hire, this would likely feed through into slower demand for office, retail, logistics and healthcare real estate space. While the sub-sectors are not uniformly exposed and each have have different operational drivers, the common risks would be weaker sentiment toward UK domestic assets and weaker economic activity. Physical risk calendar Source: Barclays Research North America North America enters the summer period following a notably cold winter, with the peak of the severe convective storm season likely already past. Over the next four months, the main physical risks are expected to come from heat stress, drought, wildfire and rainfall volatility, with above-normal temperatures forecast across much of southern North America, Central America and the Caribbean. Heat stress is likely to become a cross-sector issue, affecting cooling demand, grid pressure, livestock conditions and crop stress, particularly where extreme heat overlaps with drought. Much of the South and West, except for southern California, continues to face drought conditions, although parts of the southern Plains and Southeast could improve as summer rainfall develops. These conditions are also increasing wildfire risks across parts of the western US and western Canada. At the same time, a strengthening El Niño is expected to suppress Atlantic hurricane activity, although lower overall activity does not eliminate landfall risk. Europe Europe enters the summer period with heat, drought and wildfire conditions increasingly moving into the foreground. records.text: Hybrids generally trade structure risk for quality risk For IG-focused investors searching for ways to capture incremental spread without deviating too far down the quality spectrum, hybrids can be an attractive solution given the spread premium they offer vs. senior debt. This additional spread premia serves as ‘compensation’ for hybrids’ subordination as well as some issuer-friendly structural features, such as the ability to defer interest payments in certain situations (without triggering a default). That said, determining whether this compensation is adequate requires a clear understanding of the company-specific capital management priorities for each hybrid issuer. It also requires a thorough analysis of the potential long-term fundamental headwinds facing the issuers’ industries to evaluate the risk of financial distress (which may necessitate deferral of interest). Very few investors expect hybrid issuers to actually utilize the provision to defer interest—especially if that issuer already has a large debt capital structure which requires frequent refinancing. The assumption is that deferring the hybrid’s coupon payments may make it more difficult—due to investor push back from overlapping buyer bases—to refinance the ‘regular’ (non-subordinated) debt when the time comes. Consumption Tax Cut: +0.2pp to GDP , -1.0pp to CPI This week, the government began consideration of a plan to reduce the consumption tax to 1% starting next April. A cut to 0% would require significant time and cost for system adjustments at retailers, so the government appears to favor a 1% rate for quicker implementation. Our estimates suggest that this tax cut would boost private consumption by 0.4ppt and raise real GDP by 0.2ppt. Mechanically, reducing the food tax rate from 8% to 1% would lower CPI by about 1.4%. However, international experience shows that tax cuts are not fully passed through to prices. Referring to Germany’s 2020 example, we estimate a 1.0% decline in CPI with 75% of pass-through rate. That said, revisions to the CPI base year in 2025 (starting from July 2026 print)— including changes in weights and a reset of the index to 100—could introduce some variability, so the impact should be interpreted with caution. A key issue is how to finance the ¥4.4 trillion revenue shortfall. As Prime Minister Takaichi has suggested, the government is unlikely to issue deficit-financing bonds, and will instead rely on reallocating existing expenditures and revenues. This may involve reviewing special tax measures and subsidies, supplemented by non-tax revenues if necessary. Specia

records.text: US Economics Weekly5 June 2026 ab 12 Fedspeak: inflation risks rising, policy in a good place Last Sunday, Governor Powell delivered prepared remarks in his acceptance of the 2026 John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award (link here). He avoided commenting on the outlook and emphasized the importance of central bank independence. FRB of New York President Williams said that “Monetary policy is exactly in the right place. I don't see any need to raise or lower interest rates right now. At the same time, you know to get to your question, I do think that upside risks to inflation have increased somewhat given—or increased significantly, actually—given, you know, recent developments especially with energy prices and some of the other factors pushing up inflation. At the same time, which is very good news, we're seeing the economy be remarkably resilient, continue to have solid growth, and the labor market stabilizing in a pretty good place…We've seen the risks on the price stability go up and some of the risks on the employment side have edged down a little bit. The One Transformation remains one of the core drivers of performance at Santander, allowing for cost take-out and simplification across divisions. A simple cost structure across all divisions lowers the cost-to-income ratio at the group level and results in operating leverage going forward. For example, Portugal is experiencing both revenue growth and lower costs. On the product side, it makes sense to reduce the product suite to a contained number of products which are easy for customers to understand and choose from. The roll-out of modern technology infrastructure through Gravity improves both back-office operations and relationships with customers, as management can use real-time data to improve decision-making and tailor its product offering. So far, Gravity has been rolled out in Spain, Mexico, and Chile, while the platform is being partially rolled out in the UK and the USA: the process should be completed in Brazil over the next 3 to 4 months. He also added that, if there are signs of second-round effects pushing underlying inflation above its projected path, the BoJ would need to consider an appropriate policy response. Although Ueda did not directly point to a hike at the next meeting, his speech led markets to price in a June hike as a done deal (~95% probability). We continue to call for the next hike in October vs. market pricing in another full hike by December, although we stress that the summer/autumn months will be key for the BoJ to assess the effects of ongoing supply chain disruptions. First comes energy then comes pass-through inflation The Iran war has contributed to the recent surge in CPI inflation, particularly headline, which rose to 3.8% y/y in April (see report: US Watch: April CPI inflation: Core concern 12 May 2026). The immediate impact of the conflict has been seen in energy prices. In April, energy goods surged by 29.2% year-over-year, contributing 0.9 percentage points to headline inflation. Additionally, airfares increased by 5.6% over the two months ending in April, a rise linked in part to higher jet fuel prices. Beyond airfares, there is little evidence of pass-through to core inflation so far. However, numerous indicators suggest that this pass-through is likely to occur soon, raising concerns that inflation may repeat the pattern observed in 2022. Operating profit leaped 33.0% QoQ in the manufacturing sector, a sharp contrast with the 2.7% drop at non-manufacturers. records.text: ing a hard bargain One important issue for the USMCA discussions will be the treatment of auto production and trade. This past week, USTR Greer announced that the US would seek to incorpo- rate much higher requirements for rules of origin on vehicles as part of the renegotiation. Currently the USMCA has a 75% regional value content requirement (up from 62.5% under NAFTA), along with a 40% share of labor value content (pro- vided by workers making at least $16/hr). By July 2027, 70% of the steel and aluminum used in a vehicle must also be sourced from North America. Greer proposed raising the regional content requirement to 82%, with 50% of that value produced by high-wage workers. The goal of these proposed changes is to shift as much auto production into the US as possible. The higher labor value content requirements have been applauded by US labor unions. US auto producers want more clarity on the rules, and have suggested they could comply if given enough lead time. However, a number of lower-cost models are assembled in Mexico, and it would neither be cost effective to increase the US (or Canadian) labor value content nor to move production to the US. US auto dealers have complained about the conse- quences for affordability. How much the Trump administration is willing to bargain over these proposals remains to be seen. records.text: Inflation forwards have moved lower We are bearish on inflation expectations beyond the 2y point. In the initial stages of the Iranian conflict, the correlation between front-end rates and inflation expectations was positive. As energy prices moved higher, both forward inflation expectations and rate expectations moved higher, and this led to a flattening of the inflation curve. However, in recent weeks, that correlation has started to flip beyond the 1y point of the inflation curve. As markets started to price for hikes, forward inflation expectations have started to decline (Figure 26). This does not surprise us as hawkish Fed should cap longer-term inflation expectations. Going forward, we believe any upside surprises in inflation data will lead to a hawkish Fed pricing, which should cap any upside on longer-term inflation expectations. We expect the 3y2y-10y20y inflation curve to steepen in the medium term. As near-term inflation expectations increased, the 3y2y-10y20y inflation curve has flattened to multi-year low levels (Figure 27). With 3y forward 2y inflation moving lower in recent weeks, the curve has steepened slightly but is still relatively flat. As mentioned above, we do think that 3y2y inflation expectations will likely move lower in the near term. Positive feedback loops: A better growth outlook can spark positive feedback loops into fiscal and debt- sustainability metrics. This is particularly relevant for an economy where a rising real interest cost burden has been a big driver of weakening fiscal metrics over the past decade. Our debt sustainability analysis provides a sensitivity matrix and lays out two scenarios (one conservative and one proactive) and a possible glidepath for the state’s push towards meeting the Maastricht criteria beyond 2030. An ecosystem of higher growth potential, more sustainable fiscal spending and collapsing FX vol, should also translate into a credible lowering of Hungary’s inflation target within the next two years. This is likely to more than neutralise an above-50bp rise in Hungary’s ‘r-star’, we estimate, relative to the pre-Covid counterfactual. Our economics team estimates there is currently a shortage of approximately 3-4 million homes nationwide. One approach for increasing the supply of homes at more affordable price points is to promote access to manufactured housing. Manufactured homes (MH), colloquially also referred to as mobile homes, are residences that are prefabricated in a factory setting and then transported to their final location for installation. This method not only streamlines the construction process but also offers significant cost savings compared to traditional site-built homes, making manufactured housing a promising solution for those seeking affordable housing options. There are currently about 8.4 million manufactured housing units across the country. Prior to 2000, shipments of manufactured homes averaged about 265k a year (Exhibit 1). Manufactured housing experienced a construction boom in the 1990s driven by overproduction and lax lending standards. records.text: M Update 4 Next Week: ECB In Focus Euro area | ECB in focus: The key event in the euro area next week will be the ECB's June Governing Council meeting on Thursday. We expect the ECB to hike rates, predominantly to mitigate the risk of de-anchoring inflation expectations. Updated projections will likely show higher headline and core inflation, and lower growth (see our Preview here). And we will also take a close look at the updated projections from national central banks due on Friday. The data focus will be on April prints for industrial activity in Germany and Italy, where we continue to watch for impacts from higher energy prices. In Germany, we expect manufacturing orders at -3.5%M after a strong March print while industrial production could rise slightly (0.3%M) supported by construction activity and exports might decline in line with overall subdued manufacturing momentum. For Italy, we forecast industrial production will correct by 0.1%M. In addition, we will get final inflation data for May from Germany, France, Spain, and the Netherlands, where we will look for signs of the transmission from higher energy prices into other items, especially core. Scandi | Busy week: After a flash inflation for Sweden this week, which surprised to the upside on the back of stronger services but still remained below Riksbank's forecast, our focus turns to Norway. We expect CPI in May to decline to 3.1%Y (from 3.4%Y), mainly due to base effects, and CPI-ATE to rise to 3.3%Y (from 3.2%Y)

records.text: M Idea 4 EGBs In EGBs, we do not think the European Commission broadening the scope of its fiscal rules to exempt certain energy-related spending alters our assessment and we remain broadly neutral on EGB spreads. In our mid-year outlook, we reiterated our 2026 supply forecasts (Exhibit 4 ), noting that any more material increase in issuance is more likely to occur in 2027, with some risk of front‑loading into late‑2026. The credit channel of the fiscal innovations remains important in our view, as higher deficits can increase credit premia and pressure sovereign ratings. records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 05 June 2026 Weekly view Just because It’s time for the ECB hike next week. The market is pricing it quasi fully, there is no further data release on the schedule that could stop it now, and ECB speakers have made absolutely no effort to raise doubts. We think the message will be similar to March: no pre-commitment on the trajectory, a data-dependent approach, but still an implicit nod that absent very good news (on energy prices) or very bad news (on the economy), they’re not done here. The forecasts may even open the door for three hikes at face value, although we think the fine-print may be less obvious on that. We stick to our view: two rate hikes by the end of the summer, at most, followed by two rate cuts, at least (our base case is three) in 2027. Unlike in 2022/23, the ECB will be the first among the major developed market central banks to move. And that first-mover element may be partially what motivates the hike in the first place. The memory of the criticism that they waited too long last time is still very fresh on the central bank’s mind. At the risk of repeating ourselves, the contrast between the ECB and Fed narratives is stark. The Fed is facing an economy with robust 2% growth, core inflation above 3% as the starting point and a labour market that is creating jobs, perhaps even tightening. records.text: elative stability — if not strength — of Gilts on asset swap is supporting evidence for the view that risk premium in the Gilt curve is currently more macro-driven rather than supply-driven. Indeed, on our models, we find swap spread valuation near fair (Exhibit 4). Although we find evidence that over recent years the increase in the supply of bonds via large deficits and BoE QT has contributed to higher long-end yields, current term premium volatility seems to derive from macro risks around the medium-term fiscal outlook and near-term inflation. Reds run ahead. 1y1y rates (reds) have been the most volatile point along the US n forward curve since the onset of the conflict, re-rating by about 110bp versus end-February levels and generally leading the way in both sell-offs and rallies. That repricing has shifted the prior front-end inversion into a hump, with a positive slope between 1y and 1y1y, and inversion from 1y1y to 2y1y. We think there are multiple routes to see that relative cheapness in 1y1y moderate. It is typical to see the 1y1y point lead on the curve in sharp inflections in front-end rates (Exhibit 1). While an extension of acute front-end cheapening can see further 1y1y underperformance, we would expect the opposite to hold on a reversal lower in yields, and we think that a period of stabilization can be a source of pressure relief. We think that can happen either via more benign inflation signals that moderate the upward slope priced into the front-end (1y/1y1y flattening), or due to a more resilient growth and labor market backdrop that either shift the timing of hike risk further in or start to undo the inversion priced in further out (1y1y/2y1y steepening) if the Fed signals a more patient approach. Compared to Australia’s early 2010s min- ing capex boom, which peaked at nearly 7% of GDP, the tech dynamic appears much smaller so far. Furthermore, while there is likely still upside for technology capital expenditure, a meaningful share of data center fit-out relies on imported capital equipment. Capital imports for tech equipment have also been surging and will mechanically offset some of the gross capex impulse to GDP. records.text: US Economics Weekly5 June 2026 ab 8 Trade update: refunds, s301s, tariff tweaks, USMCA Trade policy hasn't been front and center for a while but there were a number of events worth highlighting this week. It has been nearly three months since the Supreme Court struck down tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). The CBP appear to finally be moving on the processing of refunds for those who paid the now-illegal tariffs — but it is slow going. The USTR are progressing with a number of section 301 investigations lining up more options for imposing tariffs. The White House tweaked the existing section 232 metal tariffs too. We published a note last week on our expectations for the upcoming USMCA joint review which is scheduled for July 1. In advance of that review Canada sent a letter to the US and Mexico this week outlining recommendations to renew the trilateral trade agreement for 16 years while seeking talks on sectoral tariffs. Canadian Trade Minister, Dominic LeBlanc, met with USTR Greer this week, which is the first set of formal trade talks between the US and Canada since October. This comes after talks between the US and Mexico last week, and the announcement of further talks between the two countries on June 16-17 and July 20. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 05 June 2026 3 labor in national income falls relative to capital is a blessing in disguise to absorb the negative shocks associated with the war. However, it needs to be fed with further increases in asset prices and improvements in productivity to justify sustainable rate of growth given that the tightening in immigration puts a natural cap on labor income growth absent those productivity gains. Excess global liquidity is the hidden driver But interestingly, the stock market is making new highs not only in the US but globally. Countries like Korea or Taiwan, that benefit from the AI boom as they play a critical role in the global supply chain, continue growing fast, amassing significant current account surpluses, but witnessing their currencies to depreciate in real terms vs the dollar. Why? Despite strong growth, there are not enough domestic assets to park those massive savings, which need to be recycled back to the US. That explains in part the co- movement in equity prices. But that is not the whole story. More broadly, as we have discussed extensively in our year ahead report, there is too much liquidity chasing too few assets. And we can see how this excess global liquidity materialize in increasing leveraged positioning, in particular in the US. We have been making the case that the US economy didn’t need easier monetary policy before the Iran war started, when the market was pricing in 2 cuts and the Fed was comfortable validating that view.

This helped dampen inflation outside China , especially in EM (see Emerging markets : External tailwinds to disinflation grow, dated 4 August 2025). Starting in 2026, however, we expect the trend to reverse. Sustained PPI reflation and a modest appreciation of the RMB against the USD could help China export mild inflation abroad. We forecast export prices to rise 2.5% y/y in 2026 and 2.0% y/y in 2027. Nonetheless, we think Chinese goods should retain their cost competitiveness against most competitors facing similar pressures from higher oil and metal costs. Higher costs and stronger currency: Export prices are primarily a function of two variables . ▪ PPI inflation: This is a key measure of exporters’ costs. records.text: 14 Fig. 33: CGB yields’ reaction to the 2016–18 reflation period Sources : Bloom berg, Macrobond, BNP Paribas Supply-driven reflation: As discussed on page 4, we see similarities between current reflation and that in 2016–18, which was mainly driven by the government’s supply-side reform as well as increases in global commodity prices . Between December 2015 and February 2017, year-on-year inflation surged for the PPI, from −5.9% to 7.8%, but kept to a 1.3–2.5% range for the CPI – one of the most pronounced CPI–PPI gaps in China’s history. End-demand was throttled by real-estate regulation and deleveraging, severely impeding price transmission to the consumer side. Central bank policy reaction: The PBoC cut its RRR by 50bp in Q1 2016, when both the PPI and CPI were still relatively steady. Surging PPI inflation and a steady CPI when the real economy was deleveraging needed a neutral or tight monetary stance. The PBoC left its 7-day reverse repo rate unchanged throughout 2016 but did implicitly lift short-term funding by cutting reverse repos while expanding the MLF. In 2017,it raised the 7-day reverse repo rate by 25bp and the MLF rate by 20bp. Reflation only one key variable: During this cycle of structural inflation, the link between long-term rates and PPI growth was weaker than in 2006–08 and 2009–11. US Economics May employment: Shake your foundations Payroll data point to strengthened labor demand, with a third consecutive strong job gain in May. Although the sideways trajectory of the unemployment rate downplays any urgency for a rate move, today's data challenge claims by FOMC doves that the Fed's stance is restrictive. • May's employment estimates were stronger than expectations, with the BLS reporting a 172k gain in nonfarm payrolls (Barclays: 75k; consensus: 88k) on the heels of two similarly strong prints in March (+214k) and April (+179k). We think FOMC voters will regard these estimates as consistent with a strong underlying trajectory of nonfarm payroll employment, with 3mma gains in May (+188k/m) and the preceding three-month period ended in February (-4k). • Unlike in prior months, birth-death adjustments to the payroll estimates do not appear to have contributed to the strength in payrolls seen in May. These adjustments have zigzagged so far this year, but in May they provided a stronger drag on headline employment (NSA), but the headline (SA) still showed a strong gain. • The unemployment rate continued to round to 4.3%, although it did edge down a few basis points from April. Unrounded, it stood at 4.296% (versus 4.337% in April), reflecting a stronger gain in household employment (+149k) that came amid a constant labor force participation rate (61.8%). We highlight the following key takeaways: Loan Growth and NII Loan growth still remains a bit soft. On the retail side, households remain cautious to increase consumption and borrowing given the impact of higher rates on the mortgage book, which is mostly floating. Corporates have been more resilient, although capacity utilization in Sweden remains low and some corporates chose wholesale funding over bank funding. According to Statistics Sweden data, corporate lending is accelerating and SEB has been able to capture a good share of that. In the first quarter of the year, SEB captured c.1/3 of net new lending, while in April out of SEK ~22bn of net new lending, SEB captured SEK ~7bn. Given that the last rate cut in Sweden happened in October, the impact on the PnL and balance sheet has already fully fed through; from now on, NII should evolve in line with volume growth and margin development. Fee Income Payment fees are linked to the corporate market (this is where AirPlus sits), while capital markets fees are mostly a function of the level of activity of financial markets. Lending fees are relatively stable with a run-rate of SEK ~1bn per quarter. It was a high-profile listing that was cited as having very strong retail demand. The first day of trading saw a technical issue that delayed the open until midday. The stock rose 16% to an intraday high but went on to decline 40% from that peak over the next couple of weeks. The shares troughed 60% below the highs in September, before rallying 200% by the end of the following year. A late-’90s vibe: This type of extreme volatility around new listings was also seen in the late 1990s. Many fashionable new stocks delivered gains in the hundreds of percent in the weeks after. This was then followed by huge post- bubble declines, often making lows more than 90% below peak levels. Our view is that it is the norm for IPO names to be very volatile post listing. Swings of much larger than 50% are very common. What makes SpaceX unique in this is its size. Its market cap is likely to approach $2trn on listing. We would not normally expect a mega-cap of that size to exhibit such extreme volatility. However, we suggest that the initial free float, with a tradable value closer to $75bn, is a better barometer of liquidity and volatility than the market cap. records.text: Executive Summary The 2026 FIFA World Cup is set to be the largest and most geographically dispersed in history, jointly hosted by the United States, Canada, and Mexico. The tournament has expanded materially compared to previous years, with 2026 seeing a greater number of teams (48 vs. 32 in 2022), matches (104 vs. 64), and a broader footprint (16 cities across three countries). While there is a lot of excitement around the World Cup, in our view, the lasting impact will be limited. Macro view Our Economics team estimates the World Cup could provide a small, temporary lift to US GDP by at most 0.2% over the summer, but leave little lasting macro imprint at year-end (Figure 2 and 3). The team views the FIFA estimate of boosting US GDP growth by $17.2bn as an upper-bound for two reasons. First, demand for the event seems to be running below expectations thus far. Second, a key channel through which international sporting events/cultural events tend to generate activity (and employment) is construction of infrastructure – venues and transportation. The US is uniquely positioned, in that, it already has this infrastructure in place. Any employment gains are also likely to be localized, short-lived, and concentrated in services. Localized price increases in hotels, airfares, and related services are also expected to be temporary, narrowly concentrated, and unlikely to materially move the needle on national inflation. In our view, the 2026 World Cup will create a visible but ultimately transitory services-price shock across North America, with Mexico exposed only at the margin given that Mexico will only host 13 out of the 78 matches in the three largest cities of Mexico City, Guadalajara and Monterrey in a short period (Figure 11). records.text: ce, the NEC provides flexibility within the EU fiscal framework by allowing certain expenditure to be excluded from the fiscal requirements, provided that this does not jeopardise fiscal sustainability. It was first introduced last year to accommodate higher defence spending, with a cumulative cap of 1.5pp of GDP. This week’s announcement expands the scope of the NEC to include measures undertaken since February 2026 aimed at reducing dependence on fossil fuels. More specifically, within the existing overall cap of 1.5pp of GDP, a dedicated annual allocation of 0.3pp of GDP (with a cumulative limit of 0.6pp) could be made to these energy related measures. In other words, the size of the NEC has not increased, instead its definition has been broadened. In practice, this implies that countries choosing not to use their available space for defence spending could instead allocate part of it to a narrow set of eligible energy measures. Q2) What's the approval process? It is important to understand that these changes are not automatic. In principle, and in line with Article 26 of the EU fiscal framework, countries would still need to request activation, after which the Commission would assess the case and make a recommendation to the Council on the basis of “exceptional circumstances.” The final decision would rest with the Council and require a qualified majority vote (55% of member states representing at least 65% of the population). records.text: 7 Fig. 13: Sow and pig stocks versus pork production (Q2 2020 = 100) Sources : China’ s National Bureau of Statistics, CEIC, BNP Paribas Mild pickup in headline inflation: CPI inflation hovered around zero from 2023 through most of 2025. In 2026 so far, it has risen to about 1%y/y, driven not only by higher oil prices but also by shifts in other components . We project CPI inflation to average 1.3% y/y this year and 1.5% y/y next year. While still below the official 2% target, a move from years of ‘noflation’ to mild reflation represents a positive development, in our view. Food prices contained by overcapacity: Food prices have always been a dominant driver of headline CPI inflation because they are more volatile than the other components. Over the past three years, food inflation was negative, reflecting chronic overcapacity. During the pandemic, households built up food stockpiles, which drove up prices and signaled to farmers that demand was strong. In response, farmers expanded capacity and improved productivity. However, after Covid restrictions were lifted in 2023, that extra capacity proved excessive. Pork prices are a good example. records.text: SCREENING FOR PROTECTION USING LIQUID ALTERNATIVES 1205 June 2026 Our hedging framework We model the historical behaviour of the strategies at different attachment points using non-Gaussian Kernel Density Estimation (KDE). For the purpose of this analysis, we consider three-month rolling returns of the MSCI ACWI index benchmark. This analysis offers a visualisation of the strategies’ behaviour at different levels of equity stress. We quantitatively assess a hedging strategy’s reliability through the probability of the strategy delivering a positive return using the KDE analysis and its convexity through the beta of a linear regression of the strategy’s performance against that of the relevant equity benchmark for returns falling under this attachment point. As shown on the summary table of reliability scores, Rolling Put strategies are very effective as hedging tail events with a probability of positive returns above 90%. For their part, Dispersion strategies are equally effective as protection regardless of the benchmark regime. (6) A pushback on market pricing seems unlikely, creating mild asymmetric bearish risk for € rates from the meeting. Asymmetric (mild) bearish risk for € rates from the ECB. Next week’s ECB meeting is most likely to validate market pricing, with risks skewed mildly bearish in our view. Validating market pricing means delivering the fully priced 25bp hike for 11 June and indicating that at least a second hike is likely while being non-committal on timing. The mild bearish risk comes from any communication that boosts the prospect of back-to-back hikes (with 8bp currently priced for July vs 17bp for September). We do not expect any pushback that would remove hike premium and prompt a strong rally. Moreover, in this inflation spike – and following the experience of 2022 – the ECB seems determined to avoid any impression of being ‘behind the curve’ . The short answer is no. In our view, the amendment to the NEC is marginal. The overall size of the flexibility remains unchanged (i.e. 1.5pp of GDP), as the adjustment only affects the scope of eligible spending, now including a narrow set of energy-related measures. More importantly, the expansion is limited to a specific category of expenditure tied to reducing dependence on fossil fuels. To date, such spending has been relatively underrepresented in the commitments made by Member States (see here), where meaningful spending has taken place at all. A significant share of these commitments has been directed towards price suppression measures or subsidies, which are unlikely to qualify under the NEC. As a result, we leave our fiscal forecast unchanged and reiterate the view outlined in our outlook (see here). In particular, we expect the euro area deficits to widen in 2026 (to 3.4% of GDP from 2.9%), driven primarily by the German fiscal expansion, followed by only a modest further increase in 2027

records.text: prices; all eyes on core momentum • April IP surprised to the upside, at 4.9% RBI holds rates, boosts capital inflows The RBI kept policy rates on hold, as we had expected, defy- ing market pricing that had priced in a 60% chance of a 25 bp hike. With the rupee under pressure, it simultaneously announced several measures to attract capital inflows—con- sistent with India’s inflation-targeting “separability” frame- work, where policy rates and liquidity are used to manage domestic inflation and growth dynamics, while FX interven- tion and regulatory tools are used to address external-sector issues. The focus on capital inflows also reflects the view we have espoused that current Rupee pressures are being driven more by the capital account than the current account, making capital inflow-supporting measures the more appropriate response to rate hikes. Even as the RBI kept rates on hold, it predictably marked down its 2026-27 growth forecast and marked up its inflation forecast, given the adverse supply shocks confronting the economy. GDP growth was marked down from 6.9% oya to 6.6%, and CPI inflation was marked up from 4.6% to 5.1%, in line with our current forecast (J.P. Morgan: 5.1%). Our call that the RBI would be on hold was predicated on: • Headline inflation forecasts, averaging 5% in FY27, and therefore remaining well within the inflation-targeting band; and • Core inflation (correctly measured) remaining benign and averaging just 2.2% at the moment. records.text: 15 Sources : Bloom berg, BNP Paribas So far this year, China rates have been largely rangebound despite mild reflation, which goes against historical trends. The primary factors driving down rates have been accommodative liquidity conditions, weak credit demand, and an onshore asset shortage, while faster government bond issuance in January and geopolitical tensions have provided some support. Recently, China 5y NDIRS traded out of the 1.53–1.64% range it has held from the start of the year, while the 10y CGB has been supported at above 1.7%. We think a few factors point to limited further downside for China rates. ▪ The PBoC is gradually fine-tuning its liquidity structure and normalizing excessive liquidity, despite changing its accommodative stance. ▪ Anti-involution consensus is gaining momentum (see page 5). ▪ Reflation is halting the prospect of interest rate cuts (see page 12). ▪ Tech companies are likely using deposits to fund AI-related investments . ▪ The ongoing PPI reflation is likely to be sustained . As such, we like tactically paying China 5y CNY NDIRS to capture this asymmetric risk –reward profile (see trade idea,29 May). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 1) We expect July ECB pricing, similar to that of April, to gradually fade to 0bp as the ECB does not need to hike in back to back meetings, in our view. 2) The cumulative pricing of July and September looks a bit high to us, mostly because of the July leg. 3) October pricing appears elevated relative to September and December, given the ECB’s reluctance to move at non‑forecast meetings. 4) The total amount of tightening over the next 12 months is too high in our view, with the clearest RV in 2027: the curve shows only limited inversion, with just a few bp priced, versus our baseline of around 50bp of cuts. This week the European Commission broadened the scope of its fiscal rules to exempt certain energy-related spending (see more details in Euro Area Rates: Fiscal Developments Remain Key; So Far So Good). From a macro perspective, we flag that our economists see only modestly higher deficits under most scenarios (see more in their mid-year outlook). As a result, the market may be pricing in too much ECB tightening, and we expect the intermediate part of the forward curve to rally in the upcoming quarters. A more severe rise in energy prices could lead to higher deficits, but this would likely be linked to a major military escalation and financial stability concerns, prompting the ECB to focus less on inflation and more on stability. In that case, the curve would likely steepen, with lower short-term yields and higher term premia further out.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Special Focus: 5s10s France-Germany Auction Strategy Pauses in 2026 As we approach the mid-year mark we take a look at the performance of a popular auction-based strategy, the 5s10s France-Germany box. The strategy has not worked so far this year, but we have seen sideways periods similar to 2026 in the past (Exhibit 6 ). The split in the auction schedule in France is very neat: the standard is a long auction (10y and longer) the first Thursday of the month, followed by a shorter auction (3y, 5y, off the runs) the third Thursday of the month. The auction strategy can therefore constructed as: short 5y France in the 5s10s box vs Germany the day before or the day of the long auction and do opposite (long 5y) the day before or the day of the short auction. Exhibit 7 shows more details on the two sides of the trade and the performance by year. Historically, the strategy from the long to the short auction has a better performance, but this year’s performance has lagged relative to prior years. The performance of the strategy from the short auction to the long auction the following month has improved over time, but has also underperformed in 2026. Meanwhile, tariffs elbowed their way back into the headlines, after US Trade Representative Greer proposed two separate sets of new Section 301 tariffs. The first proposed a minimum 10% tariff on some 60 trading partners (representing 99% of total US trade) in response to the “unlevel playing field” cre- ated by perceived inadequate restrictions on products made by forced labor. These tariffs are positioned to broadly replace the 10% tariffs under Section 122 when they expire in July. The second involves an investigation into “foreign struc- tural excess capacity and production” that began in March and is expected to conclude in “weeks” according to Greer. In other trade-related news, while both Mexico and Canada pledged their support for a 16-year extension of the USMCA agreement, the US made no similar comments. records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 05 June 2026 5 But demand, labor and fiscal look very different today That said, there are important differences from 2022. First, goods demand was elevated owing to expansionary fiscal policy, restrictions on service activities and work-from- home policies. This led to a spike in the goods share of overall consumption, which has largely normalized today (Exhibit 3). Strong demand coupled with supply chain issues led to shortages of goods during the pandemic era, which gave firms pricing power (Exhibit 4). Today both the share of spending on goods and inventory levels have largely normalized. Therefore, we think firms have less pricing power today than in 2022. Core PCE inflation is now at its highest reading since 1992, excluding the Covid-driven surge in inflation. Within the components, the persistence and duration of goods inflation remain evident. Durable goods prices stayed elevated and rose by 58bps in April. Inflation pressures are also evident in recreational goods (+1.61% month-over-month) and other durable goods (+1%), with the monthly inflation rate for the former near a decade-high. Meanwhile, the service sector contributed 17bps to monthly core inflation, roughly consistent with its contribution during the pre-pandemic period. Within services, housing and utilities inflation was substantial (+0.62% month-over-month), though this elevated figure was partly influenced by a rebound in rents (+0.53% vs 0.26%) following data collection disruptions from last October's government shutdown. “Super-core” inflation decelerated by 22bps to 12bps in April, while the 3-month and 6-month annualized rate fell off from a peak above 4% in January to 3% and 3.7% respectively, a still elevated level. records.text: 5 June 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 15 Euroland Strategy EUR Rates Forecast revision - Bund to 3.2% In our 2026 Rates Outlook last November, we expected a sell-off in EUR rates to lift the 10y Bund to 3.10% (it was 2.70% when we published the forecast), driven by a rise in estimates of the neutral rate in Europe (to 2.50% by end 2027) and rising term premia (amid higher German fiscal spending). The 10y Bund yield managed to exceed this level temporarily a few weeks ago and has been hovering around a 2.95- 3.10% range for the most part of the Iran conflict. However, the recent sell-off led to much flatter curves than we were anticipating, as the market is pricing an even- higher ECB deposit rate path over the next 1-2 years than we had pencilled in, while the earlier rise in term premia was reversed in Jan & Feb. As outlined in our mid-year Global Rates update, we have just raised our 10y Bund forecast to 3.20% as well as our 10y UST forecast to 4.70% (from 4.45%). The upward revision reflects our revised baseline view that the ECB is going to hike twice this year (in Jun & Sep by 25bp each), i.e. one year earlier than we had pencilled in. Most importantly, and in contrast to current market pricing, we expect the ECB deposit rate to stay at 2.50% in line with our estimate of neutral. records.text: Key Takeaways 1) Regulatory backdrop: Focus on simplification and operational resilience Policy discussions at the conference highlighted a broadly resilient starting point for European banks, with supervisors noting that one of the key remaining challenges relates to balancing regulatory complexity with European competitiveness and a level international playing field (as seen with the recent delay in FRTB implementation), with scope to simplify the overall banking framework, such as through a more streamlined capital stack and a meaningful reduction in reporting requirements. At the same time, regulators stressed that simplification should not come at the expense of financial stability or shift risks elsewhere in the system. Alongside this, competitiveness and fragmentation across the EU (e.g. incomplete Banking Union / Capital Markets Union) were flagged as key structural constraints, particularly given the substantial investment needs across various structural themes, including digitalisation, defence spending, and the green agenda. As an example of regulatory divergence within Europe, ING mentioned how the Dutch and Belgian frameworks on mortgages etc. are notably different, despite being neighbouring countries, and that a more standardised approach to pan-European integration would be supportive. records.text: ab 5 June 2026 Global Research Japan Macro Watch Green light for a June rate hike Ueda's speech was broadly hawkish, signaling a rate hike Governor Ueda’s speech on Wednesday was broadly hawkish, with remarks signaling a constructive stance toward a June rate hike. He noted that cost pass-through has accelerated and broadened across items, raising the risk that underlying inflation may overshoot. Overall, he emphasized that upside risks to inflation are larger and likely to materialize sooner than downside risks to activity. He also stated that it is necessary to thoroughly discuss whether a rate hike is appropriate, echoing remarks made just ahead of the January hike. Following the speech, market-implied odds of a rate hike rose from 78% to 92%. Ueda also attributed the recent rise in long-term yields in part to an upward shift in market inflation expectations, stressing the importance of maintaining market confidence that inflation will be appropriately contained through effective policy management. In our view, this can also be interpreted as a message to a government wary of higher long-term yields: rate hikes are not a driver of higher yields but rather a necessary tool to contain them. records.text: Japan Macro Watch5 June 2026 ab 3 Strong earnings persist, but weak capex signals a GDP downgrade The Q1 Mof corporate survey were released this week. As already indicated by strong performances among March fiscal-year-end listed firms, current profits rose 4.1%q/q, marking a third consecutive quarter of growth. On a year-on-year basis, profits increased by 14.6%, achieving double-digit growth and reaching a record high on a seasonally adjusted basis. The strength was led by the manufacturing sector (42.9%y/y vs. 1.4% in non-manufacturing), with information and communication equipment (+174%) and electrical machinery (+42.3%) posting substantial gains, supported by the AI boom. In contrast, non-manufacturing profits appear to be losing some momentum. Going forward, attention should be paid to whether higher oil prices erode margins. Despite strong earnings, capital expenditure declined by 2%q/q (0%y/y), indicating weakness. This may reflect that earnings growth has been driven more by pricing power than by increased output, partly reducing incentives for capacity-expanding investment. Both manufacturing (-0.4%) and non-manufacturing (+0.3%) capex were weak. As a result, we expect capital investment to be revised down from +0.3% to -1.0% in the Q1 GDP revision (to be released on June 8), lowering annualized real GDP growth from the preliminary 2.1% to around 1.1%. The average Moody's collateral score (the lower, the better) of German Pfandbriefe is much higher than in most other countries issuing CB (Figure 115), suggesting weaker cover pool quality. Moreover, there is a stronger average bank credit quality in other countries (for example, Canada). records.text: housing communities, where the homeowner typically does not own the land but rather pays rent to the community operator. When the homebuyer does not own the land on which the home is placed, they use chattel loans to finance the purchase. These loans come with shorter terms, higher interest rates and fewer borrower protections. The combination of shorter terms and higher interest rates makes them less affordable than if the borrower were to obtain a traditional mortgage. Also, in the case of payment defaults, lenders can more easily repossess properties backed by chattel loans (as they are treated as personal property like autos) without having to initiate a foreclosure process. In response to MH quality issues in the past, HUD published a comprehensive building code in 1976 that set minimum material quality and energy efficiency standards for manufactured housing. As part of this code, HUD required manufactured housing units to be built on a permanent steel chassis. While the presence of this steel structure may have helped improve the structural integrity of the unit, lenders likely viewed the home as more akin to a movable property than an immovable property. The presence of a permanent chassis also increased the cost of the home. Finally, even if the borrower owns the land and obtains a traditional MH mortgage, the fixed costs of origination may be prohibitively high compared to size of the mortgage. The top markets for manufactured homes are in the South and Southeast (Exhibit 2). Interestingly, several states that rank high in manufactured home sales rank low in single family home construction, suggesting the importance of local zoning and land-use regulations as a key constraining factor for the growth of MH. Over 54% of manufactured housing units are in rural areas (defined as territories with fewer than 2,500 people), while single-family homes are primarily in large urban areas (Exhibit 3). But we do see some merit in the argument for a delay to September as September is when the MPC will have data on July inflation which is when the Ofgem price cap resets higher. Perhaps evidence on direct and indirect impacts and inflation expectations become stronger when households see their gas bills rise in July. As a result, we highlight risks of delays to our call of hikes in July and September. An implicit validation of three hikes The Governing Council will express uncertainty around the staff’s baseline. This will reflect the lack of clarity around the situation in Iran/Hormuz, rather than a fundamental disagreement with the staff’s hawkish assessment of the energy shock. The Governing Council will acknowledge more explicitly than it did in March the interest rate assumptions built into the staff’s baseline, but it will then emphasize that future decisions will be data- dependent, meeting-by-meeting and that there is no pre-commitment to a particular rate path. Nevertheless, Lagarde’s comments will implicitly acknowledge that the direction of travel remains upwards on the policy rate. Her comments will likely be consistent with the next hike coming in September rather than in July. The signal from the staff forecasts is that three hikes could be needed in total. Lagarde will accept this as plausible, but she will emphasize that this depends critically on how the situation in Iran/Hormuz evolves. The Labour Force Survey (LFS) unemployment rate has risen notably over the past several years and now suggests relatively loose labour market conditions. By contrast, registered unemployment (NAV), the focus of Norges Bank, remains exceptionally low by historical standards and continues to indicate a relatively tight labour market (Exhibit 3, left). While the two measures differ notably from a methodological standpoint, the divergence highlights the uncertainty regarding how much slack there is in the economy.3 3 LFS unemployment is an ILO-harmonised survey-based measure that captures individuals who report actively seeking work, while NAV unemployment is register-based and captures individuals formally registered as jobseekers with the public employment service. NAV does understate the unemployment numbers because not all job seekers register with NAV and renew registration every 14th day, as is required to be included in the NAV figures. Only the LFS measure accounts for people with weak benefits rights (e.g., students/migrants). records.text: al variable this year is the strength and timing of the El Niño cycle. Current forecasts point to a significant event developing by mid-summer, broadly comparable to 2023–24, but with roughly a 30% probability of a stronger “super” El Niño developing comparable to the 2015–16 event (Figure 1). In a stronger scenario, El Niño could evolve into a macro-relevant shock, particularly if energy and fertilizer prices remain elevated amid ongoing geopolitical tensions involving Iran (see: Fertilizer supply shock: LatAm implications). The clearest transmission channels are likely to be through food, power and industrial supply chains. Food inflation pressures could emerge across India, Southeast Asia, Central America and northern Brazil, while hydropower disruption and rising electricity demand may pressure regional power systems. Precipitation volatility could also disrupt metals and mining operations in regions such as Chile’s Atacama and China’s Yunnan province (see: Super El Niño: The Climate Risk Trade). More broadly, the outlook raises risks around food security, water availability, and logistics disruption. At the same time, greater climate volatility may also support demand for adaptation infrastructure, grid resilience, water management, climate analytics and risk transfer solutions. El Niño Update El Niño is driven by a temporary warming of sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific, which transfers heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and alters global circulation

Because these inputs are embedded across mid and downstream industries, we estimate that at least half of the basket is directly or indirectly exposed to this cost-push factor. With broad supply-side adjustments and stronger anti-involution consensus (see page 5), the current PPI inflation rebound appears sustainable, in our view. We project PPI inflation to hover around 3%y/y in the second half of 2026 and to ease to about 1.5% in 2027, rather than slip back into deflation, even through energy prices are likely to retreat gradually. Risks to our forecasts are balanced. Our forecasts for global energy prices are subject to upside or downside risks, depending on how fast energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz normalize (see Energy: Middle East scenarios update, 1 June). In terms of domestic factors, we see upside risks if the property sector rebounds more quickly/strongly than expected or if the anti-involution campaign is implemented more forcefully, with stricter production controls and overcapacity shutdowns; downside risks would arise from an even deeper property downturn and worse involution. The small move in USDCAD is in line relative to the muted responses of the Canadian dollar to shocks as of late. Indeed, we remain somewhat cautious for net upside in USDCAD, not as much from specific Canadian factors, but rather from both elevated oil prices as well as the exceptionally strong US employment report. While the solid Canadian employment report still leaves the Bank of Canada outlook the same, with the policy rate unchanged to the end of the year, the US data have pointed to the market now beginning to price in the potential for a full rate hike over the same time and may be particularly influential on the dollar view overall. The new composite level suggests a modest GDP contraction of around -0.16% quarter-on-quarter for the second quarter, an improvement from the nearly -0.3% contraction implied by the flash estimates. Looking at the components, the upward revision in the composite was primarily driven by the services sector, though manufacturing also saw a marginal upward revision. Despite the improvement, the services sector (final PMI at 47.7) continues to underperform manufacturing, appearing more vulnerable to elevated inflation and its impact on consumer demand. The manufacturing data, released earlier in the week, showed resilience, particularly in Spain and Italy, with output metrics consistent with flat-to-modest expansion. However, a common theme across both surveys is persistent and intense price pressure. The Composite PMI input cost indicator, for instance, reached its highest level since November 2022. Overall, the May PMIs paint a picture of an economy contracting in Q2, albeit at a modest pace. While the headline figures held up better than initially feared, underlying details and forward-looking indicators signal mounting risks. Reports of significant shortages and lengthening delivery times point to intensifying supply chain pressures. Catalyst.Metric: Pension allocation strategy review and portfolio flows

records.text: The more meaningful shift for FX would be a shift in strategy by GPIF, Japan’s public pension fund. It is one of the largest holders of foreign assets (nearly $1tn in total), it tends to invest mostly unhedged, and private pensions often follow its allocation decisions. GPIF conducts a strategy review every five years and the last one occurred in 2025, leaving any big changes unlikely before 2030. That said, it can still shift its holdings within target allocation bands. The latest reported holdings stand close to the midpoint of the range in each asset class, suggesting room for some adjustment. Theoretically, if GPIF were to cut its foreign bond holdings to the bottom of its allowable range (20%) and shift those proceeds into JGBs (bringing its allocation to 30%), it could total up to $87bn. Such an adjustment would unlikely occur all at once, but it reflects some scope for notable flows if desired—or directed by the administration. So far, the timeliest data suggest that GPIF and the private pensions have continued buying foreign debt while selling foreign equities (Exhibit 5).3 3 We show in Global Markets Daily: The Japanese Portfolio Flow Data in Practice that GPIF and private pension flows are recorded under “trust accounts” in the monthly ITS data. We also noted in the piece that in periods of significant equity gains, GPIF needs to sell stocks to keep the allocation close to 25%. Banks are primarily exposed through rates and macro channels rather than direct taxation, with spreads sensitive to gilt volatility. Housing policy appears broadly supportive for social housing but negative for private landlords. Utilities remain central to the political debate; while “public control” raises headline risk, full nationalisation is seen as unlikely, with regulatory tightening the more probable path. Equities: Across equities, macro transmission dominates. Insurers are primarily exposed to gilts, spreads, and inflation, with life insurers most sensitive to widening spreads and non-life supported by pricing power. Utilities face ongoing political overhang, but nationalisation risk appears overstated and long dated. Banks trade at a discount that already reflects tax and political risk, and the sector screens as cheap vs. European peers. Real estate and Diversified Financials remain highly sensitive to gilt yields and growth expectations, though valuations already compensate for much uncertainty. Housing and infrastructure policy could shift regional investment patterns, while transport faces increased uncertainty around Heathrow expansion under a more regionally focused policy stance. records.text: consumption boost is likely concentrated in the top of the income distribution, where equity holdings are highest. We estimate that the top income quintile accounts for nearly all of the recent wealth effect on consumption growth. The rising concentration of AI infrastructure providers in the equity market means that wealth effects are unusually sensitive to the performance of a narrow set of companies. As a sensitivity check, we consider two alternative scenarios. In an upside scenario in which AI-related stocks grow by 55% and other stocks grow by 20% over the next year (implying a 30% overall increase), we estimate that wealth effects would boost consumption growth by 0.7pp. In a downside scenario in which AI-related stocks decline by 40% and other stocks decline by 15% (implying a 20% overall decline), wealth effects would turn into a 0.3pp drag on consumption growth. These estimates capture only the mechanical impact of asset price changes on consumption through the wealth effects channel. In practice, a sharp move in AI-related stocks could also generate spillover effects—shifting broader risk sentiment, affecting the valuations of other companies, and influencing household confidence—all of which would amplify the consumption impact in either direction. Though the main emphasis, since even the April meeting, was greater concern around the upside risks to inflation rather than the downside risks to growth. The challenge for the BoJ is the high bar for a hawkish surprise, and a continued message of only gradual hikes would likely prove insufficient to strengthen the currency. We also see two other reasons to anticipate continued depreciation pressures over the nearer-term, even if the administration intervenes again. Second, lingering fiscal risks will likely return to the forefront with spending plans set to be clarified over the coming months. records.text: This year, we hosted over 100 financial institutions with several hundred equity and fixed income investors from across the globe for our 30th European Financials Conference in Zurich. For European banks in particular, we see five key themes: 1) a regulatory environment focused on simplification and operational resilience, 2) a resilient operational backdrop with revenues supported by volumes, liability dynamics and fee income diversification, 3) largely stable asset quality trends despite the macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty, 4) continued cost discipline and a key focus on AI and digitalisation as levers for operational efficiency, and 5) capital allocation focused on distribution via dividends and share buybacks, complemented by M&A. With the energy price shock a bit larger than initially incorporated in the March forecasts (which already included a June hike), more long lasting, and with (slightly) more persistent energy price effects, the natural slope is for the ECB to deliver a quite well telegraphed hike. New forecasts will show a bit less growth and more inflation in the near term but, crucially, still show inflation back to target by the end of the forecasting period. With roughly three hikes now incorporated in the baseline, the message will likely come out as a bit hawkish vs March, suggesting two hikes is still a reasonable base case, but leaving the door open to do more rather than less in case of doubt. records.text: Equity Strategy: UK equities continue to trade off fiscal credibility via the gilt market. Risk premia may remain elevated as leadership uncertainty lingers, but bad news is already priced in - particularly in domestic and rate-sensitive sectors. A continued commitment to fiscal rules could support a gradual unwind in risk premia and drive a recovery in lagging domestic names. Conversely, any perceived loosening of fiscal discipline would likely reinforce current underperformance in domestically exposed sectors. Credit Strategy: Sterling credit has shown limited sensitivity so far, reflecting its global composition in IG and structural differences in HY. The key transmission channel remains gilt volatility rather than politics directly. Provided rate moves remain orderly, the near-term credit impact should stay muted. However, UK cyclicals remain the most exposed over time via growth and funding costs. Valuations are not pricing a UK-specific growth shock, leaving downside skewed to any deterioration in fiscal credibility or macro-outlook. Credit: At the sector level, policy risk is more visible. Consumer names (grocers, pubs) face margin pressure from taxes and cost pass-through, with potential support from business rates reform. Industrials remain constrained by weak construction activity, with recovery tied to improved policy clarity. Banks are primarily exposed through rates and macro channels rather than direct taxation, with spreads sensitive to gilt volatility. Housing

records.text: TRADE IDEA TRADE IDEA KEY MESSAGES The SpaceX IPO may be the summer’s most important market catalyst. It will be the largest IPO ever. The deal is headline-grabbing, but more importantly from a flows perspective, it will be a call on liquidity. It comes at a time of very strong wealth effects for US retail investors, driven in part by robust recent gains in Semis. Rule changes for prominent equity indices have also fueled headlines about large potential passive buying flows. This implies significant selling elsewhere that would have a ‘short gamma’ effect from SpaceX’s share price. IPOs have often exhibited high volatility and fat tails. With the confluence of flows expected around SpaceX’s flotation, we think this time will not be an exception. What is unprecedented is that volatility in this stock will be coupled with the largest market cap ever seen in an US IPO. We think many of the standalone SpaceX flows might be digestible. The problem is that many of these flows are potentially same-way and additive. The selling flows in equities that we expect over the next month create a risk of high market volatility. Forced buying/selling and illiquidity are almost always present at the fattest tails for markets. With VIX and VVIX at YTD lows and SMH Put Skew at lows, we see opportunities to hedge. Not for the base case of what we think will happen, but for the tails of what might. Greg Boutle, Head of US Equity Derivatives Strategy | Evan Bybee, Equity Derivatives Strategist | BN

records.text: 5 June 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 48 Deutsche Bank AG Post-eSLR expansion in primary dealer Treasury basis positions In March, we noted the Treasury-futures basis had become less attractive, which likely dampened repo demand from the hedge fund community and contributed to the soft SOFR prints in recent weeks. We offered several explanations for the compression in basis opportunities, including reduced use of Treasury futures by asset managers. Today’s chart highlights another possibility: the easing of eSLR requirements announced late last year has allowed primary dealers to expand their Treasury holdings, which they predominantly hedge using futures and thus run implicit basis positions. As dealers fund their positions more cheaply than hedge funds through triparty repo, this dynamic likely further compresses the basis opportunity set. We estimate implied dealer basis positions as the notional value of dealer net long Treasury holdings offset by short futures positions. In 2025, these positions averaged around $210bn and were broadly flat over the year. Following the eSLR announcement, which allowed voluntary early adoption of the new rule starting January 1st, there was a clear uptrend with 2026 YTD positions averaging around $260bn. The rise in primary dealer positions has coincided with a corresponding decline in leveraged fund short positions in Treasury futures, particularly in the 2-, 5-, and 10- year sectors where basis activity is most concentrated. Japan: May CPI inflation undershot market expectations again on one-off factors May CPI inflation again undershot expectations, mainly reflecting the earlier rollout of Tokyo's free water charge policy. Japan-style core CPI inflation (ex. fresh food) slowed to 1.3% yoy (vs 1.5% in April), while BoJ-style core CPI inflation (ex. fresh food and energy) decelerated to 1.6% yoy from 1.9% (consensus: 1.5% and 1.8%, respectively). Excluding special factors, inflation slowed broadly as expected, with negative food base effects weighing on CPI inflation. Meanwhile, PPI inflation rose sharply in April and should pass through gradually, lifting CPI inflation from autumn. Indonesia: Apr trade and CPI inflation data reinforce cautious near-term outlook April trade surplus fell sharply to a 6-year low, while CPI inflation surprised to the upside amid higher food prices. We expect energy-related import costs to remain sticky for some time and see emerging upward pressure on food prices amid firmer cost pressures and increasing discussions over a possibly stronger El Nino in 2H26. Against this backdrop, we expect upcoming BI policy meetings to remain "live", with sharpened focus on anchoring inflation and IDR stability. Meanwhile, we expect domestic developments to likely stay highly fluid in June-July.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 7 Financial Conditions: A near-reversal following the April 7 ceasefire Following the conflict in the Middle East and the uncertainty it brings to the next steps for monetary policy, we include the evolution of our FRB/US-based model of financial conditions, which aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. The index includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate, using the Federal Reserve’s FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since hostilities in the Middle East began on February 28, the tightening in financial conditions is equivalent to about a 20bp rise in the federal funds rate. Since the April 7 ceasefire announcement, however, financial conditions have eased by 52bps. The tightening reversed all of the easing seen earlier this year, most of which occurred between the December and January FOMC meetings and was primarily driven by a weaker U.S. dollar. records.text: EM Carry: Switching gears and carrying on. We have favoured carry accrual n strategies in EM FX against a backdrop of declining implied volatility, broadly flat YTD returns for the dollar, and reduced room for EM central banks to deliver cuts that would have steadily eroded carry levels. We have argued for a selective approach when constructing FX carry baskets, where carry levels, relative terms of trade shifts, and idiosyncratic developments all play a crucial role, and have highlighted BRL, HUF, MXN, and ZAR as our preferred longs. Among these, we maintain a constructive view on HUF driven by EU fund and Euro adoption tailwinds, which more than offset the impact of higher energy prices on external balances. This positive HUF view is not reliant on a conflict resolution (though we expect HUF to be among the outperformers in this scenario), whereas for ZAR, near-term tactics remain more sensitive to the back-and-forth on an eventual deal. MXN is more levered to US-specific cyclical pricing and more insulated from a terms-of-trade perspective. However, even as the Peso has been a relative outperformer, we find that it has still underperformed the rally in US equities, arguing for further appreciation ahead if US cyclical pricing remains supported. records.text: nuanced. Our Investor’s Guide to Japanese Portfolio Flows outlines the data to watch and the investors to follow, and how to track and anticipate foreign asset demand. We show that Japanese investors, excluding the MoF, hold nearly $6tn of foreign assets, with the majority mostly unhedged (Exhibit 1). As a result, any coordinated reallocation towards domestic securities should be a source of notable JPY appreciation. Post Bank, however, would unlikely be the driver as it tends to invest largely on a hedged basis. An increase in Post Bank’s JGB holdings could matter more for rates markets if it is indeed the result of rotating away from foreign securities rather than simply adjusting its JPY portfolio.2 Post Bank is the biggest single holder of foreign bonds in Japan after the MoF. As of March 2026, according to Post Bank’s latest financial statement, it had roughly $550bn of foreign holdings, mainly in bonds. As a mostly hedged investor, Post Bank should theoretically care most about the gap between JGB yields and hedged foreign yields. While that gap remains positive across key regions, global yields have been rising alongside JGB yields in recent months, leaving the relative attractiveness of JGBs more stable despite multi-decade highs in the 10-year JGB yield (Exhibit 2). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Critical Minerals More Stockpiling Plans “In metals and minerals is where the newest wave of stockpiling is most visible” – Patrick Schröder, senior research fellow at Chatham House. records.text: US Economics Weekly5 June 2026 ab 13 May Emp Sit: strong NFP Nonfarm payroll employment expanded 172K in May, above our (95K) above-consensus expectations (85K). Private employment rose 120K, and there was a sizeable 52K gain in government, led by a 44K rise in local government excluding education. Typically May reports look better on the first release, and then revise lower due to the pandemic's undue influence on seasonal adjustment. May employment gains have surprised to the upside in each of the last four years, and each year revised down in either the 2nd or 3rd release, by an average of -60K jobs. Part of the strength in private employment could be due to the timing of Memorial Day, with a strong gain in leisure and hospitality employment potentially coming at the expense of June. Nonetheless, this was a strong print, leaving total nonfarm payroll employment up 57K on average in the past eight months and private employment up 88K per month on average in the past four months. Preceding months' gains were also revised up by 93K, with +62K of this due to seasonal adjustment and a +31K revision to employment on a non-seasonally adjusted basis. With today's upside surprise potentially wedging back support for prior months. The unemployment rate held steady at 4.3% (4.30% unrounded, down 4bp from April), in line with our (4.3%) and consensus (4.3%) expectations. A brief flare-up of reflation expectations in April (evident in IRS pricing) was quickly dampened byforecasts of an L-shaped rebound for China’s economy. After the PPI returned to inflation from September 2016, long-term yields rose, but this was likely also due to global trades related to the US presidential election and expectations of tighter financial regulations in China. Into 2017, the dominant themes for China’s rates market were the PBoC’s tighter monetary stance and financial de- leveraging, while the PPI remained elevated alongside high commodity prices . Rates trended downwards into 2018, when the US–China trade dispute erupted, sharply raising uncertainty on the external-demand side. Simultaneously, financial deleveraging made financing difficult for private firms and led to a spate of credit defaults. Downward economic pressure replaced inflation as the dominant headwind. It took until April for CBP to put in place the systems needed to process those refunds. On April 10, CBP launched Phase 1 of its refund process for now-illegal IEEPA tariffs. In this first phase, refunds are available only for unliquidated entries—those for which final duties have not yet been assessed—and for entries liquidated within 80 days before the refund application is filed (January 30- April 19, 2026). Importantly, eligibility depends on the liquidation date, not the import date. Liquidation typically occurs within 314 days of entry, although it can happen sooner. The process is burdensome, and the burden is on the importer to claim the refund. Refunds will not be issued automatically; eligible firms and consumers must take affirmative steps to receive them. Here’s how it played out : Stage 1 – the knee-jerk “flight to quality”: Markets were buffeted by an inflation/stagflation shock (tariffs in 2025, geopolitical escalation in 2026). The initial reaction in rates around Liberation Day was a rally, but this quickly turned to a sell-off as the inflation impact started to weigh (recall that Fed Chair Powell delivered hawkish remarks right after Liberation Day) (Figure 1). Stage 2 -- reversal and amplification: The sell-off in April 2025 became self-reinforcing based on positioning excesses and a narrative. The narrative was overseas selling of Treasuries amid a less dovish Fed, worsened by swap spread unwinds and basis trade deleveraging. There is also a parallel from March 2020, where the initial rally turned into a “dash for cash” and resulted in a sharp rise in yields. In both instances, yields did not move lower amid rising risks, reducing the “flight to quality” perception of Treasuries – see Figure 1. Two things make long-end yields particularly vulnerable right now – (1) markets have heavily discounted risks of wider deficits after the escalation (low term premiums), and (2) swap spreads are falling sharply like post Liberation day (Figure 2) which entails selling of Treasuries – that can self-reinforcing. Due to federal states ranking equal to the central government in the German constitution, it is also questionable of federal states can be considered "sub- sovereigns". Moreover, due to the so-called “federal loyalty principle” and the “financial strength equalization” enshrined in the German constitution, we agree with Fitch and Scope that all federal states have the same credit quality as Bunds, which is currently still triple A by all rating agencies. While Moody's differentiates between ratings of federal states, even Moody's concedes that federal states have a very high likelihood of receiving extraordinary support from the federal government, due to its assessment of the high reputational risk for Germany as a whole in case of default by a federal states and under the "federal loyalty principle (according to which all federal states must provide mutual support in the event that one of them or the federal republic faces a severe budgetary crisis). In addition, the debt volume and structure of federal states are extremely complex, and an event of non-payment would have a corresponding impact on Germany as a whole. These arguments typically lead to a two-notch uplift versus the so-called "baseline credit assessment" at Moody's. Against that backdrop, we went on a field trip to Berlin, to discuss the policy outlook with government officials and experts in economic policy and defence (see our trip notes here). And this is also a good occasion to take stock of Germany’s growth environment and where it may be headed. Our view in a nutshell: Higher energy prices and structural headwinds present a challenging mix for German growth. Near term, fiscal policy should only partly offset these drags; longer term, broader reforms will be needed. Still, the outlook is not all negative: backloaded infrastructure spending should raise growth for longer, demographics may support a shift toward higher-yielding savings and cushion labour-market risks from rapid AI diffusion (see here and here), and policy changes could gradually lift public and private investment.
