records.text: s the norm … • … and pointing to a tightening labor market and Fed hike ahead • Next week: ECB hike and US CPI spike Yes, and it counts This week’s US employment report is important for two reasons. First, it reinforces our view that a cyclical lift in global business spending is now broadening to hiring in a manner that will cushion the energy price drag on household purchasing power. Second, it supports our view that AI is not generating a jobless expansion. There is concern that the US lift is less indicative globally, a point highlighted by this week’s sharp drop in the global PMI employment. However, incoming news points to solid global growth which, if sustained, should support our central 2026 outlook theme of a conscious labor market recoupling. Global consumer resilience was a crucial cushion last year when non-tech businesses were reeling from a trade war and pulling back on hiring (Figure 1). Continued spending in the face of weak labor income boosted global profits and promoted leaner inventory positions. Combined with a fading of trade war fears and sustained tech strength, this allowed the global manufacturing sector to move into the new year with strong momentum. Factory output increased at a 3.7%ar last quarter and this week’s May global manufacturing PMI edged up to a five-year high, with details pointing to a positive turn in the inventory cycle. rise in May but move looks mod- est; mortgage rates fall back • BoE commentary remains mixed • Survation poll shows Burnham ahead in Makerfield Politics remains in focus and a new poll from Survation this week showed Andy Burnham with a ten point lead over Reform ahead of the Makerfield by-election on 18th June. Polling can be volatile, but is a notable step up from a lead of three points shown last week. This possibly reflects increas- ing awareness of Burnham among the general public as his campaign gathers momentum. The data flow was light this week, although the final PMI for May showed the composite output index revised up by 1.2 points to 49.7. This is very low and points to barely positive growth. But the UK PMI is very volatile, and the two-month average of 51.2 would be consistent with growth of around 0.9% annualized growth—close to our 2Q forecast of 1.0%. The price measures of the PMI remained elevated, with com- posite output prices at 61.6 and services at 60.6. The service price surge is notable given the lower energy intensity in the sector. This suggests relatively fast and broad indirect energy effects, and may hint that second-round effects are more like- ly. Services imports also picked up in Mar. While this may signal rebalancing, the strength reflects cyclical, price-driven supply factors rather than a broad-based domestic demand recovery. Brent futures have stabilized near $100 per barrel. Dated Brent—the physical benchmark for prompt delivery—has also eased materially, and its premium to the front-month futures has retraced sharply from a record $36 in early April, when buyers were scrambling for available cargoes, to about $2, back near pre-conflict levels. Refined product prices have also pulled back from recent highs, and volatility across crude and product markets has fallen sharply. To be fair, prices have so far tracked our—admittedly counterintuitive— framework closely. Brent averaged near our early-March target of $100 in both March and April and ended May just $1 below our forecast. Looking ahead, our base case continues to assume that the Strait of Hormuz reopens in June. Under that assumption, Brent should average around $100 through the balance of the year, slipping below triple digits on a monthly average basis only in December. records.text: M Idea 8 The effective tariff rate and tariff receipts The tariff rate on US imports has fallen to 8.3% in 1Q26 data On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court struck down the President's authority to impose tariffs under IEEPA. Section 122 tariffs will replace IEEPA tariffs in the short term, though uncertainty rises after the 150-day period when Congress would need to extend those tariffs. Replacing IEEPA with Section 122 tariffs of 15% and considering composition effects of US imports, we estimate baseline tariffs near 11%. Our estimate of "core" tariffs (ex fuels, gold and AI-related imports) remains closer to 13-14%. In our view, near-term tariffs are likely capped below 'Liberation Day' levels—at least until Section 232 and 301 investigations are complete. In the April 2026 data, the effective tariff rate is estimated at ~6.9%, and the 1Q26 tariff rate averages to 8.3%. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 05 June 2026 7 UK Bit by bit Sonali Punhani MLI (UK) sonali.punhani@bofa.com Ruben Segura -Cayuela BofA Europe (Madrid) ruben.segura-cayuela@bofa.com Bit by bit This week a second MPC member Megan Greene argued that the case for hikes is growing. She noted that risk of acting is less severe than that of failing to act. Her comments suggest that she is close to voting for a hike potentially as soon as June (along with Huw Pill who already voted for a hike in April). But this urgency has not been seen in the majority of the committee yet. Governor Bailey was somewhat dovish last week by noting that allowing inflation temporarily above 2% is appropriate, given uncertainty and weakness in the economy and reacting too early may cause volatility. This can explain the active hold in April. He is taking comfort from the fact that tightening in financial conditions has done some of the work and that gives them some time. But he did note that tolerance would reduce if second round effects begin to emerge and second round effects are likely to be stronger, the larger and more persistent the shock is. And this week his comments were more neutral when he noted that they cannot wait for hard evidence for second round effects to act. All this means a June hike is unlikely and data/ persistence of energy prices would need to push them to hike in July. This suggests a corresponding segmentation in investor risk aversion, where intra-asset reallocation is more likely than inter-asset allocation. Within the fixed income universe, we observe significant intra-asset reallocation between domestic money market funds, foreign money market funds, and domestic long-end government bond funds. This reallocation is driven by BoT's policy cycle and yield differentials between FX-hedged foreign assets and BoT bills. What role does regulation play in moulding this behaviour? Mandatory suitability tests reinforces asset class segmentation by assigning risk scores to retail investors based on loss tolerance. Consequently, Thai fixed income investors, who constitute the majority of retail investors, naturally seek lower risk options and tend to stick to the lower end of the risk tiering. What are the regulations on FX hedging? Regulations mandate 100% FX-hedging for all foreign money market funds and penalize unhedged funds with higher risk classifications (e.g., "High" for unhedged fixed income vs. "Low-Medium" for hedged). Only Foreign Investment Funds (FIFs) that hedge at least 90% of their FX exposure are classified at the risk level of their underlying asset class. How do mutual funds impact the ThaiGB market? records.text: The Hybrid Renaissance Hybrid supply: On pace to set new records, especially in the EUR market The issuance tailwind behind the hybrid debt market—which began in early 2024 following a change to the Moody’s rating methodology—has accelerated in 2026. As shown in Exhibit 1, both the USD and EUR markets are on pace to set new annual records for hybrid gross supply. In the USD market, there are now more than a dozen hybrid bonds with $1 billion or more of notional outstanding—and some of the largest hybrid new issues were launched in recent months. The elevated gross supply of EUR hybrids partly reflects a more mature market, which has had a high share of bonds being called this year. For comparison, while gross supply is up 132% year to date vs. the same period last year, the notional amount outstanding of the EUR hybrid market has increased by a more modest 9% since the end of 2025. Utilities have been among the most active sectors in both markets, accounting for 50% and 40% of hybrid supply in the USD and EUR markets, respectively, since 2024 (Exhibits 2 and 3). Q5) What if countries do not comply with the rules? For countries not in EDP, exceeding the limits set by the control account can lead to a debt-based excessive deficit procedure. That said, even in this case, the decision is not fully automatic, as the Commission may take into account additional factors, such as the level of debt and deficits. records.text: Shifting the distribution. We think the May US labor market report sets a higher n floor on US yields for now. Firm growth and ongoing inflation risk are likely to keep the market pricing clear asymmetry towards hikes in the near term. The main factor that likely held the market back from an even more front-loaded selloff was the relative stability in the unemployment rate and wage growth. Our economists have revised their projected Fed path, pushing out the final two rate cuts in their forecast to June and December 2027. Reflecting this, we have revised our UST yield forecasts higher and now see 2y and 10y yields ending 2026 at 3.8% and 4.4% respectively (from 3.4% and 4.1% previously), levels consistent with the market converging towards a more balanced distribution of risks around the policy path by year-end alongside relative stability in longer-term forwards (e.g. 5y5y, which are currently about fair). That dovish convergence in pricing likely requires some amount of validation from the data, which we expect over time under our economists’ forecast for a moderation in sequential inflation and an uptick in the unemployment rate by year-end. On first glance, the case for patience seems to have strengthened since the last meeting in April. Core CPI fell to a five-year low of 1.5%oya and oil prices have eased on optimism over an eventual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. However, even with the economy slip- ping into a technical recession last quarter, the May LFS report this week showed a strong rebound in employment and a three-tenths drop in the unemployment rate, and markets continue to price slightly more than one full hike by year-end. But one strong month does not erase the excess supply in the labor market. The unemployment rate has remained at or above 6.5% since August 2024, well above most estimates of the natural rate. Wage growth for permanent employees slowed sharply in April, reinforcing the signal of lingering slack on net. Both the participation rate and the employment rate appear to have stabilized in recent months, but they remain below their pre-pandemic levels (Figure 1). Thus we do not expect the BoC to pivot on the back of one strong labor market report. records.text: Ben Luk 4 June 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Emerging Markets Weekly: Good vs. Bad Carry , Choose Wisely Real money flows into EM have been highly volatile, with sharp outflows in March, reversed by strong inflows in April amid ceasefire optimism and reduced contagion risks. However, sentiment deteriorated again in May , albeit less so for FX relative to bonds and equities, as renewed USD strength and higher US yields weighed on the near -term outlook, particularly as valuations and positioning bec ame less compelling after sustained accumulation over the past year. Against this backdrop, a broad beta -driven rally is unlikely to dominate. Instead, dispersion should increase as investors differentiate more clearly between resilient and vulnerable economies. Within this environment, we emphasize selectivity in carry: favoring “good carry” FX such as TRY, HUF, BRL, and newly added COP, while avoiding structurally “bad carry” in INR and IDR. We also maintain a constructive stance on tech and manufacturing proxies, including ILS, CNH, KRW, and our new overweight in TWD. records.text: Market Disruption Part 2: A Case Study In Productivity Driven Labor Displacement The Week Ahead: more inflation news for an inflation focused FOMC We expect headline CPI to rise 0.46% in May, lifting 12-month inflation from 3.8% in April to 4.2%, likely the peak for the year, with energy as the main driver. Gasoline prices fell late in the month, suggesting some relief in June. Core CPI likely increased a more modest 0.17%, leaving the 12-month rate at 2.8%, held down by residual seasonality, softer rent growth, and muted vehicle prices. Wednesday's CPI along with Thursday's producer prices will refine our current 0.32% estimate for core PCE prices in May. Inflation expectations in the New York Fed survey are likely to remain relatively stable when compared to the University of Michigan survey, while small business optimism we expect stays subdued. Elsewhere, we expect a narrower April trade deficit, modest gains in existing home sales, stable initial claims with a rise in continuing claims, and still- elevated inflation expectations alongside weak sentiment in the June Michigan survey, all against the backdrop of the Fed’s pre-meeting quiet period. records.text: US Economics Weekly5 June 2026 ab 6 Labor market indicator moving sideways We ran our indicator model of the private NFP employment subcategories, which assesses the probability of net job losses in the near future, reflected in the share of leading sectors weakening to a certain degree. The leading indicator in May remained stable at 56%, the same level since January. But that contour is quite different from last months' report, which suggested notable improvement since the start of the year in the leading data. In contrast, the 'other' indicator improved (fell) to 39% in May from a downward revised April, with a better contour over the spring relative to last month's print. Overall, the picture suggests less stress in the labor market, with stability in the leading sector and marginal improvements in the rest. Nevertheless, in the broader historical context, these are still prints that warrant caution. In particular, we expect the euro area deficits to widen in 2026 (to 3.4% of GDP from 2.9%), driven primarily by the German fiscal expansion, followed by only a modest further increase in 2027 (to 3.5%). As discussed in our outlook, excluding an oil-led recession, we see upside risks to our baseline as limited to around 15bp in 2026 and 30bp in 2027 (see Exhibit 2 ). As a final point, we would highlight that this week’s announcement is fully consistent with our previously published fiscal playbook (see here, and refined further here and here), where our core view hinges on the amount of fiscal space available under the EU fiscal rules. For some time, we have argued that euro area deficits would remain contained and that to see a materially different fiscal landscape compared to our baseline would require a clear activation or expansion of any of the two escape clauses. In our view, such a scenario would likely need to coincide with a more adverse macroeconomic backdrop, particularly a recession in the euro area, which is not our base case. And if anything, the latest announcement reinforces our thinking. The fact that the Commission, despite requests from some Member States for more fiscal flexibility (see here), opted for only marginal adjustments to the NEC suggests that the bar for more significant changes remains high. In our view, clearing that bar would likely require a downturn of a much larger scale, such as a euro area recession.

records.text: 4 Short-term outlook highly dependent on Middle East: Following our analysis in Energy: Middle East scenarios update on 1 June, we look at how those scenarios filter through to aluminium. As the Middle East conflict has constrained production and exports of aluminium, prices have to some extentbeen correlated with oil prices . Imminent ceasefire: Should rapid progress to a sustainable ceasefire occur, and oil fall to a floor of USD70/bbl, we would expect a sharp drop in aluminium prices, potentially towards USD3,500/t, as backed-up primary metal and value-added products (VAP) are released into the global market. However, we believe such a drop would drive significant end-user buying interest and ultimately spur a price rally into 2027,as the market increasingly prices in shortages . Hormuz re-opens in August: In this scenario, we would still see aluminium rally on failure to reach an earlier ceasefire and prolonged Gulf shipping disruption. However, sustained higher oil prices (at c.USD140/bbl), driving a stronger USD, and slower global demand growth would, in our view, would dampen extreme aluminium price upside potential. The modelling for this scenario is closest to the assumptions underpinning our revised forecasts. Hormuz re-opens in October: We assume further damage to critical energy and aluminium infrastructure across the Middle East as both parties escalate further to improve their negotiating positions. The current energy shock presents downside risks to economic growth and likely fiscal trajectory. The way forward: a proposed deficit limit of 3% of GDP South Africa has used nominal expenditure ceilings to manage spending growth. But when economic growth slows, revenue shortfalls widen the fiscal deficit. This has been the case in the post-GFC and Covid periods. Various measures to increase tax rates have helped narrow the gap (in 2016, the government introduced the highest rate of 45% on personal income tax and in 2018 increased VAT to 15% from 14%). However, these steps have not been sufficient to reduce deficits significantly. As seen in multiple 2025 budget presentations, when a VAT increase was rejected, tax increases are now politically difficult given that no single political party holds a majority in parliament. So, something stronger is required to put debt on a sustained downward path – either through higher GDP or fiscal measures. South Africa is already pursuing primary surpluses. Putting these targets into law could entrench fiscal discipline and limit political interference. In this context, the government could adopt a legally binding rule that caps headline deficits at 3% of GDP and provide appropriate escape clauses when shocks occur. records.text: US Rates Weekly 05 June 2026 Citi Research 8 Short end: Range-bound SOFR/IORB Repo rates have bounced from their late-May lows; however, SOFR hasn’t fixed above IORB for more than a month now (see Figure 14). Over the next few weeks, we think repo rates are likely to stay within their recent range (i.e. SOFR fixing 0bp to 5bp below IORB) on most days, and we see two main drivers for this. First, T-bill settlements will turn negative next week and T-bill outstanding will move slightly lower through June. The negative T-bill supply means that collateral funding needs will also move slightly lower from here. Second, we think the TGA balance will stay in a range between $800bn and $900bn for most of the month. While the TGA balance could increase towards $950bn in the middle of the month due to tax receipts, we see this as transitory. Our month-end estimate of a $900bn TGA is in line with Treasury’s Q2 guidance at the May refunding announcement (see US Rates Weekly: Uneasy deadlock). This means that reserves are likely to stay above $3tn through most of the month, which should also be supportive of repo markets. records.text: k’s USTR recommendation is applied, we estimate a weighted average tariff of 19% Despite the policy rate sitting at its highest level in 20 years, with real rates running above 10% this year, the incoming data point to a strong and resilient economy in the first half of the year. More surprisingly, the resilience has been visible in the sectors where monetary policy typically bites hardest: goods production, investment, and consumption. We see this as suggesting that, so far, the fiscal and quasi-fiscal stimulus implemented this year is overpowering the effects of mone- tary policy. In last week’s 1Q GDP release, the industrial sector expanded more than 4% q/q saar, and this week the April IP grew 0.7% m/m sa, close to our expectations. records.text: Canada’s weak growth forces us out of AUDCAD, while the RBA and BoE are already softening as the post‑war data pulse disappoints. But the more interesting story sits in Switzerland. The SNB remains structurally dovish, still fighting disinflation with core CPI barely above zero, even as the ECB and others drift back toward tightening. That creates a policy asymmetry the market may be underpricing. At the same time, CHF positioning is stretched—and now starting to unwind—just as geopolitical FX sensitivity fades, mirroring the post‑2022 pattern. Less fear, less need for CHF. This is a regime shift: from “buy safety” to “fade safety.” Swapping short EURNOK for short CHFNOK reflects that pivot. Less ECB downside risk, more CHF vulnerability. When crowded refuges lose their narrative, they tend to adjust quickly, especially if the central bank provides a nudge. Taken at face value, this would suggest the Fed's current 3.50-3.75% policy setting is neutral in the context of year-ahead forecasts for inflation. (Consensus expectations for PCE inflation in 2027 are 2.4%.) Reasons for and against a higher neutral rate Is it reasonable to think the neutral rate of interest has risen this far this quickly? As we noted in our Mid-Year Outlook, forecasts for AI-related spending continue to move higher, and the categories of nonresidential fixed investment associated with the AI build-out have non-cyclical characteristics (see Exhibit 3 and Exhibit 4 ). It would be reasonable to think that the AI capex spending – past, current, and projected – would be putting some upward pressure on neutral rates. In addition, our estimate of the real neutral rate is similar to estimates from Fed Staff (here) that place it at 135bp, and in the middle of estimates from Laubach-Williams (106bp) and Holston-Laubach-Williams (169bp). Our estimate does not appear out of line with a range of other official estimates. That said, it is useful to remember that these models, while helpful, have flaws and could be fooled by false signals. One common shortcoming is the endpoint problem. Burnham has said "you need strong public control and direction over both the investment strategy and the enablers of a more productive economy, such as transport, energy, water, education and housing". This is a policy agenda that has broad public support according to recent YouGov polling. It could conceivably be done within the current fiscal rules - either by balancing against a financial asset, or by offering backstops and joint ownership models to private firms in exchange for oversight/control. However, the cost is likely to be large, with estimates ranging from tens to hundreds of billions of pounds of upfront cost. • Increasing provision of social housing. Burnham has said that he would aim to use the full £39bn allocated to affordable housing provision in the last Spending Review for homes for social rent (currently aimed at 60%). More broadly, he is advocating a locally delivered model, in which central government provides funds but devolved decision makers have discretion about how best to deliver. Crucially this would not come at a fiscal cost beyond what has already been budgeted for. • Devolution of tax and spend decisions to regional decision makers. Beyond housing, Burnham's agenda focuses on devolving decision making to regional areas. records.text: US Rates Weekly 05 June 2026 Citi Research 4 Overview: Rising rates distribution, but we carry on How much more pain for 5y USTs? The Treasury sell-off continued today on the strong +172k NFP print. However, the unemployment rate was only slightly lower, now at 4.296%, and wage growth remained subdued even in leisure and hospitality where there was strong jobs growth. The Treasury market is pricing the possibility of a much lower unemployment rate, combined with higher inflation. Since the Iran conflict started, yields have generally been driven by inflation expectations, specifically WTI prices (Figure 4). This makes sense as the market quickly priced out cuts and priced in the risk of a structural revival of inflation which would require a hiking cycle. Now the question is the risk of a non-linear move in USTs due to both strong growth and inflation. However, we have argued previously that the unemployment rate would need to move down to 4%, or lower, to trigger a material Fed tightening cycle (see US Rates Weekly - March showers bring April rallies?). T oday’s UR has us questioning how high the breakeven growth of NFP is; it does not appear close to zero. Thus, this move feels slightly overdone to us, although as we wrote two weeks ago there is no obvious bullish catalyst (see US Rates Weekly - Et tu, Waller?). The recent string of above-target readings in food inflation reflects specific weather-related crop disruptions, as well as cost-push pressures in the food processing and distribution chain given the sustained conflict in the Middle East. El Niño intensifies tail risk: Beyond current food price dynamics, we now incorporate into our base case a meaningfully higher probability of a strong El Niño weather phenomenon developing in late 2026 and persisting into early 2027 (see Figure 5). El Niño events typically bring drought conditions to Brazil’s MATOPIBA (an agricultural region in the northeast) and northern region. This might affect the rain outlook for the bigger Midwest harvest at the end of the year. Moreover, the phenomenon typically brings heavier rains to the southern region, where most fresh fruits and vegetables are produced. records.text: Wealth Effects on Consumption Growth: AI Leads the Way After a temporary decline in February and March, the S&P 500 has rebounded sharply— now 11% higher than at the start of the year and 27% higher than a year ago. With home prices rising only about 1% over the same period, equity gains have been the dominant driver of household wealth accumulation over the past year. We estimate that household net worth has risen to 800% of disposable income, the highest level except for early 2022. The recent rebound in equity prices—and much of the broader rally over the past few years—has been driven by the outperformance of a handful of large US companies providing key AI infrastructure. The outperformance of these AI infrastructure providers accounted for about 20% of the total increase in equity prices in 2023–2024 and 70% since 2025. In fact, the impact of AI optimism on the equity market likely has been and will remain even larger than this pure accounting contribution of AI companies because it has also lifted risk sentiment more broadly. records.text: Another goal of this wage-setting framework is to guarantee that wage earners receive their share of the value generated in the economy, usually proxied by the “wage share” – labour costs as a share of total factor income – which is expected to stay stable over time. The upward pressure on wage settlements over recent years therefore partly reflects the wage share falling below its historical average, driven by exceptionally strong profits (Exhibit 2, left). At the same time, manufacturing labour productivity growth continues to exceed that of the broader economy (Exhibit 2, right). Together, these developments imply that the sector leading wage negotiations entered bargaining from a position of relatively strong profitability and productivity, with the “exposed” sector able to absorb higher labour costs while remaining competitive internationally. In this framework, labour market conditions and inflation expectations still matter, albeit less so than in a standard wage Phillips curve logic. In the “exposed” sector, they enter the bargaining considerations as a part of the Technical Reporting Committee on the Income Settlements (TBU) report, which provides the data used in the negotiations, such as the wage share and inflation forecast. In the “sheltered” sectors, it matters for local bargaining and sectoral wage drift. Traditional labour market slack indicators in Norway point to markedly different stories. If the Strait stays closed beyond June, our framework implies that each additional month of disruption would lift average prices by roughly $5 in 3Q26 and $15 in 4Q26, driven primarily by accelerating inventory depletion. Yet despite the absence of an agreement, the continued closure of the Strait, and ongoing inventory draws, markets appear increasingly comfortable with the status quo. So when does market psychology shift from a sanguine “Is that it?” to a more apprehensive “What if this isn’t?” Or is the market correctly signaling that the worst of the shock has already been absorbed and that oil can indeed oscillate around $100 for the rest of the year, despite the largest supply disruption in modern history? There are several channels through which the disruption may prove more manageable than the headlines imply: supply losses may be smaller than believed, inventories larger than reported, or demand losses deeper than recognized. Our assessment suggests that all three are at work. We estimate that an additional 1 mbd of supply is finding its way through the Strait, visible inventories are drawing somewhat more slowly than our initial projections, and demand losses are materially larger than expected. Exhibit 5 summarises the range of approaches, showing the range of what the weighted average best 10% of models implies in each of them. The recent decline in wage share, strong manufacturing productivity, continued labour shortages in parts of the economy and stronger inflation outcomes all point to wage growth remaining firm ahead. India: Early May activity data gives mixed signals; IMD lowers monsoon outlook With over three months of the ongoing Iran conflict, we are seeing pockets of weakness in April and early May economic data. Auto sales held up in May, while industrial production remained relatively robust in April. Air traffic and power demand (weather- related) also saw some recovery. However, fuel consumption remained under pressure in May, GST collections weakened, and foreign reserves stayed on a weaker footing. April WPI inflation surged to a 42-month high, while the fiscal deficit was the highest in eight years. Separately, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) lowered its rainfall assessment for this year from 92% to 90% of its Long Period Average, with a model error of ±4%. In our view, this suggests rainfall is likely to remain below par going into July-August as well, which are critical months for agriculture and sowing activity. Further, IMD also predicts that El Niño conditions are likely to develop during the southwest monsoon. However, better starting points in terms of ample food buffer stocks and healthy reservoir levels should act as a tailwind for food prices for a while. The drivers of hybrid issuance and investment With the broader debt capital markets open to a wide range of borrowers, many market participants have questioned why an issuer might opt for a subordinated (higher coupon) hybrid instrument vs. a more traditional financing option in senior unsecured form. Issuers in capital intensive industries—which often operate with large debt capital structures—tend to favor hybrid debt for two key reasons. First is the partial equity credit it receives from the rating agencies, which reflects its ‘equity like’ characteristics, including subordination in the capital structure and the ability to defer coupon payments without triggering a default. For a capital structure with limited ‘headroom’ within a targeted leverage or rating band, this partial equity credit can be attractive— especially since it does not involve diluting shareholders. Second is the favorable tax deductibility of hybrid interest (relative to preferred stock, for example). For a profitable corporate taxpayer, the tax shield can help optimize the weighted average cost of capital—even if the hybrid debt has a moderately higher coupon. Placing the growth of the hybrid market (across regions) in context Exhibits 4 and 5 show the evolution of the size of the hybrid asset class across regions. records.text: M Idea 2 Are neutral rates moving structurally higher? Our estimate of the neutral rate has risen 50bp in the past year Our US Economics Mid-Year Outlook highlights both the fundamental momentum in the US economy driven by the AI build-out and near-term risks to the expansion from the ongoing conflict over the Strait of Hormuz. In recent editions of the US Economics Weekly, we detailed where consensus differs from our views on inflation and how upside risks to inflation – if materialized – could alter our outlook for monetary policy, which includes 50bp of rate cuts in 2027. This week, we examine another risk to our outlook for further monetary policy normalization; whether the inelastic nature of nonresidential business investment is pushing the neutral rate of interest higher. To estimate the natural rate of interest, we turn to our trend-cycle decomposition framework that we introduced last year when examining the effect of changes in immigration policy on the macroeconomy (see here). Our framework assumes each measure of economic activity and labor markets is represented as the sum of cyclical and trend components, where the cyclical component is assumed to be common across all the inputs with contemporaneous effects. Each variable is permitted to have its own unique trend. The framework yields estimates of potential output, the output gap, long-run unemployment, and the equilibrium real policy rate, which are key inputs to monetary and fiscal policy. records.text: We have been making the case that the US economy didn’t need easier monetary policy before the Iran war started, when the market was pricing in 2 cuts and the Fed was comfortable validating that view. Asset prices inflation and a boom in private credit are hard to come by when liquidity is tight and our view was that financial conditions were pretty loose, both in the US and globally, before the war. Now the consensus narrative is that the Fed should not cut and should even hike rates because of the recent inflation dynamics attributed to the Iran war. That is not the reason why the Fed should be mindful of inflation dynamics, because at the end a supply shock can be looked through. The reason is more structural in our view: inflation has been persistently high and above the target for too many years to simply blame a sequence of supply shocks. It is the underlying inflation that should be a source of concern for the Fed, not the energy shock per se. The sector remains the leading job cutter of 2026 by a wide margin, according to the press release. The transportation sector announced 6K seasonally-adjusted cuts in May, up from 2K in April (7K not seasonally adjusted, up from 1K in April). That leaves the not-seasonally- adjusted year-to-date transportation job cuts at 40K in 2026, up from the 7K announced in the same period last year. We noted in our preview (link here) that job cuts associated with the Spirit Airlines shutdown risked showing up in the May Challenger report. In May, artificial intelligence led all reasons for job cuts for the third consecutive month, accounting for 39K announced cuts (NSA), the highest monthly total recorded for the reason since Challenger began tracking it in 2023. Cuts attributed to artificial intelligence were 40% of the May total, up from 7% in January, 25% in March, and 26% in April. Compared to the ECB’s “adverse” scenario, that would be c 10% lower for this year, but still 8-9% above the 2027-28 trajectory. Meanwhile, the market has priced a more hawkish ECB compared to March. A “regular” cut-off on 20 May would imply market pricing of close to 80bp of policy rate hikes – twice what was included in the March scenario. A somewhat lower oil price this year than in the “adverse scenario”, but with greater persistence, brings elements of the “severe” scenario into play. But more demand destruction and more ECB hikes priced should, to our mind, mean inflation back on target in 2028 on an annual average basis. True, that would imply the ECB giving the “nod” to more than 50bp of hikes. But we would caution against taking that at face value. The downward slope in core inflation would be much steeper to get to target, on average, in 2028, and most likely imply end- 28 quarterly core inflation below 2%. That, to our mind, would be the ECB’s way of flagging that three hikes or more is not unthinkable, but probably a bit too much. ab 5 June 2026 Global Research US Economic Data Solid May employment report Strong May gain in nonfarm payroll employment Nonfarm payroll employment expanded 172K in May, above our (95K) above-consensus expectations (85K). Private employment rose 120K, and there was a sizeable 52K gain in government, led by a 44K rise in local government excluding education. Typically May reports look better on the first release, and then revise lower due to the pandemic's undue influence on seasonal adjustment. May employment gains have surprised to the upside in each of the last four years, and each year revised down in either the 2nd or 3rd release, by an average of -60K jobs. Part of the strength in private employment could be due to the timing of the Memorial Day, with a strong gain in leisure and hospitality employment potentially coming at the expense of June. Nonetheless, this was a strong print, leaving total nonfarm payroll employment up 57K on average in the past eight months and private employment up 88K per month on average in the past four months. Preceding months' gains were also revised up by 93K, with +62K of this due to seasonal adjustment and a +31K revision to employment on a non-seasonally adjusted basis. With today's upside surprise potentially wedging back support for prior months. records.text: 2pp to GDP , -1.0pp to CPI This week, the government began full consideration of a plan to cut the consumption tax to 1% starting in April next year. Our estimates suggest the tax cut would reduce private consumption by 0.4% while lifting real GDP by 0.2%. Assuming a 75% pass- through of the tax cut, we project a 1.0% decline in CPI. How to finance the ¥4.4 trillion tax cut remains a key issue. As PM Takaichi indicated, the most likely approach is to avoid deficit bond issuance and instead reallocate within existing revenues and expenditures. One scenario involves securing around ¥1–2 trillion from special tax measures and subsidies, with the remainder financed through non-tax revenues. Next week:GDP revision, PPI and economy watcher survey Main economic data to watch is Q1 GDP revision (8 Jun) and May PPI (10 Jun). We expect a downward revision of Q1 real GDP from 2.1%q/q, saar to 1.1% due to a weak capex data. We see another surge of PPI in May at 1%m/m. What market pricing does capture is the evolution of myriad of factors, not least of which is the likely path of issuance and medium-term fiscal policy. So a policy shift that would see greater borrowing and increased budget execution risk will inevitably alter the market participants' perception of risk and uncertainty around the path of fiscal policy. What might market participants want to see from leadership candidates and their proposed approaches to fiscal policy? First and foremost, any discussion of big changes to the path of borrowing or taxation need to be contextualised - the failure to do this and the consequences thereof were some of the key lessons from the Truss-Kwarteng period. Changes to fiscal stance need to be placed within an overall fiscal framework that can be understood and scrutinised by external participants who then will be in a position to come to a judgement on what is being proposed. To that end, it has been notable that there has been a dialling down of the more combative rhetoric around the market that was earlier reported and as the expected leadership challenger, Burnham has been clear in his commitment to a fiscal framework. The bottom line is that the Burnham campaign probably does not want to be a source or cause of unnecessary gilt market volatility that might come back to haunt it. These actions are broader and faster-moving than the 2017–18 China measures, but may face heightened legal risk given the courts’ emphasis on statutory text rather than the administration’s interpretation of trade laws. The currently approved UK airport development plans are heavily weighted to the UK South East. This would not necessarily kill the Heathrow project outright, because it already has a policy process under way and the present government has framed the runway as a national growth project. But it would likely make the political sponsorship less secure. A Burnham leadership could reopen the balance between south-east hub capacity and regional connectivity, making Heathrow more vulnerable to delay, tougher economic tests, or a higher burden of proof around national distribution of benefits. The most likely consequence would therefore be a weaker political tailwind rather than an immediate policy reversal. The risk would be compounded if Ed Miliband had greater Treasury influence in a Burnham administration. records.text: 14 Global Economic Weekly | 05 June 2026 Emerging EMEA Tatonga Rusike MLI (UK) South Africa: Fiscal anchors – increasingly a necessity, not a choice Complete report: South Africa Viewpoint: Fiscal anchors – increasingly a necessity, not a choice 01 June 2026 Fiscal cycles: a three-chapter story South Africa has experienced three fiscal cycles over the past 25 years. The first was the golden era pre-GFC, defined by a positive fiscal stance (large primary surpluses), supported by high GDP growth, which led to a decline in debt ratio by close to 15% of GDP. In this phase, South Africa had multiple credit rating upgrades reaching a peak of BBB+ at Fitch and S&P. while Moody’s was a notch higher at A3. The second fiscal phase was post GFC into Covid, characterised by a negative fiscal stance (consistent primary deficits), with modest GDP growth and rising borrowing costs, which led to debt-to-GDP rising to 70% from 25%. Credit downgrades followed from 2012 until 2020 – with a loss of investment grade in 2017 by Fitch and S&P and reaching the lowest level of BB-/stable in 2020. We are now in the third fiscal phase: post-Covid, with a disciplined fiscal stance (large primary surpluses). The improvement in fiscal discipline has been rewarded with declining borrowing costs and the start of upgrades in sovereign ratings for the first time since September 2009. records.text: Fundamental Credit: Utilities Franck Bataille(i) BBI, Paris | Parikshit Budhe(i) Barclays, UK Energy and Water Utilities are core to the political debate As mentioned in the "Economics" section, energy and water are core to the ongoing political debate, with public opinion supporting stronger public control on these strategic sectors. Although the still ongoing UK water turmoil has made it even more topical, this debate around Utilities is a recurrent political theme during general elections. In our view, potential credit headwinds for Utilities are concentrated around three aspects: • Ownership: although some political leaders are mentioning nationalisation as a potential solution, we believe that 'public control' does not necessarily mean nationalisation. As shown by the ownership structure of Manchester Airport, a blend of public and private stakeholders could be an efficient way to ensure stricter public control while keeping alignment and support from private money. The acquisition of a minority stake or the introduction of golden shares could also be ways to ensure stricter public control on privately-owned Utilities. In the meantime, full nationalisation of the Utilities sector would be extremely costly in terms of acquisition cost (under the Regulated Asset Base model, expropriation would need fair compensation) and future investment burden. records.text: 1 The telegraph: Andy Burnham piles pressure on Chancellor Reeves over pub taxes, 13 January 2026 2 FT: Andy Burnham plans to replace business rates with land tax, 2 September, 2015 While credit has so far appeared to shrug off the political risk, the market is not completely immune to the UK political backdrop. From a demand perspective, credit investors remain sensitive to gilt volatility. While higher yields ultimately support credit demand, a disorderly path higher and uncertainty around gilt terminal values can delay buying. On this front, our rates colleagues expect a limited reaction in gilts. They see a muted rally in the event of a Burnham victory, given that yields have already retreated 25bp from the highs, while a Burnham defeat would likely see the gilt market view the position of the PM and Chancellor Reeves as more secure in the near term. Against this backdrop, we would also expect little near-term impact on the the sterling credit market as a whole. Beyond the by-election, the more direct transmission to credit fundamentals comes via growth and funding costs, primarily affecting UK names, particularly cyclicals. Across both IG & HY, UK cyclical premiums over defensives remain compressed and well below levels seen during prior growth shocks. This suggests that current valuations, which entered the period already screening relatively wide to €, are not pricing in any UK-specific growth impacts at this juncture. Where do we go next? As a reminder, we pencil in rate hikes in June and July 2026, 25bp each. Whether the second hike happens in July or September will depend on where energy prices are by then. July needs a sense of urgency. Oil prices close to $90 could delay that hike to September. At the same time, the latest inflation print increases the odds of July if some of the move in services proves not to be temporary. Cuts will need to follow, eventually. Our macro view holds firm: the path to sub-2% inflation is delayed, but all macro ingredients remain in play: a shallow recovery at unspectacular levels, with a very fragile and non-inflationary labour market, suboptimal fiscal policy, and central bank policy that always errs on the tight side. records.text: 3 June 2026 The Wide Angle Page 2 Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. now the only G7 country with a services PMI above 50 following steady improvement from recessionary levels over the past 3 months (Figure 8). n Price pressures The global input price PMIs inched higher in May across both manufacturing and services, following the sharp spike during March- April, while the output price indices stabilised after their earlier rise (Figure 3 and Figure 4). Across DM, May saw some convergence in the composite price PMIs, with US, Canada, France and Japan moving higher from more moderate levels, while the UK and Australia saw some moderation from more extreme levels (Figure 10 and Figure 11). In EM, South Africa saw a larger jump in PMI price pressures following the significant fuel price increases there. China remains a laggard on PMI price pressures despite emerging reflation there. n Price pass-through remains high in manufacturing despite a slight moderation last month, with the beta between the 3-month changes in input and output indices, on average, matching the 2021-22 inflationary period (Figure 17). Countries seeing the sharper goods price shock include the UK and Australia in DM, and Brazil in EM. By contrast, services price pass through has been more moderate, especially in countries that implemented fuel price controls or other material shielding measures (Figure 18). Accommodation and travel most susceptible to local pricing pressures A large empirical literature finds that mega sporting and cultural events generate measurable, but short-lived price increases in hotels, air travel, and related hospitality services, with little evidence of persistence beyond the event window (e.g., Depken and Stephenson, 2018; Baade and Matheson, 2016). These studies typically document limited effects on aggregate macroeconomic outcomes, reflecting crowd-out and expenditure reallocation rather than sustained demand creation. Recent evidence from large concert tours similarly highlights intense, but localized pricing pressure in capacity-constrained services that fades quickly once events conclude7 . These studies also reveal that it matters how geographically widespread the event is. Very concentrated, localized spikes in prices of hotels and restaurants, for example, seldom affect national aggregates in the CPI. Empirical literature finds that mega sporting and cultural events generate measurable, but short-lived, localized price increases in accommodation and travel-related categories. 5 June 2026 7 Barclays | Thematic Investing

Private employment rose 120K and government 52K. We had noted the strong outturn in government as a risk, but this was clearly much stronger than the +5K we pencilled in. The V - shape rise in UST yields during Liberation Day’s “Sell America” and Covid’s “dash - for - cash” was paired with decreasing liquidity and upward pressure on financing costs as dealers became more constrained. Consequently, rising repo rollover and margin risks forced a deleveraging in swap spread trades and cheapened them considerably (see Figure 2 ). Although not our base case, any concerns of a prolonged conflict that worsens oil tanker traffic may induce a perception (or even reality) that investors will continue to sell USTs on inflation worries, leaving swap spreads and funding expectations (SOFR/FF basis) vulnerable. We suggest paying close attention to swap spreads. In that vein, given that swap spreads have traded directionally with risky assets, a further weakness in risky assets can exacerbate a decline in swap spreads, and further compound pressure for rising yields. Additionally, we also suggest keeping an eye on repo markets – where stresses appear contained for now. With steady levels and Fed RMPs and TGA dynamics largely predictable, the asymmetry lies for lower SOFR/FF in the event of further escalation.

Poland’s October 2023 parliamentary elections then brought to power a government ready to address the EU’s concerns and Poland officially regained access to EU funds in February 2024. What followed was a slow pick-up in flows which only accelerated meaningfully late last year. Based on the latest available schedule, flows should rise sharply this year with peak absorption planned for late 2026–early 2027 (Figure 8). Sharp pick-up in flows possible from 2027: Hungary is likely to follow a relatively similar path, we think. The Tisza government is pushing for a rapid re-opening of its full EU funds tab, but even though a formal agreement looks likely before the European Commission summer recess begins, we doubt it would entail a blanket unfreezing of the available funds. We therefore expect an initial delay in flows to allow the establishment of a formal framework, and then a somewhat incremental approach to the re-building of flows. We think money may start to flow this Autumn at the earliest, with the real acceleration likely next year and in 2028. We therefore assume a gradual unlocking of EU funds to the tune of 3.0%-of-GDP per annum starting from Q1 2027. On the following pages we consider what this could mean for Hungary’s macro and market dynamics over the years to come. records.text: Ning Sun 02 June 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Initiate short USDCOP following the first - round election result s Colombia’s first-round presidential result sent a clear message from voters. Hard-right outsider Abelardo De La Espriella won nearly 44% of the vote, ahead of government candidate Iván Cepeda on 41%. Center-right candidate Paloma Valencia took only about 7%, underscoring Colombia’s growing tilt toward more extreme candidates. Despite the tight margin, De La Espriella outperformed market expectations. Consensus had expected him to enter the runoff in second place, but he now goes into the final round from a position of strength. With the center-right vote up for grabs, he is well placed to gain further support ahead of the June 21 runoff. While uncertainty will stay high and the first post-round polls will be key, our base case is increasingly shifting toward a De La Espriella victory. This election is particularly consequential for Colombia. Under the current administration, fiscal discipline has deteriorated, with the deficit running above 7% of GDP and debt levels rising rapidly (Figure 1). At the same time, aggressive minimum wage hikes, 23% this year following a 15% increase last year, are adding to inflationary pressures (Figure 2), especially as economic activity accelerates again this year (Figure 3). records.text: US Economics Weekly5 June 2026 ab 15 The May non-seasonally adjusted change in private employment was +762K basis, relative to +759K last May and +792K in May 2024. The NSA flow was a little larger than last year which could potentially due to the lack of 5-week adjustment and the proximity of the survey reference week to Memorial Day. The sector details shed some light here, with the +70K gain in employment in leisure and hospitality in May displaying similar strength to 2015 (+80K), 2009 (+50K), and 1998 (+57K) — all years with no 5- week adjustment and only one week from Memorial Day. June hiring in the sector was also weaker in all of these years. Meanwhile, the seasonal factor, which we define in the figure below as the difference between the NSA and SA change, was more supportive than recent years taking out -642K jobs this May relative to -739K last May and -747K in May 2024. This could be driven by the lack of 5-week adjustment this May versus the adjustment made in 2024 and 2025. Look at 2015's -650K seasonal factor, with no 5- week adjustment and the same proximity to Memorial Day. records.text: KBC Group (KBC.BR, Buy) Bartel Puelinckx, Chief Financial Officer, presented at our 30th Goldman Sachs European Financials Conference 2026. We highlight the following key takeaways: A supportive overall macroeconomic environment in KBC’s footprint: Management highlighted GDP growth for Central Europe being c.1.5pp higher than Western Europe due to benefits from European subsidies, cost competitiveness with support from foreign direct investment, and increasing disposable income. While GDP is trending at 0.6% for Belgium and Slovakia, inflation stands at 3.2% and 4%, respectively. The Czech Republic continues to be resilient, with Hungary impacted by the energy shock while set to benefit from the release of a tranche of subsidies. Bulgaria is benefitting from the recent € adoption, with real GDP trending at 2.6% and 4% inflation for 2026. Loans continuing to grow, with mortgages the key anchor product in Belgium, and net benefits expected from any ECB rate hikes: Management highlighted mortgages as crucial in the Belgian market, treated as the anchor product, driving notable competition. From a deposit perspective, meanwhile, KBC highlighted the pass-through has been low in Belgium — with future rate increases likely a positive overall, although with possible impacts on the product mix (i.e. a shift into interest-bearing/term products). records.text: Benelux ABN Amro (ABNd.AS, Buy) Marguerite Berard, Chair and Chief Executive Officer, presented at our 30th Goldman Sachs European Financials Conference 2026. We highlight the following key takeaways: Macro backdrop and strategic positioning: Management characterised the Dutch economy as resilient and noted that while the Netherlands continues to outperform the EU (supported by strong labour markets and a solid fiscal position), they are not completely immune to broader geopolitical uncertainties, and they would expect a moderate impact on their growth forecasts for the geography. Against this backdrop, management emphasised that their strategic plan is firmly anchored on self-help levers within the bank’s control including disciplined profitable growth, cost right sizing and active capital steering. Importantly, management reiterated that the assumptions embedded in their strategic plan are conservative. Furthermore, ABN confirmed that profitable growth remains their key priority while also noting that current volume growth trends remain strong across both loans and deposits. On loans, they saw +5% y/y growth in mortgages (despite the mortgage market slowing down) and +3% y/y growth in corporate loans over the past few quarters. Turning to deposits, management highlights that deposit growth has been meaningful in the last few quarters, and looking ahead, expect continued growth. records.text: The momentum behind hybrid debt issuance—which began in early 2024 n following a change to Moody’s rating methodology—has accelerated in 2026. While the elevated pace of year-to-date hybrid supply is especially notable in the EUR market, the USD market is also on track to set a new annual record. The amount of outstanding USD hybrid debt has doubled vs. early 2024. Even so, n hybrid spreads have outperformed both BBBs and BBs since that time. The recent performance of EUR hybrids vs. BBBs has been more range-bound, owing to the more mature stage of the market (and significant outperformance in 2022). For IG-focused investors searching for incremental spread (vs. BBBs), hybrids can n be an attractive solution, as they offer a spread premium to compensate for structural subordination—typically within an IG-rated parent company capital structure—and certain issuer-friendly terms. records.text: Poste Italiane (PST.MI, Not Rated) Matteo Del Fante, Chief Executive Officer, presented at our 30th Goldman Sachs European Financials Conference 2026. We highlight the following key takeaways: Distribution Network. Poste Italiane’s distribution network benefits from a strong competitive advantage because of its sheer size and reach on both digital and physical fronts. Poste’s Super App is often used to initiate sales with customers, which then finalize the purchase in one of Poste’s physical stores. Artificial Intelligence. AI can be thought of as an inside-out tool. On the inside, management thinks that it has already leveraged AI significantly to improve operational performance and lower key metrics such as cost-to-serve (which has been reduced by 30%). The largest opportunity remains on the outside, in leveraging AI to make the most out of Poste’s existing and prospective client base by cross-selling additional products. For example, Poste is confident that it can use its extensive knowledge of tech and AI to improve the operations for the public sector. Poste already has extensive experience in dealing with public sector clients; for instance, it played a key role in developing the infrastructure for the roll-out of the Covid vaccine in Italy. Payout Policy. Poste Italiane is committed to its 70% payout target and does not foresee any change going ahead. SBBs seem less likely given the relatively small size of the free float. On the usual timeline, the assumptions (oil, FX, etc.) conditioning the forecasts would have a cut-off date on 20 May, with the forecast numbers finalized on 27 May. In March, however, the Eurosystem pushed the cut-off dates much closer to the GC meeting, and we think it will be again the case in June. On our baseline, we assume the cut-off for the assumptions will be set on 27 May, with projections numbers finalized by 29 May. Postponing the cut-off date would allow for taking on board the sharp decline of oil prices observed in the second half of May: on 20 May, (dated) brent stood at 109$/bbl, but it dropped to 97$/bbl on 27 May (Exhibit 2 ). We also assume the assumptions will not be the average of the futures observed in the 10 days preceding the cut-off, but only over the three previous days, like in March. UK Politics Making Sense of Makerfield The Makerfield by-election is a near-term catalyst for UK markets, potentially unlocking a Labour leadership challenge. Outcomes remain finely balanced, but fiscal credibility, not politics alone, will be the key driver across rates, equities, and credit. Economics: Polling suggests a knife-edge result, with tactical voting likely decisive. A Burnham win would materially increase the probability of a leadership challenge, with party membership making him the favourite thereafter. Policy signals point to a more interventionist state - greater public control in infrastructure, housing, and services - while still operating within existing fiscal rules. This combination implies limited near-term fiscal space, but a meaningful shift in how capital is deployed, with risks concentrated around execution, costs, and decentralisation of decision-making. Rates: Gilts remain focused on the sequencing of political risk rather than pricing outcomes outright

records.text: M Update 2 Most of the weakness is concentrated in manufacturing. Since 2019, manufacturing value-added has fallen 5% in Germany, compared with a rise of more than 10% in the rest of the euro area. The same divergence is visible in exports and investment: German exports are down 1%, while exports in the euro area ex-Germany are up 15%; German investment has moved sideways, while investment elsewhere is up 3.5%. Clearly, the two are interlinked: companies that are losing export market share will not expand production sites. Even more alarming, the usual “confidence channel” (investments tend to rise following the federal elections) is completely absent this time around. Machinery and equipment investment has been flat since the 1Q25 election, versus an average rise of around 6% in previous cycles and around 9% when elections brought a change in government (see here). Add to that, adverse demographics and lower labor supply will increasingly be a drag, too (see our deep dive here). So where can we find some upside? Fiscal spending remains the clearest bright spot in the near term. Implementation on defence and infrastructure has been slow (see our monthly tracking here), but both areas should accelerate. Defence spending is typically backloaded, and we are likely going to see an acceleration later in the year. And industry experts we met in Berlin shared that view. Additive outflows: We think many of the standalone SpaceX flows might be digestible. The problem is that many of these flows are potentially same-way and additive. Our view is that for SpaceX, retail investors could be the largest swing factor. And if SpaceX is traded in a FOMO style similar to retail trading of Semis, it could create a very fat tail. This would then be amplified by passive investment demand. The number of shares to be bought for passive remains constant post the IPO, but the dollar value rises proportionally to the share price. With the SpaceX free float reported to be close to $75bn on IPO, it’s easy to see how $30bn of passive buying, a retail investor chase, and levered ETF and option flows collectively could quickly become challenging for the stock’s liquidity. If all are chasing to buy (or sell) at the same time, the risk of price dislocation becomes much greater. Massive index selling and blackout: The flip side to SpaceX demand is equity supply. If the USMCA renegotiation proves more prolonged than expected, the BoC may yet need to ease rather than tighten policy if domestic demand weakens further. Further ahead, if the USMCA review is resolved, or if there is at least greater clarity on the likely path, whether that means a deal or a shift to annual reviews, stronger growth should support firmer core inflation and increase the likelihood of hikes. To prevent forced selling of sound assets that are non-compliant purely due to this methodological shift, a "grandfather clause" has been introduced. Insurers can apply to retain these positions, smoothing the transition. Relaxation: Easier offshore capital raising . Rules governing overseas Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs), which insurers use to issue capital instruments, have been eased. These SPVs will no longer be assessed using the restrictive financial criteria meant for general investments. This is a credit-positive development for weaker-capitalised insurers needing to raise capital under the new TW-ICS regime. Tightening: Credit floor on foreign government bonds. Previously there was no credit rating floor on foreign sovereign bonds. The amendment changes that: insurers may only make new investments in foreign government bonds rated BBB- or above. The industry as of March holds TWD2.9tn in foreign sovereign bonds (~8% of total asset), of which ~ TWD374bn — ~ 13% of foreign bonds and ~1% of total assets— sits below BBB-. Existing holdings are grandfathered; there is no forced disposal. The FSC has also signalled quarterly disclosure of country-level sovereign exposure, bringing it in line with how financial holding companies already report. Implications on TWD. Either way, the staff expects the growth hit to be temporary, with growth already recovering in 3Q26 as the sequential drag from higher energy prices fades. In other words, the downside surprise in the growth data is not currently very large, with recent surprises also relating to Irish noise. The surprise has been much bigger on inflation. Core inflation jumped to 2.5%oya in May. It is not yet clear if this reflects stronger-than-expected pre-war momentum, a holiday distortion in May or stronger indirect effects from energy prices. Nevertheless, surveys of corporate pricing have increased sharply. This makes the March baseline for core inflation running at 2.2%oya through year-end too low. Admittedly, the flash HICP report for May came after the cut-off, but upward pressure was already building. The wage data remain more benign, but they tend to respond with a lag to higher headline inflation. The latter is likely to run above 3%oya through year-end rather than starting to moderate already in 3Q26 as projected by the March baseline. The medium-term drag from weaker near-term growth will likely be seen as modest, in line with the standard macro models and assuming that growth recovers (as projected). Although monthly injections have risen from the lows of early May, they remain below the long-term trend line, leaving considerable headroom for MXN cash demand to grow and for the basis to move higher. The markedly lower MXN FX carry and external volatility tied to the Middle East conflict have trimmed the heavy long MXN positions that the market previously held for carry-seeking purposes (Figure 2). Consequently, the likely absence of heavy rolling of MXN long positions removes the main force that compressed the basis in recent months. Moreover, with far more attractive FX carry available in BRL and COP, the market would need a significant incentive to rebuild substantial MXN long positions in the near term. This backdrop should further support an upside bias for the MXN basis. Receiving long-end basis due to upside USDMXN risk: We like to pair our front-end basis payer with a long-end basis receiver, reflecting external market volatility and the possibility of another MXN sell-off. In fact, the 10y MXN basis responded more strongly to USDMXN movements than the 2y basis over recent weeks amid uncertainty surrounding the Middle East outlook and volatile oil prices. Since 2025, China has built up its oil reserves by importing ~10% higher (~1mbpd) than its normal consumption level, making the pre-conflict bench- mark inflated by stockpiling needs. That said, China has still reduced crude throughput, as seen in the drop in refiners’ run rates for cost considerations. Refin- ers’ margins have turned negative due to state price controls on oil products, leaving refiners little incentive to keep opera- tions running at a high utilization level and making losses (Figure 2).While this has reduced refined product output, the downstream effects appear to have been limited so far. In chemicals, higher oil prices have made the coal-to-chemical route more cost-competitive. Coke oven operating rates have picked up (Figure 2), providing an alternative to oil-based chemical feedstocks, at least partially. Potential drawdowns of commercial inventories across different layers of the extended petrochemical supply chain also help cushion disruptions, reducing the risk of a larger, more immediate shock. The substitution effect is most visible in transport, which accounts for roughly half of oil product uses. In this context, the NEC offers limited support, as it does not affect the criteria for exiting EDP. It can help countries avoid entering EDP by allowing deficits to temporarily exceed 3% of GDP, provided that the excess is covered under the NEC. However, this mechanism does not work in reverse: once a country is in EDP, the NEC does not remove the requirement to bring the deficit back below 3%. This interpretation is consistent with the Council Regulation governing the abrogation of EDP (see here and here), which states: “A Council decision shall only be taken pursuant to Article 126(12) TFEU where the deficit has been brought below the reference value and is projected by the Commission to remain so in the current and following year and, where the excessive deficit procedure was opened on the basis of the debt criterion, the Member State concerned has respected the corrective net expenditure path set by the Council.”

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Special Focus: 5s10s France-Germany Auction Strategy Pauses in 2026 As we approach the mid-year mark we take a look at the performance of a popular auction-based strategy, the 5s10s France-Germany box. The strategy has not worked so far this year, but we have seen sideways periods similar to 2026 in the past (Exhibit 6 ). The split in the auction schedule in France is very neat: the standard is a long auction (10y and longer) the first Thursday of the month, followed by a shorter auction (3y, 5y, off the runs) the third Thursday of the month. The auction strategy can therefore constructed as: short 5y France in the 5s10s box vs Germany the day before or the day of the long auction and do opposite (long 5y) the day before or the day of the short auction. Exhibit 7 shows more details on the two sides of the trade and the performance by year. Historically, the strategy from the long to the short auction has a better performance, but this year’s performance has lagged relative to prior years. The performance of the strategy from the short auction to the long auction the following month has improved over time, but has also underperformed in 2026. records.text: This point is reinforced by evidence that productivity growth is poised to cool from last year’s pace. While undercutting the AI-productivity thesis, we see the alternative playing out now as more sustainable in that it will provide the needed fuel for continued growth in household spending without a further drawdown in saving rates. Growth will deliver jobs, but there remain risks to our projec- tion for growth resilience in the face of the energy supply shock. Western Europe’s disappointment highlights the poten- tial for divergent regional outcomes, while the absence of a deal to open the Strait of Hormuz risks prompting another sharp rise in prices. Next week, the US is expected to report a 0.5% m/m CPI rise, reinforcing the message that a significant drag on household purchasing power is not yet fully absorbed. The Fed to lean, the ECB and BoJ to hike We have anticipated that the combination of a cyclical lift alongside sticky and elevated inflation would prompt the Fed to hike by sometime in the coming year. LLC US Daily: Wealth Effects on Consumption Growth: AI Leads the Way 4 June 2026 | 10:35AM EDT With the S&P 500 up 27% year-on-year and home prices rising just 1%, equity n gains have been the dominant driver of household wealth accumulation and the main contributor to a positive “wealth effect” on consumer spending. Much of the rally over the past few years and about 70% over the past year has come from the outperformance of AI infrastructure providers. We estimate that wealth effects boosted annualized consumption growth by n 0.3pp on average over the past couple of years, with roughly 0.2pp of these effects attributable to AI-related equity gains. Looking ahead, we expect wealth effects to boost consumption by 0.4pp over the next year, driven predominantly by recent outperformance in AI-related stocks. The rising concentration of AI infrastructure providers in the equity market n means that wealth effects are unusually sensitive to the performance of a narrow set of companies. In an upside scenario in which AI-related stocks grow by 55% and other stocks grow by 20% over the next year (implying a 30% overall increase), wealth effects would boost consumption growth by 0.7pp. In a downside scenario in which AI-related stocks decline by 40% and other stocks decline by 15% (implying a 20% overall decline), wealth effects would turn into a 0.3pp drag on consumption growth. records.text: We have left our terminal rate forecast unchanged at 3-3.25%, though we continue to have mixed feelings about this forecast. We have long argued both that that the funds rate ought to remain somewhat above the long-run neutral rate when the fiscal stance and broader financial conditions are unusually easy, and that the true neutral rate is somewhat fuzzy, which leaves room for policymaker perceptions to matter. While we therefore see a case for leaving the funds rate unchanged, the FOMC’s longer-run dots have remained quite stable over the past year, and most participants still describe the policy stance as mildly restrictive and envision further normalization once inflation comes down. A longer pause, however, would provide more time for solid economic performance to convince FOMC participants that the funds rate is already in an appropriate place. And the argument that unusually strong investment demand for artificial intelligence calls for a higher funds rate, at least for now, could gain greater traction. As a result, we see a flat path as a plausible alternative to our baseline. We now put a higher 20% probability (vs. 10% previously) on modest rate hikes, an unchanged 25% probability on a flat path, a lower 30% probability (vs. 40% previously) on our baseline of two additional 25bp cuts next year, and an unchanged 25% probability on a recession and large cuts over the next year. records.text: US Rates Weekly 05 June 2026 Citi Research 16 A similar bearish bias also exists for EUR short-dated swaption vol, where EUR 3m10y implied vol has also cheapened by 5 normals on average over the month of the past five tournaments since 2006 (Figure 29) versus 2.3 normals of cheapening on average over the comparable period (mid-June through mid-July since 2005) for the years without the tournament (Figure 31). Admittedly, the median change in EUR 3m10y vol for the observations during the football tournament matches the median change for the non-tournament observations, which reflects a less pronounced bearish vol bias than the one seen for US rates vol. The observable calm in the market goes beyond just rates and can also be found in FX. For example, EURUSD 3m vol has cheapened by 0.7% on average during the tournament (Figure 30) versus only 0.4% of cheapening on average over the comparable period (mid-June through mid-July since 2005) for years with no Global Football T ournament (Figure 31). 11 Fig. 25: Headline PPI inflation versus benchmark deposit rate Not an inflation-targeting regime: The People’s Bank of China has multiple mandates rather than running an inflation-targeting regime: economic growth, inflation, employment, balance of payments and financial stability. When these mandates conflict with each other, the PBoC’s conduct is highly discretionary, with its policy depending on its assessment of which mandate is the most important at the time (see People’s Bank of China primer: Monetary policy, FX and rates management ,dated 27 January 2025). For instance, when an external or internal shock threatens China’s economic and financial stability, the PBoC pushes inflation to the back burner. Precedents include the 2008 Global Financial Crisis and the 2020–22 pandemic, when the PBoC responded with substantial interest rate cuts even though inflation was above its desired range. PPI appears more important than CPI: Since 2012, monetary policy has been more responsive to PPI inflation, rather than to CPI inflation, although the government has set a CPI target every year since 2005.The target has acted more as a ceiling than as the authorities’ desired rate. Therefore, the target has varied from year to year, ranging from 2% to 4.8% y/y over the past two decades, depending on the government’s assessment of the inflationary pressures for each year. Back in March, the ECB HICP projection was reasonably close to the market-implied path at the time (albeit that is for ex-tobacco rather than headline). Between the March and likely June cut- offs, the market-implied path has shifted higher by about 0.6/0.7 /0.2%pts for 2026/27 /28 respectively, with above-target inflation lasting until mid-2028 – Figure 3. The ECB HICP projections may rise by a similar amount but should be below the 4%+ peak in the adverse scenario (thanks to unchanged natural gas). records.text: If all are chasing to buy (or sell) at the same time, the risk of price dislocation becomes much greater. Massive index selling and blackout: The flip side to SpaceX demand is equity supply. Our expectation is that the retail and passive flows will be mostly financed by selling other stocks. Passive selling flows have a short SpaceX cross-gamma component. If SpaceX stock doubles (or halves), those flows also double (or half). We could hypothesize that retail and passive investors together might sell $50bn of other stocks to raise funds for SpaceX. If the IPO’s performance is very strong, those numbers could rise. If some of that selling is in levered ETFs, this produces a disproportionate market delta to be sold. In turn, this can weigh on the underlying and trigger more mechanical rebalance selling. If flows take the market lower, there is also the risk of CTAs (back to 80/100 in equity leverage) also starting selling. The passive equity selling flows related to SpaceX fall very close to quarter end. Unrelated to the SpaceX IPO, given the large QTD US equity outperformance, we estimate Q2 quarter-end might see a massive >$100bn US equity selling flow. The danger for the market is not the individual flows, but the cumulative effect. According to the methodology, iBoxx EUR Covered includes "bonds which are secured by a general pool of assets in case the issuer becomes insolvent, in particular bonds conforming to the criteria specified in UCITS 22.4 or similar directives, e.g. CAD III. In addition, bonds with a structure affording an equivalent risk and credit profile that are considered by the market as covered bonds are also included in the iBoxx Covered Bond Indices. The criteria taken into account in evaluating the status of a bond will be the structure, trading patterns, issuance process, liquidity and spread levels." The lack of a specific CB framework for ESN should not be a hurdle for ESN to be included in iBoxx EUR Covered.
