records.text: Japan Macro Watch5 June 2026 ab 2 Ueda signals a green light for a June rate hike Governor Ueda’s speech on Wednesday was broadly hawkish, containing remarks supportive of a rate hike in June. He pointed out that the Japanese economy remains resilient: corporate profits are strong, wage increases are robust, and firms are making progress in diversifying procurement away from Middle East–dependent raw materials. As a result, downside risks to economic activity are likely to remain limited. On the price front, however, the pace of pass-through has accelerated and price increases are spreading across a wider range of goods. This raises the risk that underlying inflation could overshoot. Overall, he emphasized that upside risks to inflation are greater—and likely to materialize sooner—than downside risks to growth. Against this backdrop, he stated that “it will be necessary to thoroughly discuss the pros and cons of raising the policy interest rate, from the perspective of preventing adverse effects on the economy and financial markets and achieving the price stability target of 2 percent in a sustainable and stable manner.” This closely mirrors the language he used just prior to the January rate hike (“At the MPM, the Bank will examine and discuss economic activity and prices at home and abroad as well as developments in financial and capital markets, including the point I just mentioned, based on various data and information, and will consider the pros and cons of raising the p

LLC US Daily: No Fed Cuts This Year 5 June 2026 | 5:20PM EDT We are pushing the final two rate cuts in our Fed forecast back to June and n December of 2027. The labor market has been stronger than we anticipated, and we now expect the unemployment rate to rise only a touch further to 4.4%, not enough to create a sense of urgency to lower rates. As a result, we think the most natural path for the FOMC is to delay further cuts until the effects of tariffs, the war, and AI demand have faded and core PCE inflation nears 2%. We continue to see rate hikes as unlikely, though somewhat more likely than we n initially thought. Fed commentary has turned more hawkish, and the resilient activity and employment data lower the bar for a hike. But we have not yet seen signs that the inflation shock from the war is broadening out, and with the labor market in balance and wage growth running below the rate compatible with 2% inflation, the inflation shock looks less likely to become self-sustaining. We have left our terminal rate forecast at 3-3.25%, largely because the FOMC’s n longer-run dots have been stable over the past year and most participants envision further normalization. But a longer pause provides more time for solid economic performance to convince them that the funds rate is already in an appropriate place, and we see a flat path as a plausible alternative. In the absence of hard evidence of second-round effects and amidst the heightened uncertainty, this move is predominantly meant to mitigate the risk of de-anchoring inflation expectations. The policy paragraph of the statement, featuring data dependence and a meeting-by-meeting approach, should remain unchanged. The Council will want to keep all options on the table, stressing again the high level of uncertainty, the need for vigilance, and its readiness to act. In particular, we expect that the ECB will seek further confirmation on the inflation path ahead. As long as inflation expectations remain anchored, there is a strong case for a gradual and controlled trajectory, and we see the next hike in September. We think a more rapid tightening cycle would need an entirely different assessment of the risks, with two ingredients. Page 2 inflation, uptrend in rates? ”, continues to show limited progress toward target with median and mean estimates still clustered around the low 3% range. This is consistent with our broader thematic work highlighting that inflation pressures remain unusually broad - based across goods and services and are not confined to a narrow set of categories, limiting the extent to which the Fed can rely on passive disinflation (see “What's keeping inflation above 2%? Almost everything”). In short, while our baseline remains that the Fed is on hold near neutral indefinitely (see “World Outlook: 1999 meets 1990 “), hawkish-leaning officials such as Dallas’s Logan and Cleveland’s Hammack have been highlighting the possibility that monetary tightening may be required if current trends persist. Indeed, as inflation risks rise and labor market risks recede, Fed policy may have become overinsured against downside risks to the labor market and prospects for future rate hikes might best be interpreted as a prudent reversal of this insurance as the balance of risks tilts towards inflation (see “Fed Notes: Overinsured?”). records.text: 303/06/2026 Severe strain on balance from Gulf losses Global losses already close to an annualised 2.3 Mt: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz since late February has limited the inflow of aluminium to smelters in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Qatar, prompting production cuts from ALBA, EGA and Qatalum. In addition, there have been Iranian drone and missile attacks on EGA’s 1.5 Mt/year Al Taweelah smelter and ALBA’s 1.6 Mt/year smelter, with the former shut down completely. We now estimate a deficit of c.2.6 Mt this year, a figure that is likely to grow the longer the shipping disruption lasts. Slow Indonesia smelter growth redirecting Chinese investment: Progress on three new Chinese-financed smelters in Indonesia has been much slower than the time scales normal in China: only the Tsingshan/Xinfa JV Kemajuan plant is operating ; Adaro starts later this year, and Nanshan not until end-2027. The slow pace appears to be prompting Chinese companies to increase investment elsewhere, such as in Angola and Saudi Arabia. While the small (120 kt/yr) Angola-based Huatong smelter should start in H2 2026, we do not see the Shandong Innovation Group’s 500 kt project in Yanbu, Saudi Arabia, being in production before 2029. Sceptical on US smelter capacity growth: The main aim of the 50% section 232 tariffs on US primary aluminium imports was to incentivise the development of domestic smelting capacity. This past week, USTR Greer announced that the US would seek to incorpo- rate much higher requirements for rules of origin on vehicles as part of the renegotiation. Currently the USMCA has a 75% regional value content requirement (up from 62.5% under NAFTA), along with a 40% share of labor value content (pro- vided by workers making at least $16/hr). By July 2027, 70% of the steel and aluminum used in a vehicle must also be sourced from North America. Greer proposed raising the regional content requirement to 82%, with 50% of that value produced by high-wage workers. The goal of these proposed changes is to shift as much auto production into the US as possible. The higher labor value content requirements have been applauded by US labor unions. US auto producers want more clarity on the rules, and have suggested they could comply if given enough lead time. However, a number of lower-cost models are assembled in Mexico, and it would neither be cost effective to increase the US (or Canadian) labor value content nor to move production to the US. US auto dealers have complained about the conse- quences for affordability. How much the Trump administration is willing to bargain over these proposals remains to be seen. records.text: 6 Fig. 11: Inflation during recent rounds of PPI reflation* Sources : China’ s National Bureau of Statistics, CEIC, BNP Paribas Mild pass-through is not new: A common concern is that downstream firms cannot raise prices enough to offset higher input costs when domestic demand is weak. If downstream demand drops further because of profit erosion, price gains in mid and upstream industries could evaporate eventually. Historical data shows that the concern is largely unfounded. During the major PPI reflation episodes of the past decade, upstream price increases translated only modestly into downstream inflation. Evidence from National Bureau of Statistics: From 2000 to 2015, a 10% rise in the producer-goods component of the PPI lifted the consumer-goods PPI inflation by about 2%. After 2016, the coefficient has weakened substantially: now a 10% jump in producer-goods prices adds just 0.7% to consumer -goods prices. Producer goods still dominate the basket (with about a 75% weight), so they can drive a sustained PPI reflation even with limited downstream pass -through. Sector-level patterns: In both recent reflation cycles, mining led the price surge, followed by raw materials and processing (Figure 11). Consumer-goods prices rose only in low single digits, while durable-goods prices continued to fall. We now project demand declines of 3.0 and 4.2 mbd year-over-year, respectively, corresponding to demand destruction of 4.9 and 5.6 mbd (Figures 10 & 11). That said, the picture is not uniformly gloomy across products. Demand for petrochemical feedstocks in the Middle East is showing signs of a rebound, with ethylene capacity recovering 50% from the April lows despite ongoing risks from drone and missile attacks. Jet fuel has also proven relatively resilient: although global flights have tracked 1.5% weaker year-over-year since late April, a feared wave of cancelations has so far failed to materialize. This resilience has been underpinned by strong activity in the US and by Europe, where higher jet imports and inventory draws have provided additional support. Simultaneously, the Price Law and the Anti-Unfair Competition Law were amended to outlaw predatory price wars, with maximum fines set at 10 times the relevant sales revenue. Since then, regulators have issued guidance across agriculture, manufacturing and services that ban sales below cost, restricts excessive subsidies, encourages industry self-discipline to trim excess capacity, and tightens approval of new capex projects . The policy thrust signals that the authorities view irrational price wars as a key driver of China’s entrenched deflation. Even in markets where demand and supply are roughly balanced, firms have still slashed prices to chase market share, eroding profitability and depressing share prices. Businesses appear to agree. In the EV sector, rapid sales volume growth beginning in 2021 has been offset by sharp price cuts that turned many carmakers unprofitable, contributing to PPI deflation. Avatr CEO Hui Wang summed it up: sales volume without profit is illusory; scale achieved through price wars is false prosperity. records.text: No Fed Cuts This Year We are pushing the final two rate cuts in our Fed forecast back to June and December of 2027 (vs. December 2026 and March 2027 previously). The activity and labor market data have been stronger than we anticipated in recent months, with job growth in particular picking up impressively in recent months. While we still expect somewhat below-potential GDP growth in the second half of this year as high oil prices weigh on spending, we now expect the unemployment rate to rise only a touch further to 4.4% this year (vs. 4.6% previously), not enough to create a sense of urgency to lower the funds rate. As a result, we now think that the most natural path for the FOMC is to delay further cuts until tariff passthrough, higher oil prices and other effects of the war, and the (mismeasured and overstated) effects of AI demand have faded and year-over-year core PCE inflation is closer to the 2% target. While tariff effects should begin to fade soon, the combined impact of these three forces is likely to remain roughly steady this year, keeping year-over-year core PCE inflation at 3%+ throughout 2026. Fundamental drivers of inflation still look softer. Wage growth is running ½pp below the rate that we estimate is compatible with 2% inflation, and leading indicators of rent growth remain very low. records.text: s . The 2023–25 period when China exported deflation corresponded to significant weakening of the RMB (Figure 20). However, the RMB has modestly appreciated in recent months, and we expect USDRMB to reach 6.7 by year-end from 6.78 now (see Corporate Market Monthly – May,dated 12 May 2026), mildly lifting export prices . The export-price rise has been uneven across product groups. The export prices in mid and upstream sectors have almost tracked the PPI. In April, the export prices of refined oil products surged the most, by 29.9% y/y, while fertilizers, non-ferrous-metal goods and automatic data processing equipment (mostly AI-related hardware) posted double-digit gains. By contrast, consumer-goods exports remain under pressure; apparel and footwear export prices fell 6.8% y/y and 8.2% y/y, respectively. In sum, China is moving from a period of export-price deflation to one of modest export-price inflation. The shift reflects healthier domestic pricing, a slightly stronger RMB, and a differentiated impact across industrysegments . records.text: ING Group (INGA.AS, Buy) Ida Lerner, Chief Financial Officer, presented at our 30th Goldman Sachs European Financials Conference 2026. We highlight the following key takeaways: Business performance and operating trends: The CFO highlighted a strong start of the year in Q1 across both Retail and Wholesale Banking, underpinned by healthy customer activity and disciplined execution. On the retail side, performance was supported by solid mortgage growth and continued deposit inflows at lower deposit costs than what they had done historically. On the WB side, they were able to deliver loan growth alongside no growth in RWAs, supported by their clear focus on capital optimisation while also witnessing an uptick in payments and cash management deposits. Liability margin outlook: The liability margin is expected to remain within the guided 100–110bps range in the near term, with management pointing to mid-range outcome for 2026. Beyond this, for 2027/28E, they expect potential for liability margins to temporarily exceed 110bps, given their portfolio composition (with majority share being savings accounts) and the customer and competitive behavior. The CFO notes that they take a conservative stance given historical competitive dynamics, especially related to savings accounts and do not cap the liability margin at 110bps. We close the trade idea we opened in FX: Adding short THBKRW 3m NDF on 12 March for a loss of 2.02% (USD 101k). At the time, we were bullish on the KRW and expected fundamentals and flows to prove supportive for the currency . The view initially played out – the current account balance has increased significantly and growth has beaten expectations, prompting in turn a hawkish shift from the Bank of Korea, from which we now expect two hikes this year (see Bank of Korea: Hawkish signals likely to lead to a rate hike in July, dated 28 May). Also, some flows have turned more supportive. Foreign bond inflows have followed the inclusion of KTBs in the WGBI index, while domestic retail investor outflows have cooled (Figure 1), and their investment into local assets has increased (Figure 2). records.text: lds . Parallels to Liberation Day: There are emerging parallels to post Liberation day price action in Treasuries, where long-end USTs dealt with a self reinforcing rise in yields. Here’s how it played out : (1) Stage 1 – the “flight to quality” knee jerk: Markets deal with an inflation/stagflation shock (tariffs in 2025, geopolitical escalation in 2026). The initial reaction in rates around Liberation day was a rally, but quicky turned to a selloff – as the inflation impact started to weigh (recall Powell delivered hawkish remarks right after Liberation day) - see Figure 1 (3) Stage 2 -- the reversal and the exacerbation: the selloff in April 2025 became self-reinforcing based on positioning excesses and a narrative. The narrative was overseas selling of Treasuries amid a less dovish Fed, exacerbated by swap spread unwinds and basis trade deleveraging. There is a parallel from March 2020 too - where the initial rally turned into a “dash for cash” and resulted in a sharp rise in yields. In both instances - yields did not move lower amid rising risks, lowering the “flight to quality” perception of Treasuries. Two narratives can drive higher yields currently - (1) further escalation continues, and markets keeps pricing out Fed rate cuts, or (2) concerns on deficits start to rise as investors think about a higher defense budget in the US. The exacerbation potential remains with swap spread longs and basis trade unwinds.

records.text: up 2026: Viewership drives value The World Cup will drive visible but transient macro effects, with boosts to local spending and pricing unlikely to have a lasting impact on inflation or policy. In equities, we focus on the viewership opportunity, given its scale, reach, and potential to drive more durable company-level outcomes. Ahead of kick-off, we take a closer look at the World Cup to assess the real economic and equity implications. While the tournament will be the largest in history, our view is that it will not be a game changer for the macro environment or most companies. • Macro view – Not a game changer for growth, employment or inflation. The 2026 FIFA World Cup should provide a modest, temporary summer lift to US GDP of about 0.2%, with effects wearing off in subsequent quarters, with no perceptible effect on the level of GDP at year-end. Any employment gains are likely to be localized, short-lived, and concentrated in services. Stuck in a decade-long growth trap What is still elusive is strong economic growth. For many years since the Global Financial Crisis, South Africa has struggled to grow the economy at a high pace. But our GDP nowcasting work shows a structural break in 2026 – economic growth has slowed to around a 1% average and has so far been unable to escape this low-growth trap. Structurally lower real GDP growth translates into lower nominal GDP growth. The shift to a lower inflation target in mid-2025 also implies lower nominal GDP growth, while the energy shock presents further downside risks. This suggests nominal GDP growth is likely to be in the 4-5% range over the medium term, compared with historical highs of close to 7%. That is a clear constraint on debt metrics and could further widen the gap between borrowing costs and growth (r-g), which requires a much larger primary surplus to stabilise debt. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 206/03/2026 The V-shape rises in Treasury yields during Liberation Day’s “Sell America” episode and Covid’s “dash for cash” were paired with decreasing liquidity and upward pressure on financing costs as dealers became more constrained. Consequently, rising repo rollover and margin risks forced a deleveraging in swap spread trades and cheapened them considerably (Figure 2). Although not our base case, any concerns about a prolonged conflict that reduces energy shipping traffic may induce a perception (or even a reality) that investors will continue to sell Treasuries on inflation worries, leaving swap spreads and funding expectations (SOFR/FF basis) vulnerable. We suggest paying close attention to swap spreads. In that vein, given that swap spreads have traded directionally with risky assets, further weakness in risky assets can worsen a decline in swap spreads and further compound pressure for rising yields. Additionally, we also suggest keeping an eye on repo markets, where stresses appear contained for now. With steady levels and Fed RMPs and TGA dynamics largely predictable, the asymmetry lies for lower SOFR/FF in the event of further escalation. What to watch out for? This analysis sets out why we think markets have already adopted, and should continue to adopt, a steadily more positive structural macro narrative around Hungary’s economy – see Hungary: Election tailwinds for capital flows and HUF, dated 14 April and EM rates: The case for HUF receivers, dated 20 April. It’s all about investment, flows and animal spirits: Boosting investment and addressing the absorption of EU fund inflows into the economy will likely be a top priority for the new government. Hungary’s fixed-investment-to- GDP ratio has fallen 4.0pp from the level seen before the 2007–2008 global financial crisis – and has been a major drag on growth potential. The economy has averaged a negative output gap annually over the past 15 years (Figure 1). This note provides a framework to quantify what a positive investment shock, alongside a sustained sentiment boost, would mean for future growth potential, fiscal policy, inflation and, ultimately, HUF term premia and FX performance. records.text: 12 Two critical thresholds for PPI inflation: We believe the PBoC judges PPI inflation below zero as too low and above 5% as too high. Persistent PPI deflation has always corresponded to rate-cutting cycles, such as the 2012 –15 cycle, and the more recent 2023–25 cycle. By contrast, PPI inflation accelerating above 5% usually triggered monetary tightening . For instance, the PBoC raised the 7d reverse repo rate four times in the last rate-hiking cycle from 2017 to early 2018, when CPI inflation fluctuated in a 1–2% y/y range and PPI inflation topped 5% y/y (Figures 27 and 28). Policy rate probably on hold this year: The shift from entrenched deflation to mild reflation, together with a lower growth target, reduces the need for additional monetary easing. Meanwhile, banks’ net interest margin fell to 1.4% in Q1, below the PBoC’s ‘red line’ of 1.8%, raising the bar for additional rate cuts from a financial- stability perspective. Therefore, although the PBoC still maintains an appropriately loose policy stance, we expect it to keep the policy rate unchanged this year (see China : A good start, dated 16 April 2026). Monetary tightening may require a property recovery: As the economy still faces downward pressure, we acknowledge that the next policy rate move is more likely to be a cut rather than a hike. J-curve effect: Stripping out the net trade channel (Figure 9) points to such an appreciation being virtually GDP-neutral in the short run but weighing on growth from H2 2027. The so-called ‘J-curve’ helps explain this. We estimate it can take around one quarter for foreign exporters to adjust (higher) the foreign-currency price charged to Hungarian importers (to capture part of the HUF appreciation into their profits), and another quarter for those importers to tweak their own demand (import volume) accordingly. A full adjustment may require the renegotiation of supply-chain contracts and realignment of local inventory and production capacity. We also note that Hungary’s exports do not adjust immediately to competitiveness losses. Eventually, the trade balance (in volume terms) deteriorates, weighing on real GDP. Key domestic investors like banks are constrained by regulations and prefer shorter- duration assets, while insurers and wealth management products are rotating into equities, leading to moderate demand. This mismatch between heavy long-end supply and softer duration demand is expected to put upward pressure on yields. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Oil Tracker: US ending stocks of crude oil edge lower amid increased exports and unchanged production We continue to track the evolution of inventory and production amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. US ending inventory stocks of crude oil and petroleum products, which represents the EIA's estimate of how many barrels of oil and petroleum products are physically sitting in US storage at period end, continue to move lower. Inclusive of the SPR, inventory stocks are falling by about 2mn barrels a day. The spot price of oil for immediate purchase and delivery in the physical market remains elevated, despite futures prices moving lower on prospects for a near-term agreement between the US and Iran. US domestic crude production has edged modestly higher in recent weeks, but it remains about in line with pre-conflict production. Net imports of oil (imports - exports) are declining because of increased oil exports. Because the EU has no paid-in capital, Moody’s uses the MS' shares in EU budget contributions as weights to calculate the weighted average shareholder rating (WASR) of “a1”. The EU’s WASR at Moody’s is one notch above the “Aaa”-median for supranationals of “a2” and somewhat resilient to singular downgrades. Moody’s highlights that it would require a downgrade of France and a two-notch downgrade of Germany for example to change the weighted average shareholder rating (WASR) of the EU to “a2” from "a1" currently. In the scorecard regarding the EU rating, Moody’s starts with a “A1” regarding "ability to support". Hence, without a downgrade of the WASR to “a2”, a downgrade of the EU seems unlikely, at least if EU cohesion and EU funding conditions do not deteriorate significantly. In our view, with budgets of most EU MS remaining under pressure, if anything, we expect more EU cohesion going forward. Overall, we expect the EU to remain rated Aaa at Moody’s in 2026 and 2027. We think the simple framework we have been using throughout the energy shock offers a useful playbook for deescalation in FX markets. Many of our preferred longs in recent months have been procyclical currencies that are net energy exporters (including AUD and BRL), and while risk-sentiment should remain firmly supported on a resolution and keep procyclical currencies bid, the terms of trade dimension of the shock should reverse. Along these two axes, we think the candidate outperformers on a resolution would rotate from high-beta energy exporters (the upper-right quadrant of Exhibit 2) to high-beta energy importers (the lower-right quadrant). We see ZAR, KRW, PLN, CLP , and HUF as the most likely beneficiaries in EM space, with recent HUF outperformance on the EU convergence trade an unlikely barrier to further gains from energy relief in our view, though continued equity outflows in Korea would likely undermine the resolution boost for KRW. In G10 space, we see SEK, NZD, and GBP as the top candidate resolution longs under this framework. Overlaying the potential terms of trade reversal with domestic macro and valuation factors remains key in our view though, and is a reason why we see greater value in targeting a reversal in AUD/NZD versus in NOK/SEK for instance, and why we remain constructive HUF even without a resolution. IB returns and capital discipline: Management noted that Q1 reflected the 8th consecutive quarter of positive operating jaws within the IB, attributing this to its targeted investments, including diversification within Markets (notably via Equity Derivatives, vs the franchise’s historically FICC-heavy mix), as well as continued diversification in Banking (into the relatively capital-light ECM/M&A channels, beyond just DCM), alongside ongoing growth in US-denominated deposits supported by the treasury coverage model. Management also noted that the c.£200bn pool of total RWA allocated to the IB remains dynamic, including flexibility for the business to reallocate opportunistically across products. At the time of the announcement, the minister of mines noted that "other minerals would be added to the DR Congo’s reserve based on an expanded definition of strategic minerals", which only included cobalt, coltan and germanium, as set in a 2018 decree. Since then, lithium, tantalum, niobium, tungsten, uranium and rare earths have been added to the country's strategic minerals list (mining.com). This brings higher royalties for mining these metals (10% versus 3.5%) but could also mean they are stockpiled in the future. The DRC is the largest tantalum producer, and is becoming a more important lithium producer with the ramp up of Manono. We think that a good part of the strength in leisure and hospitality could stem from the early timing of Memorial Day this year. It’s possible some of it also reflects early hiring for the World Cup, though the data don’t make a strong case for that. Memorial Day can fall anywhere between the 25th and 31st of the month. The establishment survey counts a person as employed if they are paid for any part of the payroll period that includes the 12th of the month. Thus an earlier holiday creates more opportunities to get hired in time to be counted in May payrolls. In theory this should be picked up by the seasonal adjustment process. However, a comparison of May leisure and hospitality job growth relative to the trailing three-month average suggests that when Memorial Day falls on the 25th, as was the case in 2026, then job growth runs above the trend (Figure 1). records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General SPOTLIGHT FX VIEWS Bad Carry vs. Good Carry. We have favored EM carry strategies this year, as both implied and realized volatility have retraced well below long -term averages and EM inflation dynamics remain contained relative to DM, supported in part by fuel subsidies. However, carry is no longer a uniform beta trade —idiosyncratic fundamentals are increasingly driving differentiation, and yet real money has broadly sold off most EM carry currencies despite clear divergence between the asset class (Figure 2). We continue to favor “good carry” currencies with strong macro backdrops. In Hungary, a combination of resilient exports, supportive real rate differentials, and a narrowing current account has underpinned performance, while improving domestic demand following a market -friendly election outcome suggests HUF may still be early in a broader appreciation cycle. In BRL, stronger terms of trade and a credibl e hawkish central bank offset near -term political noise, keeping us comfortable with a short USDBRL bias. We also added a short USDCOP trade , with election clarity reducing uncertainty and scope for policy normalization to compress risk premia further. Here's why: Match ticket prices will NOT be included in the CPI While exorbitant match ticket prices are making headlines, these will NOT make it into the CPI sample. Indeed, the BLS manual (and this blog) states that for a venue ticket to be priced in the CPI, a similar event has to have been held in the prior months. As a result, the CPI program does not include play-offs, the Olympics or FIFA world cup ticket prices. The BLS also confirmed this was the case in an email response to our query8 . Special train services to stadiums will likely be excluded from the CPI There are special train services scheduled to run during FIFA match days, to improve fans' connectivity to stadiums. The MBTA is running one to the Gillette Stadium in Boston, and the NJ Transit will operate one to MetLife stadium. These tickets are substantively expensive compared with regular routes. For example. the NJT match-day tickets, initially priced at $150 (now set to be reduced to $98) are well above average ticket prices for similar routes ($4.25-$13). However, given this route does not ply regularly, the CPI will likely refrain from pricing it, given no available comparison for the prior periods. records.text: 4 In theory, prices are determined by both demand and supply. However, industrial prices in China are more sensitive when supply tightens than when demand shifts .The 2016 –18 reflation episode illustrates this dynamic. In early 2016, the government launched a sweeping supply-side reform that capped output and shut down overcapacity, especially in coal and steel. The measure not only halted a 54-month PPI deflation streak but also engineered a V- shaped rebound in PPIinflation. During the same period, domestic demand slowed: real GDP growth eased a tad to 6.8% y/y in 2018 from 7.0% in 2015, real retail-sales growth fell to 6.9% from 10.6%, and fixed-asset investment growth slowed to 5.9% from 10%. Export growth, by contrast, rebounded to 9.9% from −2.8% (Figure 6). We believe the industrial capacity utilization rate is a good indicator to gauge demand–supply dynamics. Although PPI inflation swung from −5.3% at the start of 2016 to 5.5% y/y at the end of the year, the utilization rate for the year hit a record low, even below 2026’s level (Figure 7). Overall, the data suggests that once supply begins to tighten, industrial prices rise even when demand remains modest . Material supply-side adjustments: We see similarities between reflation today and that in 2016–18. We project domestic demand to remain soft and real GDP growth to ease from 5.0% last year to 4.6% this year. Bond issuance slower than last year: In our view, strong Q1 GDP growth reduces the urgency for fiscal stimulus, though if April’s underperformance is followed by a sub-4.5% print in May, the government would likely respond with faster bond issuance and fiscal spending (see China: Slower growth in April amid policy headwinds, dated 18 May). This could lead to rates edging up slightly, similar to January. Still, in the absence of hard evidence of second-round effects and amidst the heightened uncertainty, we think a rate hike next week is best seen as a mild lean against inflation and a move that is predominantly meant to mitigate the risk of de-anchoring inflation expectations. Risk assessment tilt toward a hike: As we have argued (here), the environment of the 2026 energy shock is very different to the one in 2022. While the March projections round heavily focused on second round effects on inflation, we believe concerns that demand will push core inflation higher as it did in 2022, will be less prominent now. Euro area GDP grew a mere 0.1%Q in 1Q26, and PMIs point to a flat 2Q26 (see here), at best. In this environment, a good working hypothesis is that weakness in the economy will help limit second round effects. Still, the persistence of oil prices and the surprising acceleration of core inflation to 2.5%Y in May means that the risks to the outlook for inflation are likely assessed as having deteriorated since the April meeting (see our Inflation Watch). On the transmission side, the risk of a quicker pass-through of higher energy prices into core inflation needs watching. Consequently, the main motivation for the hike we expect in June is likely a shift in the balance of risks, but not a fundamental reassessment of the outlook for price stability. This nuance should be reflected in the communication.

With OIS markets still pricing ~30bps of BoC hikes by year- end, and our economists’ NLP analysis showing BoC rhetoric turning more dovish, this suggests scope for a similar dovish lean at next week’s decision even despite today’s constructive labor market data. records.text: US Rates Weekly - Et tu, Waller?). We do not expect Wednesday’s CPI print to add fuel to today’s sell-off. Overall, we push back against the narrative that inflation is ‘widespread’ , as many categories report a sub-3% inflation, especially when constrained to core ex-shelter (Figure 5). Indeed, the category that is elevated in core CPI, transportation services ( ~12% of Figure 5), will likely normalize as energy moves lower throughout 2026. The market is also not expecting much from next week’s CPI print, with implied core CPI around 0.24% to 0.26% m/m, and our economists expecting a 0.22% m/m. Still, there is a light risk for a 0.3% m/m core print. For instance, used car inflation in CPI may catch up to leading indicators and airfares can continue to move higher. There is also a risk that computer software and accessories, which has a higher weight in PCE, could continue to surprise to the upside which may concern the Fed. Having said that, we think there is a growing understanding that this component’s weight in PCE is likely overstated. Indeed former Fed Governor Miran put out a piece on this, as discussed by our economists in US Economics - Inflation Weekly – Growing focus from Fed on AI-affected prices in PCE. Figure 4. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 804/06/2026 Fig. 21: EURHUF term structure Fig. 22: Current high EURHUF atm vol and low flies goes against the likely impact once convergence priced in Fig. 20: Realised vol tends to decline after a currency joins ERM II We think the trajectory for Hungarian assets will continue to revolve around the eurozone accession framework. This is not because entry is imminent, but because ERM II membership will increasingly become the anchor around which convergence trades and monetary policy dynamics will be priced, in our view. FX volatility within ERM II is likely lower: ERM II membership involves a bilateral peg to the euro with a standard +/−15% fluctuation band around a central rate, maintained for a minimum of two years prior to accession. In practice, the mechanism functions as a credibility device and prevailing ranges have typically been lower than what the band would suggest. Greece, Slovakia as templates: Most countries that have joined ERM II had exchange rates that were effectively pegged to the euro prior to joining. Slovakia and Greece stand out as volatile prior to joining, though in both cases vol was lower than EURHUF currently. Realised vol tends to fall: Median realised FX vol has tended to decline once a country joins ERM II (Figure 20) – but it is no panacea. records.text: Standard Chartered (STAN.L/2888.HK, Buy) Manus Costello, Interim Group Chief Financial Officer, presented at our 30th Goldman Sachs European Financials Conference 2026. We highlight the following key takeaways: Continued momentum into Q2: Within markets, management highlighted solid flow momentum so far within Q2 following strong performance in Q1, albeit while flagging a relatively tough comparison on episodic income given outsized 1H25 levels; in banking, management remains pleased with origination levels supporting ongoing momentum following the Q1 print; and in wealth, management confirmed that the beneficial conditions which enabled heightened Q1 wealth activity have remained in place during Q2 (albeit while reiterating that Q1 NNM is not necessarily reflective of the annualised run-rate). Asset quality: LLR guidance was reiterated at 30-35bp, following the Q1 print of 32bp (including a macro overlay), with management embedding a degree of conservatism in part given the bank’s extensive footprint across 54 countries, being cognisant of potential credit and counterparty risks within the current environment. Both the participation rate and a gain in employment (+149K) after a recent run of weakness likely contributed to the small tick down in the unemployment rate. The slight moderation in the unemployment rate in May also suggests that seasonal factors have begun to catch up to the shift in seasonal patterns post-pandemic, breaking the recent trend of a rising unemployment rate in May. We'd noted the participation rate was a risk, this held steady as expected at 61.8% in May. Unrounded, the participation rate rose 1bp to 61.834% in May from 61.826% in April. The broadest measure of labor under-utilization, so-called U-6, fell 0.2 pp to 8.05%. Other cuts of the survey, which can be useful for thinking about the extent of slack, were mixed in May. The teenage unemployment rate rose 0.3 pp to 14.7% in May, continuing to retrace March's decline. The unemployment rate for black and African American individuals fell 0.7 pp to 6.6% in May, its lowest level since May of last year. The close to US$ 1.5bn in dividend remittances since liberalization para- doxically signals confidence: firms repatriating dividends are simultaneously considering fresh capital commitments under the RIGI framework. This scenario was premised on a gradual normalisation of inflation towards target, a moderate growth trajectory, and well-behaved inflation expectations. Stronger-than-expected growth, above-target inflation readings, and first and second round effects stemming from the conflict in the Middle East have fundamentally altered the scenario for monetary policy. The BCB can no longer afford to continue easing without risking a de- anchoring of inflation expectations that would require a much more painful tightening later. Revisiting our call: We expect the Copom to proceed with a 25bp rate cut at its 16 June meeting, bringing the Selic to 14.25%. This decision had already been largely signalled by the BCB's communication in previous meetings, and there has been no suggestion in recent communication from Copom members that they have changed course towards a pause – although we believe that would be the wisest strategy at the current juncture. records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 05 June 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS AI, Iran war and K-shaped economy: are they connected? What is the connection between the AI boom, the Iran war and the K-shaped consumption dynamics most prominent in the US? Do they reinforce each other? What can go wrong? What do we need to watch? We argue that they are connected, they do reinforce each other, they open the door to multiple equilibria and depend heavily on the persistence of excess global liquidity. In other words, any shock that could tighten global liquidity represent a relevant threat to these positively reinforcing dynamics. Watch for oil inventories, productivity gains, inflation and upcoming IPOs. The AI boom can continue if the Iran war doesn’t derail it The impact of AI on equity valuations is often over-simplified: either valuations are consistent with fundamentals or there is a bubble. However, that characterization can be misleading, we think. The AI-driven productivity shock creates labor savings that are appropriated by companies through higher profits, both current and expected. This creates a redirection of savings towards higher income brackets that have higher propensity to save. Those savings end up bidding up asset prices, in particular of those companies that lead the AI race, validating those valuations in turn. The JGB curve n flattened this week, reflecting a hawkish repricing of the June BoJ meeting, with BOJ OIS implying nearly a 95% probability of a June hike (up from 70% last week). Governor Ueda signaled greater urgency to tighten and the need to secure market confidence that the BoJ will properly control inflation, supporting the market’s repricing and prompting our economists to pull forward their forecast for the next BoJ hike to June from July. Even with the timing adjustment, they have maintained their baseline for a roughly semi-annual pace of hikes. While the curve had flattened somewhat into the speech, the aftermath has seen yields move higher and the curve re-steepen, a pattern at odds with the intuitive response to a hawkish signal. Indeed we find that hawkish policy innovations—proxied as instances with higher 3m OIS yields and a stronger Yen—typically result in bear flattening consistent with a more front-loaded policy reaction (Exhibit 5). Although the shift at the very front-end was directionally hawkish and recent communications have emphasized the importance of securing market confidence, we think the muted move beyond the first few meetings and limited FX response suggests little perceived shift in broader reaction function at this point. We continue to see rate hikes as unlikely, though somewhat more likely than we had initially thought. The Fed has usually not hiked in response to oil shocks that seemed unlikely to spark sustained high inflation historically, and we have not yet seen signs that the inflation shock from the war is broadening out. Our composite indicator of the risk of more persistent inflation—a combination of slack and wage pressures, inflation expectations, and the breadth of inflation—remains low, though the latest jump in University of Michigan long-term inflation expectations to 3.9% has pushed it slightly higher. That said, Fed commentary has turned more hawkish in recent weeks, with many participants saying that hikes are possible if the inflation situation worsens. The resilient activity and employment data also lower the bar for a rate hike, less because they suggest risk of overheating than because a stronger starting point for the economy reduces the risk that a hike could end up looking like a costly mistake. records.text: 5 June 2026 Asia Local Markets Weekly Page 16 Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Thailand A deep dive into the Thai mutual fund industry The Thai mutual fund industry has a net asset value of ~$160bn, making it larger than both the life insurance and pension fund industries in the country, each of which manages ~$140bn. This establishes the mutual fund industry as one of Thailand’s largest set of institutions, second in size only to commercial banks. n Surprisingly, mutual fund holdings of ThaiGBs are small, averaging just 2% of the total outstanding amount. BUT this summary fact hides significant volatility in their holdings. n Their behavior in the market has proven significantly more complex over time, largely influenced by retail investment preferences and regulations. In this report, we explore the unique characteristics of the Thai mutual fund industry – including why fixed income retail investors stick largely to money market funds, why FIFs almost fully hedge their FX exposure, and the factors that drive retail allocations to government bond funds. The full report goes into considerable more detail, with a few key takeaways below. How do retail investors behave? Thai retail investors exhibit segmented investment behavior by asset class – crucially, those investing in fixed income tend to remain in fixed income, and similarly for equities. Policy-rate convergence would follow later, once the NBH has demonstrated durable disinflation, in line with the Maastricht criteria, and once the exchange rate is effectively anchored (Figure 24). Ahead of ERM II entry, the NBH would likely need to formally lower its inflation target, in line with ECB’s 2%, we think. Governor Mihály Varga has acknowledged that a formal decision on euro adoption would affect the NBH’s current 3% target (Bloomberg, 28 April). The most instructive precedent is from Slovakia, we think. At the time of its ERM II entry in November 2005, it was explicitly targeting the Maastricht inflation criteria alongside exchange-rate stabilisation. When and if the euro adoption process begins, the NBH may also prefer a relatively cautious near-term bias, to engineer the necessary disinflation and maintain the reputational heft required before any target recalibration is deemed credible by the market. This will likely keep flattening pressure on the HUF curve, akin to that seen in South Africa since its inflation target change last year. records.text: US Economics Weekly5 June 2026 ab 21 BPC estimate debt ceiling to be reached by mid-summer 2027 The Bipartisan Policy Center (BPC) estimates the federal government will reach its federal debt limit between late winter and mid-summer of 2027 (link here). This follows the $5 trillion to $41.1 trillion increase in the limit included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last July. As of now, over half ($2.9 trillion) of that headroom has been used. The timing of when the debt ceiling will be reached is highly uncertain and their report noted three trends to watch in terms of the timing: military spending related to the conflict with Iran; tariff revenues and refunds; and changing economic conditions. On the former, they note that although the Pentagon estimated the conflict had cost approximately ~$29 billion by mid-May in the federal budget actual defense outlays are not significantly above trend. Uncertainty remains on the process for tariff refunds and revenues — we discuss the latest news on this front on page 8. Beige Book: higher prices and uncertainty The Federal Reserve's Beige Book (link here) reported that overall economic activity rose at a "slight to modest" pace in ten of the 12 Federal Reserve districts in the period from early April to May 27. This is slightly better than the eight districts reporting "slight to moderate" growth in the prior report from late February to April 6. The report also noted continued business caution amidst the uncertainty of recent events.

records.text: IDR: Increasing domestic risk premium. USD/IDR broke above 18,000 for the first n time ever this week, and is now the worst performing currency in Asia. While the Middle-East conflict pushed USD/Asia higher, increasingly domestic developments are playing a greater role in IDR depreciation. Even though BI delivered a larger than expected 50bp hike on May 20th, other factors have led to an increase in risk premium. First, the government plans to centralize natural resource exports and retain export proceeds in state banks, and business groups are seeking clarity on this policy: while it is aimed at improving tax revenue and preventing exports under-invoicing, investors are worried that this added bureaucracy can delay/slow down exports. Second, Indonesia’s House of Representative passed a Law to expand BI’s mandate adding a more explicit pro-growth and employment objective to BI’s existing mandate on price and exchange rate stability, leading to investor concerns around the inflation targeting framework. Third, we expect MSCI to provide updated guidance on its treatment of Indonesian equities, including its EM status, by June 23. MSCI has already rebalanced Indonesia’s weight lower in May, leading to around USD 1.7bn of passive outflows. Any additional downgrade could trigger further outflows. High-tech industries like pharmaceuticals and semiconductors are expanding rapidly and becoming central to China's growth model. According to Bloomberg, final demand from high-tech sectors has climbed to over 20% of China’s GDP in 2026, surpassing the property sector. Furthermore, projections suggest these industries will continue expanding at around 12% annually, which could add 2.4 percentage points to headline GDP growth each year. The equity market tells a similar story, with new-economy sectors materially outperforming old-economy segments this year. China’s growth is K-shaped, not L-shaped. The best way to characterize China’s macro backdrop is not as a broad-based, L-shaped slowdown, but as a distinct K- shaped transition. While legacy sectors remain under pressure, newer industries are gaining scale, profitability, and macroeconomic relevance. This structural shift helps explain why headline growth has held up better than many investors expected. Growth resilience reduces the urgency for aggressive easing. Our economists’ 4.7% growth forecast for 2026 is well within Beijing’s 4.5–5.0% target range. This view is consistent with the tone of April’s Politburo meeting and the PBoC’s Q1 monetary policy report. records.text: Our thoughts on USD, JPY, The Resolution Playbook, EM Carry, CAD, INR and IDR USD: Divided we stand. The divided dollar spent another week wrestling n offsetting impulses but finished the week moderately stronger. On the one hand, cyclical activity data remains firmly reflationary, with a bumper payrolls report and the ISM surveys providing evidence both of better growth prospects and uncomfortable inflationary pressures, and that has pushed rate differentials in favour of the Dollar, especially versus Europe. On the other hand, while many commodity and high carry EM currencies have been resilient through the conflict, as US-Iran negotiations inch forward, the potential for lower oil prices and relief across key energy importing economies has raised the prospect of gains across lower-yielding cyclical currencies as well (see Resolution Playbook bullet). And over this period, the persistent appreciation in the Chinese Renminbi—a trend that we think is likely to be gradual but sustained beyond consensus expectations—and the stickiness of the Japanese Yen—through a combination of actual and threatened interventions—has meant that the Dollar is truly divided. As an illustration, the DXY index with a heavy weight in the Euro and other G10 currencies is up ~+1.5% year-to-date even as the broader USD Trade-weighted Index is down by about ~-0.1% (Exhibit 1). Separately, Arca is already leaning into the event’s “legacy” angle via a program to train thousands of local SMEs near high-traffic areas (including around Estadio BBVA / Fan Fest), which can strengthen customer relationships and in-market execution beyond the tournament window. Net, the benefit is less about a single “stadium spike” and more about tighter route-to-market, improved activation, and a broader uplift in local commercial activity during the event, with earnings sensitivity primarily volume-led and upside skewing to immediate-consumption channels rather than any structural reset in baseline growth. Bimbo We expect the World Cup to drive incremental at-home and on-the-go food occasions (watch parties, travel, quick meals, snack builds), which typically benefits staple packaged food categories, and Bimbo’s core portfolio (bread, buns, sweet baked goods) is well-aligned as consumers trade into convenient, shareable formats around matchdays. With scale distribution spanning modern trade, traditional trade, convenience, and foodservice, Bimbo is positioned to capture that incremental demand broadly, with the key upside lever being velocity (and mix) rather than new capacity. The key point is quality of flow-through: incremental volume can move through an existing route-to-market footprint, supporting utilization and operating leverage – so we’d frame this as a modest but high-quality tailwind, more about broad-based velocity than a concentrated host-city spike.

records.text: 5 June 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Deutsche Bank AG Page 51 Long-end EGB supply falls to a 10yr low Towards the end of last year, amid heightened market focus on the Dutch pension reform, we noted in FICOTD: The drop in long-end EGB supply that sovereign issuers were responding with a significant decline in long-end EGB issuance in 2025. Despite the number of 30yr syndications this year — notably new 30yr benchmarks from Belgium, France and Spain in February, followed by Austria in March and a German tap in May — the rolling 1-year share of long-end EGB issuance has now fallen to a 10-year low, to below 7% of total EGB supply, a level last seen in early 2016. We define long-end issuance here as maturities above 25 years. By comparison, that share peaked near 12% in 2021 and was still around 11% at the end of 2024. The overall WAM of annual EGB issuance has also declined, though not dramatically. The latest 1-year rolling WAM, including May 2026, stands at 9.7 years, versus an average of 10.2 years over 2022–2025. This limited decline reflects the fact that the reduction in supply above 25 years has been offset by greater issuance in the 15–20 year sector rather than by shorter-dated bonds, thereby containing the impact on the overall WAM of EGB issuance. Recent data has disappointed, including the Q1 GDP report which showed a second consecutive quarter of contraction—one definition of recession, and the labor market remains fragile. There are reasons not to overstate softness: GDP data are lagged, some survey indicators have improved on the margin, and the composition of the May employment report was strong with a decline in the UR despite stable participation and full-time employment gains. This prompts a key question :will the reflation continue once energy prices retreat? Reflation in this cycle has legs: Current cost-push reflationary forces are broad-based. In China, industrial product prices are more sensitive to supply than to demand, and recent supply adjustments and a growing anti-involution consensus among policymakers, manufacturers and retailers should curb irrational pricing wars, in our view. As in the past, the reflation in this cycle is driven by mid and upstream sectors, so pass-through to consumer prices will likely be modest. Still, the shift in the CPI from ‘noflation’ to mild reflation is already a positive sign. Full-fledged reflation, however, will probably require a substantial recoveryin the property market. There are a few reasons for the very poor investment performance: ▪ Hungary has received a relatively lower and more intermittent flow of EU funds; ▪ The government has been forced to limit public investment and consumption due to budget constraints; and ▪ A manufacturing recession and poor business sentiment has heavily crimped private investment in the supply-side of the economy. Investment green shoots: The most recent data has finally started to show tentative signs of improvement, which we think can be linked chiefly to a very low starting point and to base effects (Figure 2). Improving business sentiment has also been conducive to better investment performance in recent months (Figure 3). Pre-election spending helped: A pre-election boost to public spending, introduced by the then-ruling Fidesz party, underpinned the stronger domestic demand witnessed at the turn of the year. It is worth noting that the fiscal boost followed a lengthy period of falling public spending, in terms of both consumption and investment, which had been a prominent feature through the fifth term of former prime minister Viktor Orban. The economic data that has emerged since the previous meeting – including the resilient Q1 GDP print, the robust early Q2 indicators, sticky core services inflation and rising inflation expectations – paint a picture that is inconsistent with continued easing. We foresee BCB increasing its inflation forecast for the relevant horizon of monetary policy (until Q4 2027) from 3.5% to 3.6%, moving further away from the 3% target. This estimate is based on the Focus survey’s interest rate path, which has Selic reaching 13.25% this year. The increase in forecasted inflation would happen in an environment of asymmetrical upside risks that we had discussed earlier: the possibility of a larger output gap (Figure 9), stronger El Niño and the unpredictability of the Middle East conflict. Just a 50bp upward revision to BCB’s output gap estimate – aligning the central bank’s estimate with ours – would translate into a 24bp increase in the BCB’s inflation estimate for the relevant horizon, slightly closing the somewhat large gap between the BCB’s and the Focus survey’s estimates (the latter’s forecast currently sits at 4.02% for Q4 2027). 2028 inflation expectations continue to creep up, also increasing the risk of further de-anchoring of long-term inflation expectations should the commitment to the 3% target again be questioned. Volume Growth: Corporate lending is expected to drive most of the foretasted volume growth (c.3-4% annually for loans and 1-2% for deposits). When looking at growth on a q/q or y/y basis, corporates have grown across the majority geographies and segments, while Danske expects to gain market share in corporate lending across the Nordics. Net Interest Income and Hedging: Danske’s projections are based on a flat rate curve, although management notes that rate expectations and market rates have increased since the plan was announced, offering potential upside risk to NII. records.text: If asset prices are driven by the reinforcing mechanisms of excess global liquidity and the AI boom, any shock that tighten global liquidity or AI-related valuations and investment can create a correction in asset prices that will directly feed into the economy through the now well known K-shaped dynamics. If inflation dynamics force the Fed to hike aggressively and/or bond vigilantes ask for higher risk premia to hold US bonds, real rates can derail the AI boom, which can be consistent with somewhat high real rates as we currently have in the market, but not a significant repricing. On the Iran war, a key variable to monitor is the evolution of energy inventories. The general perception and imperfect data that can be gathered indicates that we can go another few more months with the current status quo in the Strait of Hormuz without creating meaningful non-linear dynamics. On the AI boom side, it seems the market will remain robust through the IPO season. Those are two important variables to monitor: a non-linear increase in energy prices can feed into an already very persistent inflation dynamics. A disappointing IPOs outcome can impact asset prices in a way that if accompanied by still high inflation can limit the Fed’s room of maneuver to accommodate the financial shock.

records.text: 5 June 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 50 Deutsche Bank AG Liquidity transmission by FHLBs Behind the scenes of the dramatic easing in funding conditions since last year, the Federal Home Loan Banks (FHLBs) likely have played an important role in money market intermediation. Today’s chart examines the flows within the cash lender side of the market and highlights a growing divergence: since the start of the year, money market fund (MMF) AUM growth net of private bill supply has risen by $150bn, even as repo lending by MMFs (proxied by TGCR and sponsored reverse repo volumes) has declined. This discrepancy can be explained by very strong FHLB discount note (DN) issuance, which has provided an alternative outlet for MMF liquidity amid negative net bill supply this year and has helped prevent meaningful ON RRP takeup at the Fed. The increase in DN issuance since mid-2025 is tied to strong demand for FHLB advances by banks as deposit growth rates have lagged loan provision amid resilient economic activity and the unprecedented pace of the AI-infrastructure buildout. Thus, while repo lending has slowed, FHLBs have aided liquidity transmission by issuing DNs to MMFs to fund their advances to banks. records.text: US Economics Weekly5 June 2026 ab 34 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Week Ahead: inflation week We expect the headline CPI rose 0.46% in May, leaving 12-month headline inflation up from 3.8% in April to 4.23% in May, which we expect to be the peak for the year. We expect the May increase was driven largely by energy, though gasoline prices began falling late in the month, pointing to some relief in June. Core CPI is expected to have increased a more modest 0.17% in May, leaving 12-month core inflation still at 2.8% in the rounding. The monthly change was likely held down in part by residual seasonality, softer rent growth, and muted vehicle prices. Alongside the May PPI data also due out next week, Wednesday's CPI data will inform our estimate of the core PCE price increase in May, which currently sits at 0.32%. We expect inflation views remain relatively stable in the FRB of New York's May Survey of Consumer Expectations compared with the University of Michigan Survey of Consumers, even as gas price expectations remain elevated and labor market sentiment remains soft. NFIB small business optimism likely remained subdued in May amidst cost, logistics, and uncertainty headwinds. The full April trade report should show a narrower deficit driven by export strength. records.text: Economics Jack Meaning(ii) Barclays, UK | Cian Hennigan(ii) Barclays, UK By-election outlook: on a knife-edge The latest polling of the Makerfield constituency shows Labour holding a slim majority over Reform UK, but well within the margin for polling errors and also the limits of tactical voting being able to swing things one way or the other. Prediction markets currently put the probability of Labour winning at c.75% (Kalshi; Betfair) but the latest Survation poll, conducted between 18-22 May, suggests just a 3pt lead for Andy Burnham (Labour) over Robert Kenyon (Reform UK) at 43% and 40% of the vote, respectively (Figure 1). Importantly, Reform UK's vote share has been eaten into by Restore Britain, a new party further to the political right of Reform, which now polls at 7%. Parties more aligned to Labour/left/liberal politics also represent around 7% of the vote, according to the poll. This means tactical voting - where voters switch their allegiance from their preferred choice to which of the two leading candidates is closest to their political views - could easily swamp the 3pt lead implied for Labour, leaving the result on a knife-edge. Because of this, we expect political uncertainty to remain high for the next two weeks. FIGURE 1. records.text: Europe Economic Weekly | 05 June 2026 5 Synthetic energy prices (ie the weighted average of oil and gas) were c 14% above the March base case in 2026 and still 8-9% higher in 2027/28 into that cut-off period, mainly due to oil prices. Compared to the ECB’s “adverse” scenario, that would be c 10% lower for this year, but still 8-9% above the 2027-28 trajectory. Meanwhile, the market has priced a more hawkish ECB compared to March. A “regular ” cut-off on 20 May would imply market pricing of close to 80bp of policy rate hikes – twice what was included in the March scenario. A lower oil price this year than in the “adverse scenario”, but with greater persistence, brings elements of the “severe” scenario into play. But more demand destruction and more ECB hikes priced should, to our mind, mean inflation back on target in 2028 on an annual average basis. True, that would imply the ECB giving the “nod” to more than 50bp of hikes. But we would caution against taking that at face value. The downward slope in core inflation would be much steeper to get to target, on average, in 2028, and most likely imply end- 28 quarterly core inflation below 2%. That, to our mind, would be the ECB’s way of flagging that three hikes or more is not unthinkable, but probably a bit too much. records.text: 5 June 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 5 Week ahead ECB rates decision and staff projections (Thu) We expect the Governing Council will deliver a 25bp point rate hike at next week's meeting, lifting the deposit rate to 2.25%. With inflation risks remaining persistent and credibility on the line, recent commentary from Council members suggests clear support for a hike, and we do not believe even a potential US-Iran deal would deter them. Our baseline view remains for two hikes this cycle, with a second move in September, though the timing of that second hike is becoming more uncertain. President Lagarde has outlined three potential responses to the energy shock: 'look through', 'measured tightening', or 'forceful or persistent' tightening. The ECB now appears to be moving firmly into the 'measured tightening' phase. We will be watching for any shift in emphasis from the "intensification" of risks to the "inevitability" of indirect inflation effects, and whether the ECB maintains full policy optionality in its forward guidance. Hawkish signals could include opening the door to a July hike or emphasizing the need to preserve credibility, while a dovish tilt might involve highlighting downside risks to growth. The new staff projections will be another critical element, as they will be conditioned on a market-priced path that includes three hikes, up from two in the March projections. We expect the new forecasts to show higher inflation and lower growth. Specifically

records.text: Norway—Why is Wage Growth Still So High? Wage growth remains one of the key drivers of the inflation outlook in Norway. While inflation has declined substantially from its peak, wage growth remains close to 5%, keeping domestically generated price pressures elevated. Real wages fell sharply during the inflation shock of 2022-23, but the subsequent recovery in purchasing power, the 2026 wage norm of 4.4% and Norges Bank’s forecast of 4.5% imply persistent pressures ahead (Exhibit 1). Understanding why wages remain so strong is therefore crucial for assessing the future path of inflation and interest rates, so we take a closer look at the Norwegian wage formation model in this Daily. Norway’s wage formation is organised around the “frontfag” bargaining model.1 Under this model, the economy is divided into two sectors – tradables (or “exposed”) and non-tradeables (or “sheltered”) – and wage negotiations are initiated and led by the internationally exposed manufacturing sector. Since manufacturing firms compete directly with foreign producers, they face the hardest constraint on wage growth as it cannot exceed what productivity and profitability allow without undermining competitiveness. The settlement reached in manufacturing therefore serves as a benchmark for the rest of the economy, otherwise called the wage norm.2 An important implication of this framework is that wage growth can remain elevated even when domestic economic conditions weaken. records.text: 5 June 2026 Asia Local Markets Weekly Page 10 Deutsche Bank AG/Singapore Singapore Rates Reading the liquidity tea-leaves We continue to field several client questions on Singapore’s liquidity dynamics. With limited high-frequency public data available, we go back to first principles for analyzing the same, including assessing the balance sheet dynamics for the commercial banking system and the central bank. n The macro factors are more dominant on the bank side, driving a persistent gap between deposit growth and credit take up. n Policy on reserve money management then determines if, and by what amount, the surplus liquidity within the banking system is withdrawn. In this note, we assess both these dynamics and conclude with our expected market implications. The macro backdrop Loan growth of SGD 40-50bn/month (Figure 12) has not kept pace with the higher supply of deposits at 100-150bn/month (Figure 13). This has resulted in loan-to- deposit ratios falling to lows of <70% (Figure 14), from >100% before 2020. This deposit-loan gap will likely persist and remain supportive of liquidity generation. Source: Haver, BofA Global Research BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH The fiscal stance is improving but is it enough? We measure fiscal stance using the primary balance. This measure strips out interest payments that are compulsory and inflexible, and the first charge on revenues. The balance between non-interest spending and revenues therefore reflects a government’s fiscal stance. In South Africa, this stance has changed over the years – sometimes weak but more recently improving while the cost of debt is moderating. The debt-stabilising primary balance is a moving target as it depends on factors such as economic growth. For a substantial reduction in debt, South Africa requires primary surpluses much higher than the level needed to stabilise debt. Large primary surpluses would help to drive a firmer decline in the debt-to-GDP ratio. An improved fiscal stance has helped debt to peak in the 2025/26 fiscal year and set it on a declining path. However, risks of lower GDP growth have intensified since the energy shock in early March 2026. That could derail the fiscal consolidation path and potential downward debt trajectory. In Central Europe, the CFO noted mortgage growth had been strong, particularly in Bulgaria, with a general rule of thumb for lending to track nominal GDP . Insurance business: Management expects sustained positive inflows, noting particularly low insurance penetration in the CE region, where the % of GDP spent on insurance stands in the low-single digits, compared with ~7% in Belgium and ~12% in the UK. In Belgium, KBC highlighted its strength in cross-selling insurance products via its bancassurance model, driving an advantage vs ordinary insurance companies, with above-market growth highlighted in non-life. Opex & asset quality: Management discussed cost savings from the increased use of straight-through processes which do not require human intervention and are highly scalable, while set against continuous investments into digitisation — with €2bn invested every three years into IT and AI, split three quarters opex and one quarter capex. Regarding asset quality, KBC reiterated its confidence in the guidance for 2026 credit costs to be well below the through-the-cycle level of 25-30bps, albeit with some stage 1 and 2 deterioration possible, largely reflecting normalisation. Valuation and risks We value KBC using a P/E valuation methodology applied 75%/25% to 2027/28E estimates, and use an 11.75x multiple. Our 12-month price target is €139.00. We remain Buy rated. The upside surprise appears partly driven by durable goods, which rose 12.4%m/m sa, as auto- related subsidies and tax cuts that began in April likely boost- ed vehicle sales. Importantly, services consumption continued to post steady gains, rising 0.3%, and non-durable goods rebounded 1.2% despite a jump in energy prices—suggesting households remain resilient at the start of this quarter. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 11 recently unveiling plans to centralise commodity exports (Reuters). A centralised trading company will handle the exports, covering palm oil, coal and ferroalloys initially, with more commodities potentially added over time. Another proposed measure would require all natural resource exporters to keep their revenues in state-owned banks. China has restricted rare earth exports to Japan: China has restricted exports of several heavy rare earths to Japan for at least four months (Reuters). Japan depends on imports from China to support its rare earth magnet production as well as its aerospace and defence sectors. The restrictive measures were imposed by China after Japan's Prime Minister made public comments on Taiwan in November last year. Since December, rare earth arrivals in Japan from China have ceased, apart from some yttrium shipments. China is still exporting rare earth magnets. Japan has started releasing stockpiles to ease some pressure while investments in overseas producers and projects may provide some offset. However, this diversification away from China will likely take years to materialise and will likely not alleviate shortages in the short term. This highlights the importance of stockpiles, with Japanese companies holding more stockpiles since 2010 when a similar slowdown in Chinese exports was seen. Test cases: Applying our debt consolidation framework, we look at two scenarios (S1 – conservative, S2 – proactive) and their progress under different assumptions for growth, inflation, interest rates, FX and structural primary balance adjustments (Figure 14). S2 envisages a faster primary balance adjustment which returns to a primary surplus and a halving of the general government deficit to below 3.5% of GDP by 2028, alongside stronger growth and a faster drop in funding costs. Under both scenarios, we generate moderating deficit and debt trajectories. However, the more proactive S2 scenario generates debt ratios that we think are closer to what the European Commission would likely deem acceptable progress under a timeline for euro adoption around 2032 (Figure 15). S2 does show a more plausible path towards meeting Maastricht benchmarks, but highlights that for such a strategy to be successful, non-negligible progress would still be required in terms of both the structural primary balance adjustment (from 2027) and stronger growth (and in terms of lower funding costs – but we see this as a by-product of the first two). Term premia compression matters: As we argue on page 9, we see a continued convergence in back-end yields towards eurozone levels as the first in a sequence of events that assists the kind of fiscal consolidation we outline above. records.text: US Rates Weekly 05 June 2026 Citi Research 15 Vol: Football lull The World Cup begins this month. Historically, short-dated rates vols in US and EUR tend to stay low or grind even lower during the football tournament, which supports our near-term bearish vol bias. 2s10s rate curve also tends to move more modestly and less than the market’s current 1m expectation. Hence, we reiterate our short curve vol recommendation via costless 1x2 straddle/strangle switch. Rates vol tends to stay low or decline during the tournament As counterintuitive as it may seem given the uncertainties and headline risks around the Middle East conflict, we believe that an extremely divided Fed that is handcuffed by opposing inflation and employment tail risks will continue to dampen short-expiry implied vols, especially on front-end rates, over the near- term (Rates Vol Lab - Hedging 30y buyers strike risk). While implied vol can certainly bounce on news headlines, we believe that it would be difficult for upper- left vol to remain elevated over a sustained period given the Fed’s gradual approach. Thus, we continue to like selling upper-left vol on any near-term bounce, barring a significant upside surprise in the inflation data. records.text: European Rates Weekly 04 June 2026 Citi Research 8 Bunds: persistently richer than they should (for a reason). The key question to us is whether the superior international hedging properties of Bunds will survive the combination of (i) the transition of the ECB to a demand-driven liquidity provision framework and (ii) the structural shift of Germany’s Federal government towards a looser fiscal stance. For this purpose, we can re-cast the differential between Bunds and USTs (both swapped to SOFR) as the simple difference between the actual bond yield differential (blue line in Figure 10) and the one implied by the ex- ante PV equality of two streams of floating rate payments in $ (SOFR) vs € (ESTR) over a 10y period (light blue line in the chart). The positive difference between the two – which captures the fact that Bunds have persistently traded richer than the assumption of perfect international bond substitutability would infer – trended higher between the post-pandemic and October 2022 before stabilizing around 30-40bp and then dropping by some 20bp in the second half of 2025 through to early this year. A G4 pecking order of bond richness. Compared to Bunds, the bond differential vs USTs has been persistently negative for JGBs (meaning that these have been trading cheaper than the perfect risk-sharing benchmark) while it switched from slightly positive to slightly negative for Gilts in May 2023 (Figure 11). The main source of the slow down is household operations, where a 5.4% price increase that was by far the largest monthly increase in its nearly 30-year history accounted for half of the non-rent core services price increase in April. Additionally, airfares are projected to see a somewhat smaller (but still notable) increase compared to recent months as elevated jet fuel prices continue to pass-through to ticket prices.  Upside: We view the risks as tilted toward the upside of our May projection. A May core CPI increase anywhere between 0.12% and 0.26% would not be surprising. The biggest upside risk in our view is a larger increase in airfares where the pass-through of the rise in jet fuel prices could be more concentrated in May than we have anticipated. We also see upside risks to lodging away from home from potential World Cup-related rate increases that are not captured in our source data from Smith Travel Research due to differences in sample timing. Further the bi-monthly sampling for most cities could mean that the slowing we have pencilled in for household operations in May does not appear until June.  Downside: Downside risks are less clear.
