We dipped our toe with a light bullish structure, on the back of a possible deal on the Iran conflict via risk reversals last week (see US Rates Strategy - On the other side of a deal). Such structures are easier to hold on a terminal basis, and we still like the trade. Specifically, we are short 95.875 SFRZ6 puts and long 96.625 SFRZ6 calls, which has a take-in, into next week. Over the medium term, we are still constructive on USTs, but this requires an end to the Iran conflict. Then the narrative may move away from higher inflation risks and towards a possible growth shock later this year. Indeed, the latest NFIB small business survey recorded a multi-year low for hiring plans, which may portend lower payroll growth ahead (Figure 6). In general, labor market data appeared stronger at the start of ’24 and ’25 before weakening into Q3. Hence, the bar will be high for the Fed to deliver rate hikes, which means long UST positions should capture attractive carry and rolldown. Note: Futures trading involves substantial risk of loss. Forecasts might leave the door open for a bit more. Time for the well telegraphed hike We expect the ECB to hike all three policy rates by 25bp next week. With the energy price shock a bit larger than initially incorporated in the March forecasts (which already included a June hike), more long lasting, and with (slightly) more persistent energy price effects, the natural slope is for the ECB to deliver a quite well telegraphed hike. New forecasts will show a bit less growth and more inflation in the near term but, crucially, still show inflation back to target by the end of the forecasting period. With roughly three hikes now incorporated in the baseline, the message will likely come out as a bit hawkish vs March, suggesting two hikes is still a reasonable base case, but leaving the door open to do more rather than less in case of doubt. If El Niño develops more rapidly or strengthens beyond baseline expectations, regional impacts could shift materially, particularly across Latin America and South Asia. records.text: At the same time, the Norges Bank Regional Network Survey (RNS) labour shortages indicator provides some support for a relatively loose labour market hypothesis, with the reported shortages at the cycle-low in 2026Q1 and notably below the post-pandemic highs (Exhibit 3, right). While the measure on average tends to lead nominal wage growth, suggesting a potential downside impulse for wage formation, the relationship remains less strong in the years when wage share dips below the historical average (shaded in Exhibit 3, right) and those that follow, highlighting the “frontfag” model features. While aggregate labour market conditions remain broadly supportive for wage growth normalisation, labour shortages appear fragmented across sectors and are not concentrated in manufacturing. Vacancy rates and labour shortage indicators remain more elevated in parts of services, such as oil-related services and hospitality, while manufacturing tightness has moved closer to historical norms (Exhibit 4). Firms in these sectors may need to offer larger pay increases and show a stronger wage drift than in manufacturing (pushing economy-wide wages above the norm) despite exhibiting lower productivity growth simply because the local labour markets remain more tight. These changes include relaxing transition rules and offshore capital-raising while tightening standards for new foreign bond investments to BBB- or higher. The immediate impact on the TWD should be limited, as existing assets do not require forced selling. While portfolio flows remain stable, a key headwind for the TWD is the potential for insurers to lower their currency hedging, which would increase USD buying and cap appreciation. Taiwan's life insurers manage one of Asia's largest overseas investment portfolios, with total assets reaching approximately $1.2tn and foreign holdings constituting around 60% of that total. Regulatory concerns over sovereign credit risk, combined with the new TW-ICS solvency framework that began in January 2026, have prompted the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) to amend the rules governing these investments. While the changes are framed as "two relaxations and one tightening," their net effect on the TWD is limited. What are the new rules? Relaxation: TW-ICS transition relief. We think the primary reason for the move was heavy take-up of the facility by local banks as FX I/Y were trading below 5.75%. ASW will remain tight: Though HGB ASW remain very tight by CE3 standards, foreign inflows and low FX I/Y will likely keep a lid on ASW, in our view. We also think the government will not be in a rush to meaningfully change the measures that incentivise local banks to hold bonds. Hungary is also currently not meeting the Maastricht criteria on long-term interest rates, which further adds to the incentive to keep HGBs supported, in our view. Second, it supports our view that AI is not generating a jobless expansion. There is concern that the US lift is less indicative globally, a point highlighted by this week’s sharp drop in the global PMI employment. However, incoming news points to solid global growth which, if sustained, should support our central 2026 outlook theme of a conscious labor market recoupling. Continued spending in the face of weak labor income boosted global profits and promoted leaner inventory positions. Combined with a fading of trade war fears and sustained tech strength, this allowed the global manufacturing sector to move into the new year with strong momentum. records.text: hallenges for public finances in 2Q26 After Moody’s credit downgrade, Mexico’s public finances look strained: more fiscal consolidation is needed, but so is investment to break out of a low-growth rut. April figures underscore the tension. The wide deficit has barely narrowed in nominal terms to MXN$178.5bn (vs. MXN$181.8bn a year ago), while the primary balance fell 41.7% ytd to MXN$171.3bn in the first four months. The main obstacle has been weak revenue growth even as spending remains rel- atively contained, leading us to forecast a 4.8% of GDP defi- cit—above the Finance Ministry’s 4.1% target (Figure 1). Revenues declined 6.4% y/y in April and 2.2% ytd, reflecting softness in both oil and tax income. Oil-related inflows have lagged despite higher prices, pressured by a strong peso and policies aimed at limiting exports to support energy self-suffi- ciency. On the tax side, collections have been challenged by a drop in overall tax revenue (-6.4% ytd) and only modest V AT growth (0.4% ytd), partly offset by stronger excise receipts even with the gasoline subsidy. Going forward, as activity improves, tax collections should rebound. We initiated the position shortly after media reports suggested the Japanese Ministry of Finance had intervened in markets to strengthen the JPY. Our rationale was based on historical precedent that suggests fading unilateral intervention is a favorable strategy so long as it is not accompanied by a shift in the macroeconomic backdrop. Fundamentals have remained bullish for the pair. Energy prices remain elevated due to constrained flows through the Strait of Hormuz, weighing on Japan’s terms of trade. US data has continued to be strong and has driven markets to price in tighter monetary policy by the Federal Reserve. There has been an uptick in hawkish commentary by Bank of Japan officials, but we think this has been insufficient to support the JPY on its own, largely because the BoJ is still being viewed as behind the curve. In May there was a move up in advance notices of redundancies by employers (Figure 3). But the rise is small compared to the usual chop in the series. Some MPC members have been con- cerned about the sharp move up in mortgage rates driven by market expectations of multiple hikes. Following some dov- ish commentary, there is evidence of this impact receding, however. After surging 120bps through to March, quoted mortgage rates fell back by around 20bps in May. The other crucial factor is oil prices. They have undershot expectations despite the Strait remaining closed. We think this could prove to be the deciding factor regarding a July rate hike. While we can see as many as three dissents appearing for the June meeting, our sense is that oil of $90 or below would buy the MPC as a whole more time if it were to persist into July. KEY MESSAGES The sharp recent rise in Treasury yields leads us to see some parallels to post-Liberation Day price action. At that point, the initial knee-jerk “flight to quality” didn’t last and turned into a self-reinforcing rise in yields. Right after Liberation Day, the Fed seemed less dovish and a narrative of overseas selling of Treasuries emerged. This was amplified by swap spread unwinds and basis trade deleveraging. In the current setup – if the narrative turns towards wider deficits after the escalation, long-end looks especially vulnerable given the recent decline in term premiums. Additionally, already tightening swap spreads, and potential basis trade unwinds, risks a rise in Treasury yields that becomes self-reinforcing - similar to post-Liberation Day. Continued re-pricing of Fed path to a less dovish one can also reinforce a selloff in Treasuries. records.text: Katya Vashkinskaya +44(20)7774-4833 | katya.vashkinskaya@gs.com Goldman Sachs International European Daily: Norway—Why is Wage Growth Still So High? 5 June 2026 | 8:33AM BST Wage growth remains one of the key drivers of the inflation outlook in Norway. n Inflation has fallen from its peak, but wages are still growing at nearly 5%, keeping domestic inflation elevated. Norway’s wage growth is staying high mainly because the “frontfag” bargaining n system sets the economy-wide wage norm. This year’s 4.4% settlement reflects strong conditions in manufacturing: high productivity and a “wage share” that remains below the historical norm. Labour market conditions in the broader economy still matter, mainly through n wage drift rather than the wage norm itself. While some indicators point to softening, registered unemployment remains low, and relatively more tight sectors such as oil services and hospitality could still push wages above the norm. Taken together, the “frontfag” model, sector-specific labour tightness, n productivity, and wage-share catch-up explain Norway’s wage dynamics better than a standard wage Phillips curve. Our framework therefore points to persistently firm wage growth and some upside risk to Norges Bank’s wage forecasts, consistent with our expectation of another Norges Bank hike in September to 4.5%. We expect a 25bp hike from the ECB at the June meeting, taking the depo rate to 2.25%, in line with market pricing. During the press conference, markets will likely focus on the guidance on the future path of policy rates. We think ECB guidance will likely remain data-dependent with a tightening bias and we expect no explicit signals around the July meeting. Forecasts will also be key to assess the ECB's reading of the ongoing energy shock on the Euro area economy and inflation dynamics. Beyond June, we still look for a further ECB hike in September, broadly consistent with markets pricing around 50bp of cumulative tightening by then. The ECB OIS curve, however, further prices additional hikes after September, with roughly 65bp priced by December and about 70bp by March 2027. We do not think the ECB can deliver more than three hikes in this cycle given the starting level of the economy and policy rates, with 75bp hikes being an upper-bound for ECB pricing in our view. The experience of COVID and the 2022 price spike may have taught governments, businesses, and consumers how to sustain economic activity while using less energy. Remote work reduced commuting, digital tools replaced a portion of business travel, supply chains became more flexible, and energy efficiency rose on both corporate and policy agendas. The result has been faster and more pronounced oil demand adjustments—weakening the traditional link between economic activity and oil consumption. Early demand indicators from March are consistent with this interpretation. In the HY market, these segments have seen some degree of underperformance; however, the reaction has still been relatively muted, once composition impacts are accounted for. For £-IG, a key explanation for why the market has not shown signs of investor concern is that UK issuers only account for 55% of the index by market value, with many of those still having international operations and revenues. In other words, £-IG credit is not a particularly clean way to express a view on UK risk compared to other asset classes. In HY, on the other hand, while the index is dominated by UK-domiciled credits (accounting for over 90% of the amount outstanding), and underperformed their € counterparts through the headline volatility, a large portion of the widening £HY - €HY premium is attributable to the distinctly lower quality of the sterling market. Single-B and lower-rated assets account for 73% of the £HY index versus just 36% in €HY. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 504/06/2026 Getting the house in order: Fiscal rectitude will form an important part of any turnaround in Hungary’s economy and in HUF-asset prices over the medium-term. We note that the previous government’s policies around the minimum wage and social subsidies, as well somewhat inefficient spending across state and quasi-state institutions, encouraged anxiety around Hungary’s unsustainable fiscal stance (see Charting global fiscal risks, dated 17 June 2025). We do not, however, think the central issue lies in the primary deficit, which until the pre-election year had been narrowing (Figure 12). ‘r–g’ problems: Instead, we see Hungary’s main problem as its growing debt service cost burden which has more than doubled as a ratio of revenues since 2019 (Figure 13). With an average term to maturity below five years, the need for higher short-term interest rates to curb inflationary impulses linked to weak productivity has structurally added to the state’s fiscal burden. Does he use the lofty, almost soaring rhetoric of prior speeches? Or stick to the template of the last three Chairs, who largely called it like they see it? We do not know. If not, then markets could react mistakenly, or price in or price out rate hikes based on misunderstanding. Investors are asking whether a “Warsh Fed” will truly deliver policy tightness in practice —and they are expressing that doubt through positioning. Non-US accounts continue to hedge USD exposure aggressively, while domestic investors are only tentatively leaning back in. That divergence matters. records.text: Wider spreads could drive down life insurers We regard UK domestic life insurers – Legal & General, Standard Life, M&G, and Chesnara – as well as the more diversified composite insurer Aviva to be most vulnerable to UK risk perception, primarily from the sentiment perspective. From a fundamental perspective, Solvency 2 capital models of life insurers have a positive gearing to higher gilt rates; however, with the resulting additional capital not viewed as distributable, we consider commitment to fiscal discipline to be crucial for any contender for the PM role. On the other hand, the potential for tax changes, such as the harmonisation of the capital gains tax and personal income tax, may strengthen the appeal of tax-efficient life insurance savings products and help inflows. Increased inflationary backdrop may help non-life insurers as cycle hardens For the domestic non-life insurers Admiral and Sabre, we regard inflation and regulation to be the main risk pass-through mechanisms. A potentially expansionary fiscal framework would further elevate inflationary risks, in our view, but UK domestic insurers may be in a more favorable position to pass on that pressure to customers. Pricing for motor and home insurance have started to stabilise and increase in recent months, which may allow insurers to maintain margins even if claims inflation accelerates from the current low single-digit level. records.text: Fiscal policy still relevant for European spreads. We continue to be positive on n front-end sovereign credit as a carry expression in European rates markets. With inflation risks now more balanced, there are reduced prospects for much higher rates volatility, and the market already prices the extent of the upcoming ECB hiking cycle, in our view. The fiscal response to higher energy prices has so far been muted, including in places like France which had provided substantial relief back in 2022/23. But pressure remains on European budgets, especially should flows through Hormuz stay muted. For instance, this week the European Commission decided to allow some exemptions for “energy resilience” measures in the context of fiscal rules, worth 0.3% of GDP for the years 2026-28. While this remains modest, against this backdrop we think front-end EGBs should be better protected should energy price upside re-emerge, in which case we’d expect the credit curve to steepen curves. Macro risks not supply risks key for Gilts. Despite a strong narrative around n political and supply risks for the UK bond market, 10y Gilts have quietly performed quite well on asset swap over recent weeks. Gilt risks have relaxed since mid-May with our term premium estimate declining by around 25bp. We think the relative stability — if not strength — of Gilts on asset swap is supporting evidence for the view that risk premium in the Gilt curve is currently more macro-driven rather than supply-driven. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Macro Projections: More Inflation, Less Growth European Economics Team Overview: Headline and core inflation up, growth down Lower growth, inflation up: As per usual in June, the ECB will publish updated projections prepared by national central banks (NCB). From a broad perspective, we expect four main takeaways from the updated baseline forecast: (i) headline inflation will be revised higher in 2026; (ii) the quarterly profile will likely show an undershoot at some point in 2027, but HICP will be back on target in 2028; (iii) Core inflation is likely to be seen a touch higher over most of the forecast horizon; and (iv) annual growth in 2026 and 2027 will likely be revised down. We also expect the baseline forecast to be accompanied by alternative scenarios, likely entertaining much higher energy prices but displaying a more balanced trade-off between growth and inflation than in the March scenarios. That’s a tough one: Anticipating the exact figures the ECB will come with next week is however particularly challenging as uncertainties abound. First, while on the usual procedure, the cut-off date for the assumptions would be on 20 May, we suspect it was pushed to 27 May, with a significant impact on the path of oil prices taken on board (see below). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 1) We expect July ECB pricing, similar to that of April, to gradually fade to 0bp as the ECB does not need to hike in back to back meetings, in our view. 2) The cumulative pricing of July and September looks a bit high to us, mostly because of the July leg. 3) October pricing appears elevated relative to September and December, given the ECB’s reluctance to move at non‑forecast meetings. 4) The total amount of tightening over the next 12 months is too high in our view, with the clearest RV in 2027: the curve shows only limited inversion, with just a few bp priced, versus our baseline of around 50bp of cuts. This week the European Commission broadened the scope of its fiscal rules to exempt certain energy-related spending (see more details in Euro Area Rates: Fiscal Developments Remain Key; So Far So Good). From a macro perspective, we flag that our economists see only modestly higher deficits under most scenarios (see more in their mid-year outlook). As a result, the market may be pricing in too much ECB tightening, and we expect the intermediate part of the forward curve to rally in the upcoming quarters. A more severe rise in energy prices could lead to higher deficits, but this would likely be linked to a major military escalation and financial stability concerns, prompting the ECB to focus less on inflation and more on stability. In that case, the curve would likely steepen, with lower short-term yields and higher term premia further out.

records.text: M Idea 2 Economics: More Room on Paper, Very Little in Practice Skander Garchi Casal & Jens Eisenschmidt What happened? This week, the European Commission (EC) published its Spring Package (see here), providing, among other things, an annual assessment of Member States’ fiscal positions. It includes country-specific recommendations and, importantly, an evaluation of compliance with EU fiscal rules. The most important announcement within the package was the introduction of additional flexibility in the implementation of these rules. Notably, the Commission may allow an expansion in the scope of its pre-existing national escape clause to include measures undertaken since February 2026 aimed at reducing countries’ dependence on fossil fuels. As we argue below, these changes appear marginal and do not change our fiscal view. We see only very limited additional upside risks (if any) relative to our baseline deficit forecast from the announcement. In what follows, we address a number of key questions that we believe are particularly relevant for investors. Q1) What is the national escape clause (NEC)? An important focus of the announcements was the use of the national escape clause (NEC). Before turning to the recent changes, it is helpful to step back and recall how it works. In essence, the NEC provides flexibility within the EU fiscal framework by allowing certain expenditure to be excluded from the fiscal requirements, provided that this does not jeopardise fiscal sustainabilit

Management continues to target c.5% growth in both loans and deposits, framing this as a longer term objective, supporting overall profitability targets. Furthermore, on deposits, management has highlighted a shift in their acquisition strategy moving away from broad-based campaigns towards more targeted initiatives. While upfront economics of these campaigns remain negative (in the first four months), profitability is achieved through customer retention and lifetime value. These campaigns also cater to existing customers to help them increase their deposit balances (unlike certain peers which focus solely on new customer acquisition). records.text: Societe Generale (SOGN.PA, Buy) Leopoldo Alvear, Chief Financial Officer, presented at our 30th Goldman Sachs European Financials Conference 2026. We highlight the following key takeaways: Macro backdrop and operating trends: Management noted that while energy prices remain elevated, it is early to assess any meaningful direct implications on their underlying business or Group asset quality trends. From a credit standpoint, they note that Q1 remained resilient, and they do not see any signs of underlying stress with cost of risk at ~25bps, in the lower end of their 25-30bps target range for the FY. Across businesses, they outline the following key trends: French Retail: In French Retail, Q1 NII increased by c.10% y/y excluding PEL/CEL n effects, driven by a combination of lower cost of funding/deposit repricing (with mix stabilisation over the last 3 quarters), asset repricing and volumes. Looking ahead, management expects these drivers to remain supportive, although it reiterated guidance for a more muted progression in NII, with no change to underlying expectations. BoursoBank: BoursoBank remains a key growth driver, with the Group reaching n c.8mn customers ahead of plan last year and now approaching 9mn clients, with only ~1,100 employees, relatively low RWA consumption and ~60% RoNE levels. Importantly, management highlighted a shift in focus towards profitability for clients alongside growth. Looking forward, the strategy remains centered on deepening client engagement

records.text: l: Median realised FX vol has tended to decline once a country joins ERM II (Figure 20) – but it is no panacea. SKK appreciation towards a stronger conversion rate on the date of EUR adoption led to higher volatility. The central rate may be a good guide for EUR conversion, but is not necessarily fixed. In principle the +/−15% band – and a tendency for one- sided adjustments in the central rate (towards a stronger currency, as in the case of the SKK) – implies the risk of devaluation has fallen. Currencies within ERM II are not allowed to fluctuate by more than this range and are supported by intervention if necessary. Although there has not been an instance of a currency leaving ERM II after entering, the precedent of the ultimate collapse of ERM I shows that a necessary condition for the mechanism to work effectively is economic convergence. So, not only would EURHUF volatility be lower in ERM II, but eventual EUR adoption would mean it reaches zero – the clear implication being that if a convergence path is followed, long-term EURHUF vol should fall. With current long-term EURHUF vol near 10% – and given the upward-sloping term structure seen over the last year – we suggest that such a sequence is not yet in the price. If Hungary joins ERM II then EURHUF may trade like a ‘currency peg’, i.e. with very low day-to-day spot volatility, but subject to tail risks that may include adjustments to the central rate or pressure on the ERM from economic divergence. records.text: 5 June 2026 Global Fixed Income Weekly Page 52 Deutsche Bank AG Covered Bonds and SSA Pfandbriefe - CB market reference Note: This note was originally published on 4 June 2026. "Jumbo" Pfandbriefe - outdated term - introduced to support investor demand "Jumbo" Pfandbriefe were the large-volume segment of the German Pfandbrief market. While "Jumbo" Pfandbriefe had to strictly comply with the statutory requirements of the German Pfandbrief Act - like all Pfandbriefe - they were additionally defined by specific voluntary minimum standards set by the Association of German Pfandbrief Banks (vdp), for example, a minimum new issue size of EUR 1bn (details under the link here). In our view, the term "Jumbo" Pfandbrief is outdated and was introduced in May 2025 when low liquidity of Pfandbriefe was an issue for investors. Back then, the "Jumbo" Pfandbrief requirements were introduced to support demand by international investors. Nowadays, most EUR benchmark CB - also issues with a size of "only" EUR 500m - are priced with the same standards. German Pfandbriefe - still the reference product in the CB markets German Pfandbriefe typically have commercial real estate (CRE) exposure in the cover pool. Moreover, in contrast to numerous other CBC markets, there are plenty of double A (instead of exclusively triple A rated) Pfandbriefe. That will leave markets to focus on the pol icy aftermath, with a string of important central bank meetings across major economies in the next three weeks. While market pricing remains fairly certain in most cases what will happen, guidance will be key to whether economic policy uncertainty continues. Inflation continues As we highlighted in this month’s Inflation in Focus, And now five percent, US inflation has only shown modest signs of deceleration in May. According to State Street PriceStats, the month looks set to post another 0.5%m/m plus rise, which has lifted annual inflation rate up to 5%. Having first risen through 4%yoy on 31st March, the pace of acceleration has at least slowed, but is still troubling. The only good news here is that our sector data still suggests much of the rise is in energy prices, with minimal signs of contagion outside of that. US data surprises and USD recoupling Robust headline inflation is so far doing little to disrupt what has been a remarkable run of upside surprises in US economic data. records.text: ing rigidities complicate fiscal consolidation in 2Q26 • Next week, benign dynamics should ease May CPI to 3.99%oya; IP and manufacturing up 0.5%samr • Consumption and GFI improve in March but domestic demand faces important challenges • Mexico and Canada propose a USMCA extension as the US opts to impose new wave of tariffs News this week was mixed in terms of policy updates, nota- bly on the fiscal front and USMCA, while the macro outlook is now complete for 1Q and we move to early 2Q. Domestic demand in March confirmed that investment and consump- tion are gradually recovering, as sentiment indicators for 2Q are evidencing important challenges. Growth volatility has been in place for a while and we still expect it to dominate as regional and domestic uncertainties linger, short-term World Cup-related consumption takes center stage in the next few weeks, and external demand remains supported by resilient non-auto manufacturing exports. From a North American perspective, in addition to the World Cup kick-off next week on June 11, the USMCA back-and- forth news remains in the spotlight — the main reason for investment sluggishness. Mexico and Canada have announced their intention to extend the agreement, while the US remains unaltered in its pro-tariff approach to global trade. Challenges for public finances in 2Q26 After Moody’s credit downgrade, Mexico’s public finances look strained: more fiscal consolidation is needed, but so is investment to break out of a low-growth rut

The combination suggests a flattening impulse, particularly in the context of hawkish repricing elsewhere in DM. JPM’s Hawk Dove Score (HDS) natural language processing measures of central bank tone have pushed higher across G10 (Figure 3H a w k d o v e s c o r e s h a v e m o v e d c o n c e r t e d l y h i g h e r i n r e c e n t w e e k s a c r o s s G 1 0 . . . ), catching up to the RBA. Relative to that input, front-end rates are looking somewhat rich again on models calibrated to central bank tone and global data, with AUD least so, and NZD richest (Figure 4. . . a n u m b e r o f f r o n t - e n d s n o w s c r e e n r i c h o n m o d e l s f i t t e d t o c e n t r a l b a n k t o n e a n d U S d a t a ). We continue to hold the AUD-USD 2Y1Y (IRS-SFR) tightener entered in early May. As shown above, AUD yield levels are less offside than others relative to the evolving global policy bias. The most likely driver of AUD outright cheapening from these levels is global, and on a spread basis AUD is high beta to changes in relative hawkishness

records.text: US Economics Weekly5 June 2026 ab 30 For Q4, nonfarm business productivity growth was unchanged at 1.6% (saar), while unit labor cost growth was revised down sharply to 2.1% (saar) from 4.6% previously. On a two-quarter annualized basis, nonfarm business productivity growth now stands at 0.9%, down from 1.2% prior to this week’s revisions. Over the same period, unit labor cost growth is 2.0%, versus 3.4% previously. Overall, productivity growth appears to have moderated in recent quarters. That said, Q1 is often a weak quarter, and the two-quarter annualized pace in 2026 (0.9%) remains above the 0.3% recorded in Q1 2025. ADP estimates private employment posts a broad-based gain ADP estimates private employment rose 122K in May, a broad-based gain, and up a bit relative to the 105K pace they estimated for April. Goods-producing employment expanded 8K in May, with construction up 8K and manufacturing up 3K. Service- producing employment rose 114K. Education and health services employment remained solid, up 57K. Trade, transportation and utilities employment rose 36K, professional and business services employment rose 11K, and leisure and hospitality employment rose 8K. The only services sector to shed jobs was information (down -9K).
